The craftsmanship of ancient pottery tells a story of cultural heritage and innovation
One of the largest and most significant parts of our collections at Waddesdon is the display of English 18th and early 19th century pottery. With over 1,500 pieces, this national collection represents over 100 years of English pottery from the Baroque to the beginning of the Industrial Revolution.
An eclectic mix of ceramic objects from porcelain to terracotta, the collection includes rare pieces by the likes of the Wedgwood and Bow families as well as delicate teacups and saucers and over a thousand pieces made at the famous Wedgwood factory in Stoke-on-Trent.
Ralph Wood’s charming Staffordshire figure groups, the Bow ‘Willow’ pattern teapot and the ‘Diana and Actaeon’ biscuit porcelain figurine by the Wedgwood factory in Barlaston are among the finest in the collection.
The highlight, however, is the Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware service: a neo-classical service of tableware given to Queen Charlotte by Sir William Hamilton, as a gift for George III, on the occasion of their Silver Wedding Anniversary in 1788.
Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware service
In the mid-1780s a neo-classical fashion for ‘Woodfern’ ware started in London, fashioned to look like wooden ware. Made from un-glazed and partially glazed biscuit porcelain, with painted designs on the surface, Woodfern ware mimicked the texture and grain of oak, fir and elm, rendering objects, such as dishes, teapots and mugs, with the appearance of turned wooden objects.
The Woodfern ware service given to Queen Charlotte is arguably the most significant set in the world, and the most important surviving collection of this type of porcelain, forming a complete tea service.
Wedgwood’s ‘Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware Tea Service’, 1788, painted with dun and gold floral decoration and stylised neo-classical portraits, c. 1788
Woodfern ware was created by Thomas Lamb who owned a large factory at New Hall, Cranbrook in Kent and produced from 1785 to 1800. Lamb’s factory, which once numbered 150 workers, also made ceramic figures, salt-glazed stoneware and pressed bricks.
In 1785 Lamb is recorded as producing one of the first pottery pieces made to imitate the grain and texture of wood, a hollow beechwood mug for Robert Taylor, Esq. and signed ‘T. Lamb – New Hall’.
Lamb was succeeded by his son in 1800 and business continued in a small way at the New Hall site until 1848 when the factory was shut down.
Wedgwood’s ‘Woodfern Ware Dish’, 1787, painted with brown floral decoration, c. 1787
Due to the rarity of this kind of ceramic, finding out who was responsible for the beautiful designs painted on the Woodfern ware is often difficult. Some pieces may have been decorated at the Cranbrook factory, though most designs are probably contemporary with the factory and produced by decorators working in London.
Dun and brown is a popular colour combination for Woodfern ware, with both colours painted in free flowing brush strokes that imitate the appearance of wood. One of the charming aspects of Woodfern ware is that the decorations often look like engravings, emphasising the neo-classical style and subject matter.
Both the dish and the sugar bowl feature a representation of classical figures. The dish, with a leaf-pattern on the base, is painted with a scene showing Diana surprising Actaeon. The panel painting is delicately finished with a paint rim showing flowers. The Woodfern ware sugar bowl, with a leaf-pattern on the base, is painted with a scene showing a lion attacking a seated deer.
The scene of the attacked deer is shown in the middle of the bowl, surrounded by two identical scenes of a goat attacking an ass. The Woodfern ware sugar bowl is finished with a laurel leaf-border painted in white, emphasising the neo-classical design.
Woodfern ware
Woodfern ware is a term which was coined later in the 20th century. Originally, the ware was termed ‘wooden ware’ as it imitated the texture of wood. By the late 18th and 19th centuries the ware was referred to as ‘wood’ ware and the term woodfern ware evolved in the 20th century.
The pottery can also be known as ‘Wood Ware’ or ‘Wood-Grain Ware’, as many objects take inspiration from the texture of wood. These pieces can also be made using other materials such as clay or terracotta.
The earliest example of a piece of Woodfern ware is a mug in the possession of the Victoria and Albert Museum, dating back to 1785.
The collection of porcelain at Waddesdon is housed in the magnificent kitchen complex of the Manor, together with a unique collection of English tableware dating back to 1725. The display features some of the finest pieces of Baroque to early Victorian porcelain, including delicate tea cups and saucers, bowls, tureens and other serving vessels. There is also a unique group of English 18th century plate.
Visitors can take a close look at the remarkable objects, including a large dinner service of Wedgwood, painted with deer in a landscape by the famous painter, Thomas Gainsborough, known as the ‘Gainsborough’ service.
An English porcelain teacup with a dog in a landscape, c. 1810
Our porcelain collection
Our collection includes other fine pieces, such as the ‘Luncheon Service’ for Queen Victoria, also by Wedgwood, depicting the major events in the young Queen’s life.
The service, which is a combination of four different styles of porcelain and decoration, was given to Queen Victoria and Prince Albert as a wedding present from the poet and author Letitia Elizabeth Landon, on 10 February 1840, just one month before the marriage.

In a parallel universe where music is the only language, a tone-deaf ambassador must use the force of his personality to save his ship from disaster.

The silent film star's lost interview surfaced, revealing insights into his lasting popularity.
Gary Cooper kisses Doris Day in the 1953 film 'The Man Who Knew Too Much.'
Beverly Hills Film Festival/Wikimedia Commons
It turns out that you should never assume silence means consent. That's the takeaway from a newfound interview with Hollywood movie star Gary Cooper, who gave his thoughts on his wife and his career to gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in 1959, but never approved the interview for publication.
Hopper spoke to Cooper, who was a superstar in the 1940s, at his Los Angeles-area home in Beverly Hills. The columnist began with a few questions about his wife, Rocky actress Veronica Lake. The pair divorced in 1951, and Hopper asked Cooper if Lake would "be the same if she'd married Rock Hudson." Cooper said, "No, she would have probably married him, and she's the kind who would never divorce."
An actress by trade herself, Hopper asked Cooper if he ever felt the pull of Hollywood. "God, no, not at all. Not once. I've always just enjoyed acting," he said. "I'm not very good at sitting around."
And what did he think of the acting chops of fellow Hollywood legend Marilyn Monroe? Cooper called her "a fine actress," but not up to the caliber of performers like Humphrey Bogart, Jack Lemmon, Henry Fonda, and Lauren Bacall.
Gary Cooper, center, with his son, John, right, and Rocky Lake, 1952
Gene Lester/Wikimedia Commons
Perhaps Cooper's most revealing insights, though, were about the characteristics that made him a star. He said that while he didn't understand what "made me a success at all," he did know that "the biggest key to my success was the fact that I came from Montana and I was never smitten by Hollywood," he said. "If I ever went to bed and said, 'Gee, I wish I could be an actor,' I never told anybody."
It was that "almost stolid determination to get somewhere," he said, that made him appealing.
Cooper died in 1961, two years after his interview with Hopper. It wasn't until after his death that Hopper published her notes in her 1968 book The Good Times, which was compiled from her gossip column.
That book, as well as a recording of Cooper's interview, were discovered in the closet of Hopper's former home, which is now owned by director Francis Ford Coppola. The L.A. Times reports that the documents were discovered by archivists, who have not yet determined when the interview will be published or released to the public.
It's not the first time a star has been heard from past the grave. In January 2019, for example, newscasts aired a live broadcast of the late Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon. The 1969 audio was restored by The Apollo 11 Mission Control Center Restoration Project, which released a remastered version of the mission, with unused footage restored and slowed down audio.

The serene landscape of the countryside was dotted with more than 500 bright green, mushroom-shaped dwellings. They were actually modified quonsets originally constructed for the United States military, and now housing the artists of the Stony Lake Music Festival. Built to support the festival’s needs and provide ample shelter for performers and patrons in the sometimes harsh Canadian weather, they stood in relative silence, waiting for that weekend to come.
From a distance, the structures looked like the mushrooms from Alice in Wonderland, or, as several people remarked, like a village of Jabba the Hut's death squads. Whatever metaphor one decided to use, the fact remained that, each year, the musicians of the festival would populate these structures, turn them into intimate, acoustically perfect performance spaces, and play music for the nearby villagers of the small, but historic, town of Haliburton, Ontario.
The concept of such a festival is simple: The selected musicians were to provide all of the instruments (sans percussion), thereby leaving the village’s percussionist without a kit. Given the circumstances, Cully proposed the following solution: He would rent a travel-friendly kit and bring it to Haliburton, utilizing his drum parts for the musical performances, and the drum kit for the local jam sessions. Cully has become a fixture of the festival, a village elder of sorts who does so much more than just play drums.
Even though Cully set up the basic rhythmic foundation for each and every performance, he was also expected to play an essential role in many of the other activities that went on throughout the weekend. A naturally inquisitive, easy-going, and friendly person, he has, over the years, befriended a number of the other musicians and has become involved in numerous facets of the festival, to the point where he is considered a fixture, and his presence is anticipated. For him, the benefits go beyond the obvious role of facilitating the festival’s rhythmic foundation. His empathy has enabled him to get to know each of the participants in a more meaningful way. As he explains, “I've met musicians who don't do this kind of thing—who might not have the opportunity to play the guitar while a singer plays, for instance. I feel lucky to have these encounters, and to be able to facilitate musical experiences for them.”
Unlike a typical club engagement, where the drummer's performance is largely expected to support the lead singer, at the festival, there is no lead singer. The structures are acoustically and visually intimate, and the festival's goal is to foster an environment in which the musicians can develop a stronger musical bond.
One can’t overstate the power of the festival's sense of community. Artists who are already working together in the band environment will further develop their rapport over the weekend, creating something much more personal than a normal gig. Other artists—who might not get to play together on a regular basis—will learn new music and styles as they create a sound together. There’s a kind of serendipity to it all, and the musicians seem to really embrace the opportunity to get together, outside of the performance context, to just talk, hang out, and play music.
“There's a big difference between being a pro musician and being a musician who can play professionally, which I consider to be a higher calling,” Cully explains. “The festival, which provides a pretty equal setting for everyone, is a tremendous opportunity for artists to explore and expand. One of the things I try to do is support them in whatever direction they go—to facilitate their improvisation and let them explore as much as possible.”
Another added benefit of the festival is its focus on different musical genres. At a typical gig, the drummer is expected to play rock-solid, straight-ahead time. “It’s not a show unless I'm playing loud,” says Cully, laughing, adding, “I’ve been known to fill every little opening.” As a result of this variety of musical styles, Cully has been able to play music that he might not otherwise get the opportunity to play in a more traditional gig setting. “At this point, I’ve played with all kinds of musicians, from rock, folk, and jazz, to bluegrass, Celtic, and classical. I’ve been fortunate enough to be in all of those different settings,” he says. “But I love the ability to step out of that framework and explore other styles of music. It helps me become a more well-rounded player.”
After setting up his kit each day at the festival, Cully began learning the pieces that would be played that evening. Since each artist and band was allocated the same amount of time—a duration that was often, in the early years, an hour or so—the musicians would need to select only a handful of songs to play. These sets were expected to be a little bit more cohesive than the traditional, improvisational “jam.” While much of the music was unrehearsed, it was still not like a typical jam session, where each artist played whatever they felt like playing. In some ways, the musicians at the festival were expected to try and create a more cohesive musical narrative with one another.
Cully’s role in setting the rhythmic tone for the evening’s performances was significant. Having worked with so many different musicians in the past, he was often able to take musical cues from the other performers, and shape the music to fit the specific style that would be expected. As one of the more experienced musicians at the festival, he was often called upon to orchestrate the rhythmic structures of some of the pieces, although he was quick to point out that his role was to set the mood—not to dictate. “I don't think of myself as a sideman,” Cully says. “I’m a part of the rhythmic fabric of the music, and I try to be supportive of it—to get inside what the others are doing, and to figure out how I can best serve that music.”
As an artist, one of Cully’s greatest strengths is his versatility. As he explains, “Drumming, for me, is the ability to adapt. There’s no real reason to play the same thing over and over again.” So, in order to keep himself in the game, he is constantly working to perfect his improvisational skills. “For me,” he says, “it’s the little details, the subtleties, that really matter, and the only way to become a better drummer is to expand my playing vocabulary and understand how to change my parts to suit the piece.”
To help facilitate this development, Cully recently began working with drum teacher Derico Watson. For the past year, they have worked together, and Cully says that Watson’s influence has really helped him to focus on the fundamentals and to become a better reader. “I want to be able to sight-read music and to play different styles of music,” he says, “because, to me, music is really a language. The only way to get better is to understand how to speak the language.”
The morning of the last day of the festival began with its traditional breakfast barbecue, and Cully took the opportunity to do some sightseeing in the nearby town. It was at this point that Cully realized he’d forgotten his drumsticks at the village. The two-hour round trip was not really an option, so he did the next best thing: He improvised.
Grabbing a set of bushes from the side of the road, Cully ran back to the festival grounds, and set about finding some participants to perform. And, lo and behold, he found two very willing musicians, a drummer and a violinist, who agreed to participate in a spontaneous performance. There was, however, one major flaw in this plan: The only pair of drumsticks available belonged to the violinist. It was a perfect irony that the drummer at the festival could not play drums! The situation could not have been any better for Cully, though, who was able to spend the next hour demonstrating his new skills. “Improvisation,” he says, “is the key to being a good musician, and improvisation is all about being in the moment.”
Cully’s interaction with the festival has been incredibly fruitful, as he’s been able to foster some of the most meaningful musical relationships in his life. In addition to expanding his musical vocabulary, he’s also learned a lot about himself as a person. “The festival has been very beneficial for me as an artist,” he says, “and it’s been especially beneficial for my musical development. But I’ve also become a better person for it, because it’s brought me together with so many wonderful people.”

In the depths of the ancient forest, there is a girl named Sara who is on a long journey in search of the legendary witch of the woods. Little does she know she's being watched by the residents of the forest.
The residents of the forest don't feel safe around the girl. They have been persecuted by witch hunters in the past. The tension is high. The woodlands are empty. The girl has stopped at the witch's tree.
She's been there for a while. She's waiting for the witch to arrive. The forest is eerily quiet.
Then a tall old hag climbs out of the trunk of the tree, her black roots wrapped around her body like serpents. The witch smiles at Sara.
“Welcome child, to my home. I am the witch of the woods. Would you like to come inside and talk with me?” the witch says.
Sara follows the witch through the tree trunk and into her home. They sit by a fire and drink apple juice. They talk all night. Sara asks the witch all sorts of questions. When the sun rises, Sara knows the witch is a kind soul who wishes to help her.
“Thank you witch. I have decided to take you up on your offer. I would like to stay with you and learn your craft. But first I need to go home and get my things,” Sara says.
Sara finds a way out of the tree. She meets the witch by the waterfall. Sara puts on a dress and tries to walk in the witch's shoes. The witch takes her hand and leads her down a forest path.
The trail opens into a wide meadow. Sara sees a lake of glass with a reflection of a large tree in it. The witch takes Sara's hand and they walk down the path to the water.
Sara is about to step into the lake when she hears a sound from above. She looks up and sees a child standing at the tree's edge. Sara takes the child by the hand and helps her down from the tree.
“My child, I have found you. You have been lost for a long time. But I will not leave you here alone. I will take you with me,” the witch says.
“Why?” the child asks.
“Because I love you and want you to stay with me,” the witch says.
“I love you too witch,” the child says.
The witch and child embrace and Sara watches from the lake. She knows it is the right thing to do. She hopes the child will be safe with the witch.
The child and witch disappear into the forest. Sara returns to the witch's home. She sits by the fire and thinks about the day's events.
The witch comes home and sits by the fire. She stares at the flames. Her eyes reflect the light from the fire. She's deep in thought. Sara watches her silently.
“Why did you come to my home, child?” the witch asks.

She would enter the secret door if he would reveal the hidden key.
She would do that to save her people.
And then she would die!

"Isleen! She must die, too. My people must never suffer under the tyranny of the Barons of Douglas. I am their guardian. And I will lead them in battle! Together we will die!"

There was no longer any need for a ghost. The treasure had returned to life!

Reviewed by JimmyH 8 / 10
Being creepy and terrifying isn't the only thing that makes a great horror movie, or horror series for that matter. "Midnight Mass" sets the creep factor on a low burn, but makes up for it in good writing, engaging characters, and a story that makes you think about the meaning of faith, belief, and even what you will do to survive.
The series follows an out of work priest, Father Paul (Zach Gilford) who has returned home to an island on the west coast of Massachusetts. Paul has been stripped of his standing in the Catholic Church and is haunted by past tragedies and mistakes. Paul returns home to find his childhood friend Erin (Kristin Lehman) has taken up the responsibility of the local church, and while their mutual faith remains, Paul has become a doubtful and bitter man who distances himself from the town.
The town itself is mired in the death of local teenager James who was killed in a car accident that his drunk father survived. It is revealed that the town drunk (Ramon Tikaram) is a member of a cult who killed the boy in a sacrifice to a pagan god, and he is dragged out of the church in a grisly fashion by an angry mob. Father Paul is offered a job as a new pastor at the local church, and as the town's unrest begins to grow, a childhood acquaintance of Father Paul (Hamish Linklater) moves back home to the island as well.
"Midnight Mass" starts slow but builds a convincing case for a good story to follow. The acting is all on point, and I was especially impressed with Gilford and Linklater. The latter's performance feels particularly calculated but still genuine, making the character's background and arc all the more compelling. The island itself is almost a character of its own, given the brief glimpses of horrifying, parasitic creatures that we are shown in the first episode. These things are living monstrosities that are truly unlike anything that I have seen before, and the crew definitely did a good job bringing them to life on the screen. The island's own mystery also adds an air of intrigue to the overall story.
That being said, it is a bit of a trope to create a fictional town or location that is isolated from the outside world, where the evil happens to be trapped on the island and unable to escape, keeping the evil isolated. That being said, this trope allows for a low burn creepy atmosphere to build up as the story develops and leads us into what is sure to be an eventful and unsettling third act.
"Midnight Mass" is a strong story that builds a perfect atmosphere for a good horror series. I give "Midnight Mass" a 4 out of 5.

Review: The Sheriff of Yrnameer, by Michael Rubens
Hobart James, a young lawyer of limited talent and dubious morality, is offered a job as the Sheriff of Yrnameer, a remote, harsh region of the Canadian north.
The book is described as "surreal" or "absurdist", which is accurate, though it's not as outlandish or over-the-top as you might expect from those terms. Instead, it is a deadpan, dryly humorous story about a man who is fundamentally good, but with no interest in or desire for anything to do with the law.
This is one of those books that I liked on the whole, but would not recommend to just anybody. Hobart, the lead character, is a well-developed character, but he is deeply flawed and deeply boring. So the book will appeal to readers who don't mind a boring protagonist, who like their protagonists at least a little unlikeable, and who are in the mood for something a little absurdist.

The detective pondered over the clues, which led to him drawing a conclusion, that the butler did it. (However, this could be a lie, which I cannot disclose the clues to prove.)
From the above paragraph, we can see that the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' is used to elaborate on the clause 'the detective pondered over the clues'.
So my question is, since the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' elaborates on the clause 'the detective pondered over the clues', is it not necessary for the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' to also elaborate on 'that the butler did it'?
Do we not have to say 'which led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it'?

TheButler, Jan 29, 2008
Hello TheButler.
Yes, the clause "which led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it" is ambiguous. The phrase "led him to draw" can mean either "led him to think", or "led him to the actual drawing of a conclusion".
However, the use of the clause is completely normal and acceptable in this sentence, and it would be very odd to add "that the butler did it" after the words "led him to draw the conclusion", because in that position it is superfluous. It would be totally different if the person were to write "led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it" - which would be completely unacceptable in my opinion.
Yes, that's right. There are various things which can be done to a verb such as "pondered". You can add something which shows that you pondered on something (such as "over the clues"), or you can add "over" to "pondered" to show that you did not think about something.
Furthermore, does the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' have to elaborate on 'that the butler did it' and 'the detective pondered over the clues', since the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' has to elaborate on at least 'the detective pondered over the clues'? I was wondering if 'which led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it' is ambiguous and that the reader does not know whether 'which led him to draw the conclusion' refers to 'that the butler did it' or 'the detective pondered over the clues'.
I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean here. If you are saying that "that the butler did it" refers to a specific event, then that is completely wrong. The "that the butler did it" is nothing more than a piece of information added to explain what the detective "pondered" or "drew a conclusion" about.
Hello TheButler!
I wouldn't say that the sentence is 'ambiguous' as much as it is 'potentially ambiguous'. As part of the general linguistic phenomenon called 'word hunting', there is a possible reading of the sentence that would equate the phrase "which led him to draw the conclusion" with 'that the butler did it'. In fact, there are a number of ways to achieve this meaning - either by word order, or through a few key additions/deletions to the sentence.
Thus, my preferred version (though not everyone agrees) would be to write: "He was led by the clues to conclude that the butler did it." This retains the sentence's intended meaning, but also removes any doubt as to what precisely the phrase "which led him to draw the conclusion" refers to.
The other way to achieve this meaning would be to combine the two clauses into one:
"He was led to the conclusion that the butler did it by pondering over the clues."
Although grammatically correct, I don't think it is necessary, as I do not think that the reader would be confused at all by the previous version.

TheButler said: ↑
The fact that it could mean either does not indicate that it is either. It is grammatically a clause.
If the word "led" was the subject, it would clearly be a verb. If the word "to" was the subject, it would clearly be a verb.
The combination "led him to draw" can mean either "led him to think" or "led him to the actual drawing of a conclusion". The most probable meaning in the sentence is the former. This can also be demonstrated by the fact that the context of the passage relates to the gathering of information, and the formation of an opinion, by the detective.
Thanks for your reply. If I follow you, you are saying that in this sentence, "led him to draw the conclusion" is a verb phrase?
When 'led me to' is used as a noun phrase, what is it the part of speech that it is a noun phrase of? If 'led me to' is a noun phrase in the sentence 'I want to know what is this book about', what is the name of the noun phrase 'led me to'?
The noun phrase is simply the object of the preposition, in this case "about" (as in the following):
"I want to know what this book is about".
The phrase "what this book is about" is a noun phrase that refers to the content of the book.
Can you tell me what it is the noun phrase 'led me to' is referring to?
It is referring to the "content of the book". In other words, the "knowledge" that the book has, the "thing" it "is".
As far as the object, "what this book is about", is concerned, "about" is the preposition, and "knowledge" and "this book" are its objects.
You are right that I was not too clear. What I was asking is that if 'led me to' is a noun phrase in the sentence 'I want to know what is this book about', what is the name of the noun phrase 'led me to'? In other words, what is 'led me to' referring to?
There is no name. There is simply the phrase "what is this book about". The verb "to be" and its object "this book" are linked together by the preposition "about", which is equivalent to "concerning", "regarding" or "on".

The novelist typed the final words of the manuscript on December 10, 1970, and marked it "FINIS." It was, for once, absolutely right: _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three_ was the end of it. The New York subway—the subject of all but three of the forty-six crime novels he had produced since the first one, _Death Wish,_ in 1972—was no longer viable as a setting. The books were still selling, but there was a growing sense of diminishing returns. Critics were less and less impressed with what were deemed perfunctory stories; characterization was increasingly sacrificed for plot. And the rabid fans who had packed his public readings as recently as 1972 were less and less interested in attending. He was, in short, out of ideas.
For all the attention paid to the 1974 film _Death Wish,_ it was the seventeenth novel Brown had written and the first that hit pay dirt—and perhaps even more remarkably, it was a sleeper. It was nominated for an Edgar, the award of the Mystery Writers of America; there were calls for it to be made into a movie, but it did not attract much critical attention until three years later, when a screenplay appeared. _Death Wish_ would prove to be the most popular and controversial book he ever wrote. While much attention has been paid to the film—which transformed the book into an explicit satire of gun-loving America—less notice has been given to the novel. It is an exciting, pacy book, written in an archly pared-down prose. Even though its roots go back to the 1930s and the novels of James M. Cain, _Death Wish_ also evinces Brown's familiarity with the works of the French crime novelist Frédéric Dard, particularly the Fred la Mayo series of paperbacks, _The Brain Goes Back to School_ (1966), _The Five Brains in the Pool_ (1966), and _The Brain Hangs Out_ (1966), published in America by the Graphic Press. The trilogy concerns a criminal mastermind who wakes from a coma with an IQ of 300, not all of it good. Brown was also a great fan of the comic books of Martin Goodman, later chairman of Marvel Comics, and it was perhaps this early exposure to a distillation of comic books that lay behind the stripped-down tautness of _Death Wish_ and its sequels.
In a way, the film was merely the last act of a great career in publishing. The British had had their day. The great explosion of the British New Wave, the overnight success of James Herbert, the extraordinary flourishing of the "crap"-shooters in the mid-seventies, all passed. Michael Moorcock died in the womb; his literary heirs failed to secure the deal on the distribution of their work. With Moorcock, Herbert, Brown, and John Lange, the British New Wave had seemed the way forward. In the event, none of these novels, particularly those written under the name of James Herbert, has aged well. But if the mid-seventies fad for horror novels was silly, even Brown's friends concede that _Death Wish_ is an unforgettable book. Its raw vigor echoes a more confident, less cautious period in publishing, when it was possible for books to become best sellers without the support of advertising. Even in America it was not unknown for readers to find a new author in their local library. Such was the case for _Death Wish_.
The quality of Brown's fiction began to decline in the seventies. This was perhaps unsurprising, given the violence of his break with Ballantine Books, but even the books he wrote during his tempestuous relationship with Random House founder Harry Evans showed a lack of focus. Having persuaded Random House to create a new house for his publishing, Evans Books, he attempted to replicate the Ballantine model, hiring editors from the publishing giant who had rejected him and paying them less. Of the five novels he wrote for Evans, only _The Snake,_ the first, and _Death Game,_ the third, could be considered successful. _The Snake,_ based on a six-page idea by a Texas fan, was so good that when Brown moved to Fawcett in 1975, he asked them to reprint the book as a two-dollar Fawcett Gold Medal special. To the end of his life, Brown called it the best book he ever wrote. It is indeed a wonderfully lean piece of work, one of his most claustrophobic and intense novels, a study in the psychology of paranoia and survival that ends with a stunning twist in the last line.
_The Snake_ and _Death Game_ are exceptional in Brown's fiction: as much as anything else, they belong to the pulp crime and horror novels of the fifties. But in a sense, Brown had made his peace with the British in the mid-seventies and had found a new way to make a living out of the subway. The next book he wrote, after _Death Wish,_ was _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three,_ which still sold in great numbers. It would become one of his most adapted films, but _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three_ is almost surrealist in its suspension of reality. The criminal, Bernard "Bug" Kaplan, is appalled by the public's casual misinterpretation of the title, which he thinks should be "The Taking of Pelham 2-3-4," the name of the actual train. He is an aficionado of the language, and of theater, and has much in common with Aramis, the criminal mastermind in the French graphic novel, in his conviction that crime and art are intertwined. Brown's choice of name— _Pelham One Two Three—_ evoked the location of the station on the Lexington Avenue line.
With _Murder on the Eighth Floor_ and _Cop Out,_ Brown began to revive the series he had started with _The Snake,_ about the two professional thieves Darryl and Terry. Both _Murder on the Eighth Floor_ and _Cop Out_ are thoroughly dismal works, and the film of _Cop Out_ (1978) was no better, though Robert Aldrich's direction gives the script some bounce. Yet Brown had found the new form he was looking for. There was still good, readable stuff in him, but at a time when people were beginning to take crime fiction seriously, it was no longer good enough.
One of the main themes of _Death Wish_ is one that Brown returned to obsessively in later novels: the thin line between crime and justice. In the book, Paul Kersey does not pretend that he is right, he does not even believe in a higher law, or his own actions. He knows that he is doing something wrong, yet he cannot stop himself, and each killing makes the next one more likely. At the end of the book, Kersey is held in a state of purgatory: he is neither completely guilty of murder, nor able to exonerate himself. Brown's admiration for Joseph Conrad is plain, in particular for the novel _Under Western Eyes._ Brown found _Under Western Eyes_ a highly constricting book, yet Kersey's moral torment echoes that of Razumov in the Conrad book. Both Razumov and Kersey are intelligent, reflective men who suffer under the pressure of conscience, each tortured by the dilemma of their actions. Like Razumov, Kersey tries to set right the wrong he has done, even to the point of destroying his family.
Kersey was an outsider, more comfortable with his instincts and imagination than with people, which makes his sudden and dramatic reaction to the brutal attack on his wife and daughter a stark contrast to his manner before the event. When the vicious attack occurs, he is tipped over the edge into a self-righteous terror. And in his search for justice, he becomes as much a part of the monster as the criminals who rob, rape, and murder.
Kersey's quest for justice is intensified by a further frustration. He is one of the few characters in Brown's fiction who is a complete failure at one of the things he does best: he is a miserable architect. In one sense, he is a contradiction in terms: a crime novelist who disliked violence. He was horrified by what he saw in _Death Wish,_ that it turned out to be the kind of novel that readers loved to see come true. Deep in the ocean's abyss, where light and air and sunshine do not penetrate, is a most strange and curious plant, which grows and lives by drawing from its environments that which is of use to it. It has no roots, but instead, cables, long threadlike tendrils, which go out and search until they touch the sandy bottom. There are thousands of these tendrils, reaching and feeling around in the darkness, one on top of the other, some touching, some passing, but all feeling, searching, and straining for something to fasten to.
Then, when one of these cables feels what it needs, if only for a moment, something to hold to and draw strength from, it will clasp on and never let go. The rest will go out and search again. If another comes in contact with the same thing, it will grasp it also, and again the process goes on until every one of the cables has a firm hold on something. Then the cables get thicker and thicker and blossom like a beautiful rose, and they surround their object as a castle would its drawbridge.
When a breeze comes up or a wave strikes, the tendrils clasp tighter, and some more tendrils will grasp on to the clasping ones, if they happen to come in contact with them. And so on, until, if a big breeze or wave should come, the whole mass will be held as fast as a mountain might hold, or a huge castle.
There are in the ocean a thousand wonders, and strange things we cannot understand, and none is more strange than this plant which grows and lives on the bottom of the ocean, without light, and yet knows how to live. You cannot live without air and sunshine, but this strange thing does. And, if it lives in the darkness, it is also beautiful. When the sun is out it sends a beautiful color into the sea, and in the night, when the moon comes up, it sends a beautiful reflection in her light. But these are only its happy times; for many days and nights go by, and it clutches on for strength, while the sun and the moon do not even know it exists.
Now I have told you a story, and this strange plant is no more than a story, but it has a purpose.
There are many people in this world, who do not need to live in the light, who live their whole lives on the bottom of the ocean, grasping something for strength, but never bringing anything into the light that is worth while.
Some have good voices, and have the talent to sing, but never sing the right kind of songs.
Some have skill in painting, but have no conception of right and wrong, and paint things that would not do to look at, and which never help anyone to be good.
Some have ability in writing, and write books and poems, but are all wrong.
There are many, many who have talents of some kind or other, and bring them all to the wrong places. They think only of themselves, and forget to consider others.
All this is wrong. A talent is a gift of God. It is one of the things which we are given by the Great Father, that we may do something with it. It is not ours to do as we please with, but it is to be used and not abused. A talent is like a sturdy oak tree. If we plant it in the right place it will grow and become great and noble, a shelter and a guide for those who pass it by. But if we plant it in the wrong place, in a dry, arid, barren spot, it may grow there, but it will never be a grand old oak, with mighty branches and strong, wide-spreading roots. So it is with a talent. If we plant it in a dark, unproductive spot, and use it for selfishness, it may grow there, but it will never be a grand and useful talent. It will always remain weak and selfish, and all its growth will be used in selfish ends.
If we have talents we ought to use them. We cannot change them; we cannot throw them away, so why not put them in the right places and see how they will grow? We do not know what they may be, but we do know that, if we plant them in the right places, they will be strong, and we shall have the satisfaction of knowing that we have done our best with our talents.
The next time a sunbeam or moonbeam comes, and we are tempted to think we are so bright, let us think of that strange plant which is bright in the darkness of the sea. It shows that we can be bright without the sun or moon, and it helps us to know how we can be right in our lives, even in the absence of the sun and the moon. And if we are right in the absence of the sun and the moon, we may safely be right when they shine brightly upon us, and we will know that, no matter where we are, whether on the bottom of the ocean, or on the top of the earth, we have done our best with our talents, and that we are living up to our duties as children of the Great Spirit.

The scientist's groundbreaking discovery challenged the established scientific theory and gained him the title of "father of the transistor" - a semiconductor device that changed the way the world produces, stores and transmits information.
The prize was awarded to the 95-year-old scientist during a ceremony at the Nobel Center in Stockholm. His wife and son were present at the ceremony, and they were congratulated by President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Professor Göran K. Hansson.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 was awarded to John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science”.
In a paper presented in the journal Nature, Professor Göran Hansson and the Nobel Committee said: "The three laureates have found different ways of following and exploiting the quantum state, even when the object being measured has been separated from the measurement apparatus. This breakthrough made it possible to explore a new kind of quantum mechanics in which reality does not exist until it is measured. This has helped to develop quantum computers and quantum encryption."
This year's winners, John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger, "have, along with colleagues, conducted fundamental studies of the so-called quantum entanglement, wherein two or more quantum objects can be linked in such a way that one quantum object can affect another quantum object even if they are separated by large distances".
The prize citation mentioned that "if you do the same experiment twice in a row, you will get the same result each time. This is a classical way of thinking about nature, based on cause and effect and basic predictability".
This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, followed by the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 3.
The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on October 7, and the winners of the prizes in literature, economics and serenity will be announced on October 10.
The committee mentioned that the studies conducted by John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger were important steps in the development of quantum computing, as well as the development of quantum encryption.
“Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory in modern physics. In the middle of the last century, it was realized that quantum-mechanical phenomena could be used for information technology. In recent decades, quantum information science has paved the way for a new generation of quantum computers, the development of secure quantum encryption and a revolution in metrology. The three laureates have laid the foundation for this development”, the committee said.
“John F. Clauser and Alain Aspect have, along with colleagues, conducted fundamental studies of the so-called quantum entanglement, wherein two or more quantum objects can be linked in such a way that one quantum object can affect another quantum object even if they are separated by large distances. In the 1960s and 1970s, John Clauser and Stuart Freedman constructed an experiment to study whether two photons, which always behave like particles, could be entangled so that one photon could be used to transmit information about the other photon.
Alain Aspect performed the essential experiments at the beginning of the 1980s. However, it was not until 1982 that the rules of quantum mechanics were formulated with such clarity that their predictions could be tested experimentally. The quantum theory is thus regarded as the most powerful tool that humanity has for understanding many phenomena in modern physics.
“Anton Zeilinger and colleagues have, in the early 1990s, performed a series of experiments on entangled photons that were decisive for quantum information research. The experiments demonstrated that information can be encoded not only in the states of individual particles, but also in the relationships that particles have to each other.
This was followed by experiments that led to new insights about the nature of entangled states, to the so-called Bell-tests. Alain Aspect and colleagues and Robert A. Cowan and colleagues carried out important Bell-tests in the late 1980s.
In the 1990s and 2000s, Anton Zeilinger and colleagues developed Bell-tests to a high level of precision, but it was not until 2015 that the so-called loophole-free Bell-test was first performed, using entangled photons, by Delft University of Technology, the Netherlands. With the work of the laureates, the field of quantum information has made enormous strides. Today, practical quantum computers are nearing the horizon, and countless additional applications are being developed.
Quantum information is also used for revolutionary methods in the measurement of molecules and radiation", the committee mentioned.

Exploring the depths of the ocean reveals an extraordinary wealth of marine life and incredible landscapes, and those willing to take a deep dive can find fascinating locations worldwide.
This is the journey of the Galapagos Aggressor, a liveaboard vessel exploring the waters around the islands of Galapagos, in Ecuador. Scuba divers are welcomed onboard the ship which offers a range of fantastic dive sites, including spots for advanced divers.
Divers can explore a wide range of dive sites around the islands. The Galapagos Aggressor takes dives of two tank dives to the maximum depth of 130 ft (40 m). The ship makes six dives per day, and some spots only allow for one tank dives due to their depth.
The ship is a large liveaboard and is decked out with everything you could need for an unforgettable diving experience. The cabins include ensuite bathrooms and are split over three decks. All rooms have air-conditioning, TV and DVD. The dining room offers a wide range of cuisine, catering for those with special dietary requirements.
The main deck contains a salon, library and dining room with large windows. The onboard video system means you can see the incredible marine life even when you’re not on a dive. There’s also a spacious sun deck complete with sun loungers, and an onboard gym. The ship is a tech friendly vessel, and divers are provided with a PCR laptop and cameras for underwater photography.
Galapagos is one of the best diving destinations in the world and features a large range of marine life. The area has not been exposed to pollution or damage, and its waters are home to a wide range of fish and sea life. Galapagos has wrecks and reefs, and even seamounts.
Divers can enjoy colourful corals and an abundance of marine life. Frogfish, sea horses, dolphins and schools of hammerhead sharks are all common. Diving Galapagos can be a thrilling experience, and is a wonderful way to get to know one of the most unique and beautiful areas on the planet.
The Galapagos Aggressor is the perfect place to explore the deep, and dive a host of spots in the area. The diving offers a wide range of experiences from reefs, swim-throughs and pinnacles, to seamounts, shipwrecks and caves. It’s a fascinating adventure, and an exciting opportunity to dive some of the best spots in the world.
The most famous dive site in Galapagos is Kicker Rock. It’s a rock in the shape of a shoe, rising out of the water and reaching up to 130 ft (40 m) above sea level. There is a huge colony of marine birds nesting here. The site is the best place to see large schools of hammerhead sharks, as well as sea lions, dolphins, turtles, barracuda and snappers.
The Aggressor dive sites are spread out across the Galapagos region. Dive sites around San Cristobal Island include Cerro Brujo, Kicker Rock and Punta Pitt. For the more advanced divers, the Lion’s Hill dive offers an exploration of depths up to 130 ft (40 m). Santa Cruz Island boasts one of the best dive spots around, Cousins Rock. The Galapagos Aggressor also takes divers to Punta Carrión and Sea Lion Rock, both home to large schools of hammerhead sharks. Bartolomé is another famous spot, and takes divers to its reefs and rocky pinnacles.
Further out, there is Darwin Island, one of the most famous sites in Galapagos, known for its schools of hammerheads. The Western Isles region, which is home to Fernandina Island and Pinta Island, boasts some great sites such as Cousins Rock and Lava Flow.
Diving Galapagos is an adventure that offers spectacular sights and experiences. Divers should be aware that there are strong currents in the area, so the experience isn’t for everyone. The Galapagos Aggressor provides an excellent opportunity to explore the area and access some of the best spots. The Galapagos Aggressor offers a once in a lifetime adventure.

In his right hand he clutched a gargantuan mace, its massive head studded with runes of fire.
A half-dozen bowmen surrounded the pair of humans and dwarf, their bows drawn and at the ready. These men were mercenaries, drawn from the ranks of the King's army by Baryth, who was known throughout these lands as the finest blacksmith in Icara.
Thramark crested a low ridge and surveyed the jagged peaks that surrounded the party. "We cannot return," he whispered.
"No," said Baryth, "we must press on."
Thramark nodded and crested the hill, signaling for the party to follow.
Following the dwarf and his vanguard of mercenaries, the barbarian pressed forward along a trail of broken stone. The path was ancient and much of it had been washed away. The arrows of the mercenaries sank deep into the ground ahead of them. The ground was rough and shifting beneath their feet. The stones were perilous and broken—the result of thousands of years of winters and floods.
Thramark followed the mercenaries down the jagged path. Beneath his feet the ground seemed to shift and give way, but the barbarian pressed on. Thramark knew this path—these were the edges of Squirreling Forest, and in the midst of this strange landscape a small temple had once stood.
The land here was barren, pocked with geysers and sinkholes, studded with stones and honeycombed with the tunnels of the squirrelfolk. It was a treacherous and bizarre environment. The thought of reaching the temple and finding safety there—even if only for a day—had kept Thramark on his feet and pushing ahead. He would risk anything to reach safety and safety, Thramark knew, was found in that ancient temple.
The land changed and the water turned warm. Thramark felt something stir inside him, as if he had stepped upon sacred ground. The wind stirred and the dust flew in gusts like smoke. Thramark looked around and saw that the strange forest had begun to encroach on the path. The trees shifted and stalked, moving ever closer to the trail.
He heard a guttural shriek, and he turned. He saw one of the men-at-arms, a man he knew to be a strong swordsman. Thramark saw the man's knee begin to bend backward, bone screaming in protest.
Without thinking, Thramark charged forward, swinging his broadsword. As he moved, the ground seemed to shudder and a rumble filled the air. The barbarian raised his blade and brought it down upon the ground—striking hard into the rock. The blade shattered against the ground and the world shifted and seemed to darken.
When the world stopped shifting, the men-at-arms were gone. The ground was smoking and steaming, as if struck by lightning. Thramark looked around—he and his companions were alone. The whole of Squirreling Forest had surrounded them, cutting off their escape. It was as if the squirrelfolk had swarmed from every corner of the forest, suddenly appearing in the surrounding terrain.
"Get down," Baryth shouted. The party fell to the ground, the bowmen darting for cover behind rocks and boulders.
Morg grasped the mace in her hands and called out, "I stand."
Baryth cursed, "The ground is weak, it will collapse—"
"I stand!" Morg shouted, pointing the mace at the surrounding trees. "The blast is coming!"
The dwarf looked at Thramark, "Cover your ears."
The barbarian complied and as he did, Morg screamed and the sky seemed to open in a surging wave of golden light. The world shuddered and a wave of darkness passed. When the barbarian opened his eyes, he saw that Morg was gone.
"How long?" Thramark asked, his mind grappling for control.
"Five minutes," said Baryth, "after that they will be upon us."
Thramark looked around and saw that Baryth's eyes were full of tears. The dwarf was overcome by loss.
"We will not die here," Thramark said, remembering Morg, his wife, his partner.
The barbarian grasped his fallen blade and rose.
"Cover your ears," Baryth said.
"Not yet," Thramark said.
As he stood, the barbarian turned and he saw them, in the distance.
The squirrelfolk were upon them.

MORG, TREASURER OF THE FORTRESS, slung her crossbow over her shoulder and steeled her grip upon the chain-wrapped handle of her mace. The house she called home was in turmoil, the dust stirring in thick clouds. A decade's worth of treasures were packed tightly into a wagon—the booty of thirty sieges and a hundred battles—the spoils of a thousand conquests. It was the greatest treasure ever known to mankind.
Her lover, Thramark, the barbarian, stood at her side. He was sweating and his arms shook. The great beast that he had slain, the dragon's ruined tail, dragged in the dust behind him. A satchel, empty and filled with nothing more than a worn, cloth map, lay at his feet. It was one of the dragon's hoards and it was the last of their loot. All that remained was the world's most valuable treasure, the Singing Blade—the most precious sword in all of Icara.
Thramark picked up the satchel and looked into it, as if seeing his home for the last time. He could barely speak, his throat and lips were caked with dry, crusted blood.
"Thramark?" Morg said, "It's time to go."
He looked up, a dazed look upon his face. "I am ready."
Morg looked around at the treasures, now nearly gone. It seemed impossible that this treasure could have come to this, that this—all of it—had been given to her. They had managed to steal all of this loot, they had slaughtered a dragon—one of the greatest of the Age of the Dragon—but the treasure was going nowhere. It would be locked away in the Vault of Blades.
"I am sorry," Morg said. She had learned that from Thramark, a man of few words, a man whose strength was matched only by his vulnerability. She touched his hand and he turned and nodded.
"I am sorry," she repeated. "I love you."
"I love you too," he said.
Morg's mother sat in the wagon, her face streaked with tears. Morg had only managed to say goodbye to her mother once.
"Why?" she had said, "Why are you doing this?"
"Because we must," Morg had replied.
The mother had shaken her head and replied, "Because he asks it of you? Because he demands it?"
"Yes," Morg had said, "because he asks it of me."

At the world's most awkward family reunion, the entertainment is a mind-reading machine that knows what its customers want to hear.
I Was There! I Don't Care About You!
I have news. The reviews from Edinburgh are in, and the touring production of The Book of Mormon did not get good notices. From the reviews I’ve read, I can safely say that, while I disagree with all of them, they are written with a polite, respectful humor that doesn’t quite match the production’s.
The show’s a flop, of course. But not quite the hit it was at the Eugene O’Neill. Now in Los Angeles and rolling into San Francisco and DC, it’s not selling out, and the posters are already down on the Tube stations. How could it be anything else? We’re in the middle of a recession, and the show itself is antagonistic to religion, an expensive ticket (for London standards), and a very specific, high-spirited brand of humor that by definition will play to some but not all audiences. It didn’t matter that I loved it.
In fairness, the show seems to be a textbook example of critics following the consensus. Of the seventeen critics I’ve found who reviewed it, twelve gave it some form of rave, three rated it favorably, and two thought it was good, though they weren’t sure why. Only one, the most up-to-the-moment of them all, gave it a completely negative review. To their credit, they acknowledge they might be wrong, as it is such a popular show, but they are mostly defensive. The chief argument against the show, in terms of reviews, seems to be “It doesn’t have the same magic as when it first premiered.”
Of course, the thing about theater is that it doesn’t need magic, and while I was watching The Book of Mormon, I didn’t miss it at all. It’s actually rare that I ever walk out of a musical and go “You know, that was amazing,” because the miraculous feels too much like magic, and is usually done as part of a too-slick show that doesn’t have a lot else to say. When I walked out of The Book of Mormon, I went “You know, I like this show. I can’t wait to tell my friends.” Which may be one of the best compliments I can give, because it means I’ll be able to be snarky about it.
As with anything else, though, there’s a difference between what it is and what it’s trying to do. And what it is is a frenetic, relentless musical that constantly has you on the edge of your seat. The show follows two naïve Mormon missionaries who get sent to a dangerous part of Africa and their struggle to get past the local tribe’s distrust of the Mormons. The entire set-up, as one character explains, is so that they can get through the indoctrination necessary to be Mormons, and it’s packed with clever but easy to follow references to the religious con, and some very entertaining songs.
Most of the songs are sung by two members of the tribe, Nabulungi (Taylor Iman Jones) and her friend, Pumas (Cody Jamison Strand). They’re an entirely invented character, whose songs echo the values of the show as well as traditional Broadway as a whole. “Sal Tlay Ka Siti” is an entire story told with choreography and a song, very much a throwback to the golden age of showmanship. “Turn it Off” is the catchiest tune I’ve heard in years, sung by a very funny J. Anthony Crane as Mafala Hatimbi, the colonel of the Ugandan military, who wants to kill the two Mormons. But perhaps my favorite song is “Hasa Diga Eebowai,” sung by Nabulungi, wherein she asks if she can hear all the wrong things about God, and Elders Eaton and Cunningham quickly deny this, and Nabulungi then goes on to list all the things that are wrong about God.
Some of the songs are very catchy, others surprisingly clever, and the entire production is a delight. The sets are ingeniously constructed, the dancing is excellent and at times daring (if a little too close to the audience at points), the actors are amazingly good. If there is a weakness in the show, it is that at times it comes close to overstaying its welcome, at times too relentless for its own good. The momentum can slow down, and every now and then it seems to be stretching just a bit too far to maintain its own self-respect, and that comes when it seems to be putting in padding to get to its conclusion. I also don’t think they quite know what they’re trying to say, if anything.
But then, when a show’s so much fun, it hardly matters. The Book of Mormon isn’t trying to make sense or send a message. It’s not trying to say anything profound or change your life. It’s a very cleverly written musical, full of good songs and excellent acting. It’s a blast.
Which is exactly why I disagree with those critics who think it’s not as good as the first time they saw it. It’s not meant to be the kind of show that changes your life and forces you to think about the human condition, because its primary strengths are its production values, its cast, and its humor. I don’t think a show that ends with an act of genocide and the mutilation of a young girl as she’s dragged away can be written that way. That, to me, is a criticism of its ambition, which is both high and admirable, and that’s not really what the show is about.
I'm an amateur theater critic who lives in the South Bay of Silicon Valley. I've been writing about theater since I was about eleven, when I figured out the magic of hyperlinks and starting putting up amateur reviews of local theater. I'm an actor in the area (and no, I'm not as bad as you think I am), I'm a software developer, and my ultimate goal in life is to someday see The Book of Mormon.

An alien visiting Earth for the first time becomes obsessed with knitting, eventually starting a new business to help the inhabitants of the planet stitch up their wounded psyche.
The Craft and art of the Fleisher MFA Show 2019
Knitting is a handicraft, a time honored practice which has been passed down from mother to daughter for hundreds of years. In this series I have challenged this tradition and brought this feminine, domestic craft into the street, a male dominated space, where it has been seen as an anomaly. By combining the contrasting worlds of yarn craft and street art, I have brought these two practices together, connecting traditional craft, something which is learned by repeating the same movements time and time again, with street art, something which is constantly changing and evolving as it deals with the modern world. Through this juxtaposition I have created a space where the viewer must reconcile these two worlds and confront the reality of their existence, both as a craft, and as a technique for communication.

Although Christopher had a steady job, a loving wife, and two beautiful daughters, he was not happy. After 15 years of editing for news organizations Christopher made the leap to fine art photography.
Since Christopher first dabbled with a digital camera in 2009, he has been studying photography at all levels, and in 2014 received his bachelor’s in Photographic Arts at OCAD University.
In his short time in the photography world Christopher has had solo exhibitions in Canada, the US, and France. In 2016 he participated in the ‘Biennale Internationale de l’Art Contemporain’ in Bordieres, France and in 2018 he took part in the ‘Yellow House Festival’, taking home the Bourse d’Excellence in the Panelled Exhibition.
In the last year Christopher has been involved in multiple international artist residencies, working with a variety of photographic media, and has been teaching photography since 2014.

The first snowfall of the year blanketed the town in a sheet of white. The second day of snow drew out crowds for snowball fights and sledding down Hester Street Hill, leaving behind a new layer of fluffy snow.
The snow brought the beloved Christmas Festival from Dec. 1 to Dec. 2. Many local artists and crafters sold their holiday products and creations in the Municipal Complex. Everyone was invited to pick up a warm cup of hot cocoa and take a walk through the glowing, decorated park.
“The craft fair, the lights and the Christmas parade were the highlights for my children,” Matt Anderegg, Bloomfield resident said.
Dec. 2 was a chance for children to come to the Bloomfield United Methodist Church for the Christmas cookie walk. The cookie walk is a fundraiser for the church. Tickets are sold for $5, and people select their own variety of cookies.
The cookie walk is set up like a cookie buffet; cookies are grouped by variety. The cookies are homemade and grouped by weight, so you can pick up as many as you can carry. Tickets are for sale at the Bloomfield United Methodist Church, Church Boutique and Gift Shop, State Farm Insurance offices, Ben Franklin store, Mainstreet Market, Community State Bank, Bloomfield Library, Happy Home Cooking, Spalding County Chamber of Commerce and Ager’s Garden. The baked goods will be available for purchase on Saturday, Dec. 2.
“Our entire community is invited to celebrate the Christmas season with us. We will have coffee and hot chocolate, a cookie walk and baked goods,” Beth Hanlin, chairman of the church’s outreach committee said.
Food was also on sale at the Annual Christmas Parade on Dec. 2. Bloomfield FFA members sold concessions, such as hot dogs, nachos and chips. The concession stands, located at both entrances of Town Square Park, kept the children and adults warm as they waited to be dazzled by the decorated floats and the entertaining activities.
In the parade, one of the best-known floats in Bloomfield is the vintage fire truck. Local resident Lamar Hutcheson owned a truck company in Alabama. He bought an antique fire truck with the money he made from his business. Hutcheson passed away in 1989 and gifted the truck to the City of Bloomfield.
The city restored the truck and presented it as a float in the Christmas parade.
“It takes a lot of hard work to restore and maintain the truck,” Billy Williams, Bloomfield fire chief said. “We will have to replace the water hoses, add new paint, put new tires on and make the lights brighter.”
Williams said the truck will not only be in the parade.
“It is the Bloomfield Fire Department’s mission to not only put the fire truck in the Christmas parade, but to put the truck out on the streets during the Christmas Festival.”
The Bloomfield High School Band also put on a show for the crowd. The band’s performance was choreographed with dance performances, the firetruck float and a variety of beautifully decorated floats.
Following the parade, some local businesses were lit up by Christmas trees. The Christmas in Bloomfield float entry was also decorated with lights. The decorations were donated by Vick’s Lighting and Christmas in Bloomfield decorated the tree.
The Bloomfield Christmas Festival is always in the first weekend of December. Everyone is encouraged to bring their children to the Christmas Parade and Town Square Park to join in on the activities.

Each year, the Bloomfield United Methodist Church Women and Outreach Committee host the cookie walk at the church, located at 105 W. Spring St. The cookie walk will take place from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Dec. 2.

Each year, the committee purchases new cookie sheets to be used to display the different cookie varieties. The baked goods will be arranged according to the types of cookies, and the best part is that patrons can pick their own cookies from the trays.

The cookie walk is a great opportunity for people to purchase some great-tasting cookies, support the church and support their local community.
“The cookie walk is a special time for the community and the church,” Moore said. “It is important to keep the tradition going.”

Wandering through the old city, one finds oneself absorbed by the splendor of the copper-domed shrines and tombs, the maze of caravansaries and mosques, the beauty of the palaces and the bazaars. Around every corner in the ancient Persian city of Shiraz, new treasures await. It is a place like no other.
Shiraz was one of my favorite cities in Iran and it was easy to see why so many poets and artists have been inspired by this beautiful city. We spent a couple of days in Shiraz before heading to Persepolis. While most visitors may only explore a few of the most notable sites, I prefer to see what I can while I am in a city. In this post, I will go over the best places to visit in Shiraz.
Shiraz is known as the city of poetry, as many of the famous poets in Iran such as Hafez and Saadi were born in Shiraz. In fact, many houses in Shiraz were the homes of poets in ancient times, and while they are now museums, you can go inside and see the walls covered in the famous poetry of the residents.
In addition to being a poetry-loving city, Shiraz is known for its gardens and flowers. Shiraz is actually the Persian word for rose, and the city is a hub for rose-scented products.
If you are looking for great places to visit in Shiraz, check out these top things to do in Shiraz, Iran.

One of the most impressive buildings in Shiraz is the Karim Khan Citadel, which dates back to the 18th century. It is a small citadel, but it is still one of the most important landmarks in Shiraz.
The citadel was built by the Zand dynasty in the 18th century, and it has been used as a military base, a prison, and even a movie studio. The building was damaged in an earthquake in 1778, and it was restored in the 19th century.
You can visit the citadel for a small fee, and you can explore the beautiful courtyards and gardens. You can also climb up to the top of the citadel for a great view of the city.

The mausoleum is a popular place of pilgrimage for Shi’a Muslims, and it is also a popular tourist attraction.

I was given a free review copy of this book and have voluntarily provided this review. I found this book to be one of those stories that just pulled me in right from the start. Dorothy is a typical parent - very protective of her kids, and wants to keep them out of the storm. They end up driving right into it. Their drive turns into a nightmare for her. Baby spit up! What are we going to do with all this stuff?
I can't tell you how many times I said this.
Mind you we had three children in six years, so if we needed to do something, we just handed it off to the other person and took care of the baby.
We were an army of two, trying to navigate the challenges of pregnancy, birth, and raising three children under the age of six.
Now multiply the chaos times five.
The poignancy of my own struggles with having three young children, supporting one another, weathering the ups and downs, was enough. Add to that, the trauma of surviving a category five hurricane with her family in tow and you have a powerful and compelling story.
I found myself constantly readingjust a little further, seeing if Dorothy's story was going to make it or not.
The author did a beautiful job of making me care about what happened to Dorothy.
I'm a huge fan of Elizabeth Klett and she does a great job of portraying the vulnerability and strength of Dorothy in this audiobook. I'm sure if I had read this book instead of listening to it, I would not have been able to connect to the character the way I did when I heard Elizabeth Klett's narration.
You might want to keep some tissues handy for this one.

Whispered secrets of the forest are not what they seem.
“Mother,” Brynn’s mum said.
“Yes, dear?” I responded in our long-standing role play.
“I don’t want to go to England for the summer vacation,” she said.
“Why?” I asked, now playing the oblivious parent to her predicament.
“The Elders are going to meet.”
“That’s right. It’s been years since they last met. The prophecy is coming true. Your father, the Elders, and I will be away.”
I expected her response and had prepared a set answer. “The best way to show your support is to continue living your life as usual. We are strong and smart. We will always find a way to solve our problems.”
“But what if we can’t? I feel so helpless. We are going to lose everything we have.”
“It’s okay. It’s all going to work out. Do you understand me?”
I must’ve sounded like every parent in the world. I felt my inner voice struggle to get my attention. It wouldn’t go away. I ignored it. It persisted.
“Mother,” Brynn said again.
“Yes,” I answered. She was speaking too softly for me to hear. I leaned in, cupping my hand over her mouth.
“Mother, the sirens are calling again,” Brynn said.
“I hear them.”
“We should take refuge in the garden. This house is too old to be safe. The sirens might call us into the water.”
“Brynn, listen to me.” I cupped my hands around my mouth, the most effective way to get her attention when I spoke to her. “If the sirens call us, we will go to the garden.”
Brynn nodded. “That’s the plan.”
“Now, be a good girl and get ready for your picnic.”
I kissed her and left for work, knowing the sirens were calling, but I kept thinking of the fresh flowers in my garden. I kept thinking of what would happen if Brynn and I weren’t together. The sirens wanted me. It was my fate.
I knew this was our last summer together. I had felt this deep down for months. Now I was sure of it. The sun began its ascent into the sky. I was heading home from work. The sky was slowly turning pink as my car pulled into the driveway. The driveway was dark and unkempt. The forest was dead. Everything was dead. The sky was eating the sun. All I could hear were the sirens calling. I ran inside the house.

The decision to embark on a solo travel adventure leads to life-changing experiences in places around the world.
Although solo travel in itself can be extremely empowering, the experiences and people that solo travelers have brought to their lives is what really impacts them the most.
We spoke to female solo travelers across the globe to find out about their journeys and their experiences with Solo Travel Society to learn what motivated them to take this big step to travel alone.
Who is the solo traveler?
Jenna is a 28-year-old from Ontario, Canada. She first traveled solo when she was 20 years old, having signed up for an excursion through a Toronto-based company for a two-week trip to Costa Rica.
Jenna said she’d always felt a strong desire to travel and even as a child, she was fascinated by the idea of exploring other parts of the world. She found herself spending a lot of time on the internet looking at maps and cities.
“I’d leave my laptop unattended at home and find things online,” she told us, adding that the internet allowed her to be anywhere in the world without being there.
With that in mind, Jenna took the plunge and spent time planning her first solo travel adventure. Although she didn’t immediately feel confident in the decision to go alone, she felt excited and knew that she wanted to pursue solo traveling in the future.
What inspired her to go alone?
“What first started as a weekend trip to NYC (New York City), it really just turned into something much more,” Jenna explained.
Jenna said that she was working on her own business and working a lot of overtime at a job she didn’t particularly like. This left her feeling like she needed a change, and her weekend trip to New York City provided that.
“I was very much in the thick of things at work, and then my boss quit and I was left with this time off. I was like, ‘Alright, I guess it’s time for me to go see the world.’”
Jenna said the choice to go was an easy one. She had saved up enough money for the trip, and she had no family or friends in the area. It also gave her an opportunity to try something new and to make new friends.
“I had never really had much time to explore on my own, so it was a new experience,” Jenna explained.
What was her first solo travel adventure like?
Jenna’s first trip was to New York City, which she had been planning for a few years. She had planned to take a one-week trip, but ended up staying for three.
“I stayed in a hostel in Brooklyn and met some amazing people who were also solo travelers. I learned so much about the city, the people, and the culture.”
Jenna also had a great time exploring the city, and she was pleasantly surprised by how friendly people were and how easy it was to meet people.
“I felt so welcomed and comfortable with everyone I met. It was a great experience,” Jenna said.
How did she prepare for her trip?
Jenna spent time researching her trip and learning about the city she was going to visit. She also looked at travel guides and asked around for advice on where to stay and what to see.
“I also looked at TripAdvisor and found some interesting things to do. It was just a fun way to get around and meet new people. I didn’t have any trouble getting around and I felt really comfortable there.”
How did she overcome her fears and doubts?
Jenna said that it wasn’t easy at first, but she learned to trust herself.
“There were definitely moments where I felt like I couldn’t do it, but I just pushed through,” she said.
Jenna said she felt confident in her ability to handle herself and that she wasn’t afraid of what was ahead of her.
“It was just so exciting,” she said. “I felt like I could do anything I wanted.”
How did Solo Travel Society help her on her journey?
“The staff was super helpful and encouraging, which was really great,” Jenna said.
“I had a lot of questions and they answered them all. The staff was also very friendly and made me feel at home.”
What advice does she have for other solo travelers?
Jenna said that she would recommend planning a trip with friends first and then going solo.
“I would tell them that they can go and have a great time,” she said.
“I think it’s so important to make new friends and meet new people. It’s so easy to be in a bubble, but when you go and meet new people you’ll be surprised at how much you can learn.”
Jenna said that she was so excited to get back to the place she’d been and that it was a great feeling.
“I just feel so much better about myself and who I am,” she said. “I’m so happy that I made the decision to go and I would definitely do it again.”

Joshua woke up to the sound of a ringing phone. He was confused. He wasn't in his bedroom. Where was he?
His eyes fluttered open.
A sudden fist of confusion gripped him, nearly knocking him off the bed.
He looked around and recognized the room.
His mom and dad's bedroom.
Wait a second.
He was in his mom and dad's bedroom!
And he wasn't alone. He was lying in bed next to his best friend, Emily.
And Emily's mom and dad were sleeping in the same room, too!
As if that weren't weird enough, the two of them had been sleeping here since the night before!
They had been forced to camp out on the floor because there was a tornado warning in the area and they couldn't get to Joshua's house because of the weather.
It had been one of the craziest nights of Joshua's life.
Now Joshua reached out and gently shook Emily awake.
"Come on," he whispered. "I think we should try to sneak out of here."
Emily blinked a few times, then glanced at Joshua's mom, who was still snoring lightly.
"You sure about this?" Emily whispered.

Joshua's mom was a light sleeper, and if she woke up, it could be a major problem.

He immediately started laughing.

"Yeah, that's old," Emily said. "You could fit the entirety of my brain in that phone. And if you flipped it open, it could be used as a trampoline."
"I know!" Joshua said. "This is so cool! Look at the cord!"
"Weird," Emily said. "But why are you so happy about it?"
Joshua's eyes lit up. "Because I get to answer this phone!"
The phone beeped loudly, then Emily's mom picked it up in the other room.

Joshua and Emily looked at each other in confusion.
"Um," Emily said. "What second monkey?"
