A breakthrough in renewable energy presents solutions to long-standing problems of climate change.
In the field of renewable energy, two important facts were established.
The first is that fossil fuels produce higher yields of energy per unit mass, compared to solar and wind energy.
The second is that wind energy is subject to the vagaries of wind speed, which produces unreliable power generation for electric grids.
Further, solar and wind energy are not flexible, and thus cannot be used as backup power for the grid.
To address these issues, researchers at the University of Alberta are developing a solar-powered hybrid wind-electric generation plant. This energy system is made of novel wind turbines that generate wind energy at a constant, uniform speed.
“Our technology utilizes vertical-axis wind turbines,” said Ryan D’Souza, a researcher at the University of Alberta. “These are ideal for hybridization with solar power because they are scalable to a smaller size, which means they can produce power at night and when there is no wind at all. They do not make a lot of noise, and they do not require towers, cables, or multiple gearboxes. This means they can be built into building structures and even onto cars.”
The process is not without its caveats, however.
“To be economically viable, the energy produced by the solar and wind turbines needs to be stored and distributed,” said D’Souza.
Storage solutions are becoming more efficient, however, such as the recently proposed creation of a new liquid electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries.
To solve the distribution issue, the University of Alberta team is considering transporting excess energy via the use of pipes, though there is still a long way to go in developing such a system.
Nevertheless, the researchers believe that their renewable energy plant can significantly contribute to the transition away from fossil fuels.
“Our system produces electricity at a higher capacity factor compared to solar and wind farms,” said Ryan D’Souza. “This is because it can produce wind and solar energy concurrently, resulting in a higher electricity yield at the end of the day.”
For this reason, the researchers believe their solar-powered hybrid wind-electric generation plant could offer a practical solution to the problems of unreliable and unstable wind and solar power, and thereby serve as an important link in the transition away from fossil fuels.
Reference: Ryan A. D’Souza, et al., Hybridizing Wind and Solar Power to Solve the Intermittency Problem: A Conceptual Study, Wind Energy Science (2021). DOI: 10.5194/wes-2021-5

A book club for superheroes becomes contentious when they can't agree on a supervillain to read.
"You better get it right!" I yelled as I slammed the phone into the cradle. I'd been waiting by the phone for the last hour, but my writer friend, Adam Davis, never called. I was tired of being disappointed by his lack of enthusiasm. Today, however, I was too mad to worry about hurting his feelings. What kind of person doesn't get excited about superheroes?
I'd had the idea for a superhero book club for a few years, but Adam was the only one who I felt would fully embrace the idea. This was a chance for us to collaborate on a project and rekindle our friendship.
When Adam and I were in college, we both aspired to be writers. We were both English majors, and we became close through a shared love of superheroes, especially the TV show, The Adventures of Lois & Clark.
The show came on right after "The Arsenio Hall Show." One time, the two were competing against each other for the highest Nielsen ratings. Our friends, Joe Schaffner and Erik Bryant, and I went to both Arsenio and Lois & Clark tapings. I was in L.A. the week of Lois & Clark's debut, and I saw the TV show before I even knew that it was a TV show. I remember liking it a lot and giving Adam a heads-up that I thought it was good. After seeing that first episode, I kept a close eye on it, and the two of us began to watch it regularly.
Our enthusiasm for the show brought us closer together. One afternoon in his dorm room, Adam showed me a copy of Amazing Heroes #191. It featured a cover story about the show and an interview with Teri Hatcher, who played Lois Lane. I was excited to see the cover story and read the interview. We often hung out in each other's dorm rooms or apartments, discussing the latest episode and debating plot developments. He had a creative writing class in which he got a good grade by writing a paper on Lois & Clark. Adam and I never tired of watching the show and talking about it. We also tried to make our own Lois & Clark and The Adventures of Captain Planet videos. The "Lois & Clark" video didn't make it past the trailer phase, but we finished the "Captain Planet" pilot.
After college, we stayed in touch. I became a comic book writer, and he did some copywriting and freelance writing before becoming a lawyer. At one point, I was working on a comic book that I was hoping to pitch to DC Comics. I asked Adam to come up with a character, so he created this guy, Gravity Man. Gravity Man could make the ground move under his feet, so he was always fighting crimes that took place on large expanses of flat land, like parking lots and bridges. I loved the concept and was excited to do something with it. When my plan to pitch DC fell through, I ended up putting it in a short story for The Writer magazine.
When I was working on my book, So You Created a Wormhole: The Time Traveler's Guide to Time Travel, I remembered that Adam had written a great time travel story for his creative writing class. I remembered that, even as a college student, he was good at superheroes.
After finishing the book, I was a bit disillusioned. I was tired of the bitter, constant battles that I was having with Marvel. I'd recently walked away from a good paying gig for Marvel. Because of my tendency to question authority, I was always rubbing people the wrong way at Marvel, and I'd had just about enough.
At the same time, I was also feeling frustrated with DC Comics. DC and I had been having a lengthy back and forth regarding payment for my Aquaman: Sword of Atlantis issues. The crux of it was that DC was not honoring the three-month delay stipulation in my contract, so they were withholding payment until the three months were up. I was annoyed that I'd had to bend over backwards to get the delay in my contract, and I was annoyed that they were not honoring it. It all felt like a deliberate slight. On top of that, when they did finally pay me, they sent me my check along with a huge invoice, making it clear that they were letting me know that they expected me to pay my royalties on the book.
I was discouraged because I had a son and a mortgage to pay, and if I hadn't been able to work at home, I would have been working at a crappy office job with a crappy paycheck. But I wasn't making enough money working for Marvel or DC. Even though I felt like I was right about the payment, it was time to give up the fight. The guy in charge of the payment said that, although they were going to continue to honor the delay, they wanted me to invoice them every month, so I sent him a list of books with the month they were supposed to come out, and I added the date of each issue's release. He had to have known that it wasn't my fault that they weren't meeting their release dates, but he said that I was supposed to invoice them anyway, so I did.
My frustration with comics companies had reached a boiling point. So, I decided that I wanted to branch out a little and try some other types of writing. I started writing a nonfiction humor book for the St. Martin's Press imprint, Gramercy. The book was called So You Created a Wormhole, and the joke was that the book was a guide to time travel. The conceit of the book was that it was written by someone who had just created a wormhole and was asking questions about the time travel experience. It was a fun book to write, but there were some serious challenges.

This time, after several hours of labor, I decided that I should probably come back to the hospital so I could be there for the birth. I didn't like the idea of missing my son's birth. We were up all night, so I had very little sleep the night before I was to leave for the convention.
The show I was attending was the Baltimore Comic-Con. It was a three-hour drive from Chicago, and it was going to be a long day. I was all packed up and getting ready to leave the house when Judy woke me up to tell me that she was having contractions. This time I thought she was just waking me up to tell me about her dreams. After we got the kids up and ready for school, I took Gabriel to daycare, Judy got our daughter ready for school, and then she took her to school. After dropping off my son, I got into my car, and Judy gave me the news. Her contractions were five minutes apart, and they were painful.

I called the hospital to tell them that Judy was on her way in, and I called the guy who I was going to the convention with. He was in the Chicago area, and he told me that I should just drive to Baltimore, check in at the convention, and then drive back. While I was on the phone, Judy called me to say that she was ready to go to the hospital. My mom was already at the hospital by this time, so I told Judy that I'd go home, pick up my stuff, and meet her there.
Judy gave me a quick rundown of all of the preparations that had been made. Her mom had put together a bag of items that she wanted me to bring with me. Her mom had also brought along a pillow and a blanket. Judy suggested that I bring along a book to read. I figured that I would probably get pulled away from reading the book, so I didn't pack one. I threw together a bag of things to take with me, and I told Judy that I'd meet her there.

Jack Blackwater is a young dragon attending his first year at the Academy for Adventurous Beginners, a unique school for magical creatures. Although he doesn’t quite fit in, with his icy breath and intimidating size and strength, he is immediately drawn to Eliza, a fire-breathing red dragon who is the most feared student in the school. The two bond over their common experiences as outsiders, and she recruits Jack to assist with her plan to prove her family’s value to the rest of the dragon population by stealing the first gold coin minted by humans.
But the mission doesn’t go as planned, and Jack and Eliza are caught by the legendary beast hunter Will Scarlet. But Will is on a mission of his own, to track down a missing child. And the man he believes is the kidnapper? A friend of Jack and Eliza’s—a young dragon who vanished on the same day as the missing boy.
The lines between hero and villain quickly become blurred, and Jack, Eliza, and Will must decide where they stand—and what they are willing to do to protect the creatures they’ve come to love as family.

Teaser from the short story
At the beginning of the tube, the door was ajar, leaving a rectangle of light in the dark hallway. When she got closer, she saw a tall, slender man on the threshold. He was a blur of movement when he stepped inside and shut the door.
The hall was lined with long, red brocade curtains that seemed to absorb what little light was let in through the door. The light from the entrance showed the contours of her companion’s shiny black hair. The soft curls were unkempt. The thick, long strands fell over his shoulders. He wore all black and was obviously in his prime. His tall, athletic frame moved with a fluid motion that would have impressed even the most discerning of judges at a body building contest. However, his good looks were not the only attribute that made her tingle. He emanated power.
Isilizwi hesitated. She should have been more alert, but her attention was on the tall man’s retreating form. As if her perception had shifted, she saw the end of the hall, instead of the wall that was there before. The hall was longer than it should have been, she realized, as she ran down its length. Her heart pounded in her chest.
The man stopped and turned, finally noticing that he was not alone. He gripped her by the shoulders, and then kissed her roughly. She realized that she should have been afraid. Instead, Isilizwi allowed herself to be taken, to be seduced. His movements were precise and fluid.
He lifted her off her feet. Her arms wrapped around his neck as her hands roamed through his black hair. She bit her lip and he noticed the movement, kissing her again. He broke away.
“Come with me. I will show you. I will show you everything.”
Her pulse raced. Isilizwi was intrigued. This was a man that knew what he wanted and was determined to get it. Isilizwi did not care that he was being unreasonable or even that he was being arrogant. She was attracted to his power and his determination.
“What if you don’t come back?”
“What if you don’t?” His voice was silken and gravelly, much like his smooth black skin.
Isilizwi did not answer him. She did not need to. He knew she was staying. It was what she wanted.
As soon as she had made up her mind, he vanished.
Isilizwi blinked and looked around. She was standing on a bright orange planet. Red sand spun around her feet and the dry air blew through her hair. It was hot and she immediately wished she had worn less clothing. Even the sun was difficult to look at. However, the heat was not what drew her attention.
The dead city around her rose like an oasis in the desert, its wide, flat structures reaching up into the deep, blue sky. Its silver walls reflected the hot rays of the sun, shooting the light into her eyes. She squinted and followed the light with her gaze. Where the sun’s rays met the reflective wall, they dispersed into a rainbow of colours.
Her companion moved forward. He led her into the center of the deserted city and to a circular tower that rose above the buildings around them.
The carvings along its sides seemed to tell a story. Figures rode along, dragons and horses roaming behind them. The warriors had brown skin and their hair was tied back in tight braids. Some of the warriors were naked, while others wore bright, skimpy clothes.
Isilizwi followed her companion into the building, the sunlight receding behind her. She stopped when he pushed the door open.
The interior of the building was just as warm and dry as the desert around them. The warmth was the only source of comfort in the lifeless building. The room was circular and empty except for a small pyramid in its center. The tablets around the pyramid were sculpted into the walls. The pictures painted on them were of fierce warriors riding to battle on their horses, bringing down their enemies with one swing of their swords.
Isilizwi ran her fingers over the smooth, beige surface of the walls.
“I’ve been here before. I recognize this place.”
The man reached over to the pyramid and touched the sides of the wide structure, patting the smooth surface.
“They called this the pyramid of death.”
“The pyramid of death? Why would they call it that?”
“The one who built it was known to love death.”
“That is an unusual name. Can I touch it?”
Isilizwi moved past her companion and touched the pyramid. It was smooth and cold and had no cracks or imperfections. The only thing that set it apart from its surroundings was its slight shine. She traced her fingers along the sides and glanced over her shoulder, but the man was gone.
She was standing in the middle of the room when the door opened. She was ready to demand the man return. Isilizwi turned and gasped. The tall, black haired man stood in the doorway, his hand on the door.
“What happened to you? Where were you?”
“I was here. We were always together, you and I.”
“I don’t remember.” Isilizwi closed her eyes and shrugged. “Why am I here? What am I doing here?”
“I’ll show you everything.”
Isilizwi looked at him. His voice was cold and bitter. There was a time when she loved this man. A time when he took her away to other worlds and showed her things she had never dreamt of. He was cruel. Isilizwi knew that he was the most selfish of lovers. He used her until she could bear the pain no more and then left her.
“What do you want? It is your turn to show me.”
The man grabbed her shoulders and kissed her hard, pushing her down onto her knees. His fingers moved up her skirt and grabbed hold of her thighs. He kneaded her skin. Isilizwi closed her eyes and tilted her head back. She relaxed and enjoyed the feeling of his fingers on her skin.
Suddenly, a bright light filled the room. Isilizwi blinked and opened her eyes. She was standing in front of a silver tower, its curved surface shimmering in the glow of the full moon.
The man stepped out of the shadows. He approached her and reached out. She noticed the scimitar in his hand. It was silver and glinted in the moonlight.
“I did not think I would see you again.” His voice was gruff and husky.
“I don’t understand. Where are we?”
“You belong here. You always have. We always have. This is the place we have chosen for our first love, our last love.”
The man’s eyes burned with desire. Isilizwi shuddered when he lifted his head and tilted it to the side. The moonlight had silvered his skin and brought out the black of his hair. He held the scimitar close to his side and winked at her.
“Are you ready? Come.”
He pulled her along by her hand. She saw the metal of the scimitar clink against the sides of the walls. She had the strange sensation that she was wearing a long, flowing robe. The material dragged along the floor as they walked through the silent building.
The man reached for the ornate handle of the door. The handle was wide and shone in the moonlight. He turned it and pushed. The door was heavy and she could hear the creak of hinges. She stepped inside and saw that it was a library.
The room was large and ornate, with the walls lined with books. Isilizwi ran her fingers along the smooth, creamy spines.
“This is the library of life.”
“I thought libraries had books.”
The man laughed. “There are thousands of books in here, but they are books of the soul.”
“How does that make sense? Books are just words and paper.”
“No. A book is the key to understanding everything.”

Dark Shadows is an American gothic soap opera that originally aired weekdays on the ABC television network, from June 27, 1966, to April 2, 1971. The show was created by Dan Curtis. The story bible, which was written by Art Wallace, does not mention any supernatural elements. It was unprecedented in daytime television when ghosts were introduced about six months after it began. The series became hugely popular when vampire Barnabas Collins appeared a year into its run. Dark Shadows also featured the first same-sex kiss in American daytime television between two men and the first interracial kiss between a white woman and black man. The serial was distinguished by its vividly melodramatic performances, atmospheric interiors, memorable storylines, numerous dramatic plot twists, unusually adventurous music score, and broad and epic cosmos of characters and heroic adventures. Now regarded as something of a classic, it continues to have a dedicated fanbase. Although the original series ran for only five years, its scheduling as a daily daytime drama allowed it to amass more single episodes during its run than most other science-fiction/fantasy genre series produced for English-language television, including Doctor Who and the entire Star Trek television franchise. Only the paranormal soap opera Passions, with a total of 2,231 episodes, has more.

The craftsmanship of ancient pottery tells a story of cultural heritage and innovation
One of the largest and most significant parts of our collections at Waddesdon is the display of English 18th and early 19th century pottery. With over 1,500 pieces, this national collection represents over 100 years of English pottery from the Baroque to the beginning of the Industrial Revolution.
An eclectic mix of ceramic objects from porcelain to terracotta, the collection includes rare pieces by the likes of the Wedgwood and Bow families as well as delicate teacups and saucers and over a thousand pieces made at the famous Wedgwood factory in Stoke-on-Trent.
Ralph Wood’s charming Staffordshire figure groups, the Bow ‘Willow’ pattern teapot and the ‘Diana and Actaeon’ biscuit porcelain figurine by the Wedgwood factory in Barlaston are among the finest in the collection.
The highlight, however, is the Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware service: a neo-classical service of tableware given to Queen Charlotte by Sir William Hamilton, as a gift for George III, on the occasion of their Silver Wedding Anniversary in 1788.
Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware service
In the mid-1780s a neo-classical fashion for ‘Woodfern’ ware started in London, fashioned to look like wooden ware. Made from un-glazed and partially glazed biscuit porcelain, with painted designs on the surface, Woodfern ware mimicked the texture and grain of oak, fir and elm, rendering objects, such as dishes, teapots and mugs, with the appearance of turned wooden objects.
The Woodfern ware service given to Queen Charlotte is arguably the most significant set in the world, and the most important surviving collection of this type of porcelain, forming a complete tea service.
Wedgwood’s ‘Queen Charlotte’s Woodfern Ware Tea Service’, 1788, painted with dun and gold floral decoration and stylised neo-classical portraits, c. 1788
Woodfern ware was created by Thomas Lamb who owned a large factory at New Hall, Cranbrook in Kent and produced from 1785 to 1800. Lamb’s factory, which once numbered 150 workers, also made ceramic figures, salt-glazed stoneware and pressed bricks.
In 1785 Lamb is recorded as producing one of the first pottery pieces made to imitate the grain and texture of wood, a hollow beechwood mug for Robert Taylor, Esq. and signed ‘T. Lamb – New Hall’.
Lamb was succeeded by his son in 1800 and business continued in a small way at the New Hall site until 1848 when the factory was shut down.
Wedgwood’s ‘Woodfern Ware Dish’, 1787, painted with brown floral decoration, c. 1787
Due to the rarity of this kind of ceramic, finding out who was responsible for the beautiful designs painted on the Woodfern ware is often difficult. Some pieces may have been decorated at the Cranbrook factory, though most designs are probably contemporary with the factory and produced by decorators working in London.
Dun and brown is a popular colour combination for Woodfern ware, with both colours painted in free flowing brush strokes that imitate the appearance of wood. One of the charming aspects of Woodfern ware is that the decorations often look like engravings, emphasising the neo-classical style and subject matter.
Both the dish and the sugar bowl feature a representation of classical figures. The dish, with a leaf-pattern on the base, is painted with a scene showing Diana surprising Actaeon. The panel painting is delicately finished with a paint rim showing flowers. The Woodfern ware sugar bowl, with a leaf-pattern on the base, is painted with a scene showing a lion attacking a seated deer.
The scene of the attacked deer is shown in the middle of the bowl, surrounded by two identical scenes of a goat attacking an ass. The Woodfern ware sugar bowl is finished with a laurel leaf-border painted in white, emphasising the neo-classical design.
Woodfern ware
Woodfern ware is a term which was coined later in the 20th century. Originally, the ware was termed ‘wooden ware’ as it imitated the texture of wood. By the late 18th and 19th centuries the ware was referred to as ‘wood’ ware and the term woodfern ware evolved in the 20th century.
The pottery can also be known as ‘Wood Ware’ or ‘Wood-Grain Ware’, as many objects take inspiration from the texture of wood. These pieces can also be made using other materials such as clay or terracotta.
The earliest example of a piece of Woodfern ware is a mug in the possession of the Victoria and Albert Museum, dating back to 1785.
The collection of porcelain at Waddesdon is housed in the magnificent kitchen complex of the Manor, together with a unique collection of English tableware dating back to 1725. The display features some of the finest pieces of Baroque to early Victorian porcelain, including delicate tea cups and saucers, bowls, tureens and other serving vessels. There is also a unique group of English 18th century plate.
Visitors can take a close look at the remarkable objects, including a large dinner service of Wedgwood, painted with deer in a landscape by the famous painter, Thomas Gainsborough, known as the ‘Gainsborough’ service.
An English porcelain teacup with a dog in a landscape, c. 1810
Our porcelain collection
Our collection includes other fine pieces, such as the ‘Luncheon Service’ for Queen Victoria, also by Wedgwood, depicting the major events in the young Queen’s life.
The service, which is a combination of four different styles of porcelain and decoration, was given to Queen Victoria and Prince Albert as a wedding present from the poet and author Letitia Elizabeth Landon, on 10 February 1840, just one month before the marriage.

Pottery fascinating facts
The first pieces of porcelain were produced in China, most likely in the city of Jingdezhen.
It was not until 1712 that the first successful porcelain factory in Europe was established in Dresden, Germany.
A factory was established in Meissen, Germany in 1710.
The first English porcelain factory was established in Chelsea, London in 1743.
Tea first came to Britain in 1660, after the Restoration.

Sir William Hamilton was the British ambassador to Naples, when his wife Emma became mistress to the British Prime Minister, Lord Nelson. She was known as Lady Hamilton.

With three weeks to go before the first votes, the coalition talks are underway. The two parties who need to be discussed as early as possible are the CDU and the Greens.
With three weeks to go before the first votes, the coalition talks are underway.
The two parties who need to be discussed as early as possible are the CDU and the Greens.
This became clear in a conversation with the co-chair of the Greens, Annalena Baerbock.
Baerbock is campaigning in the Hanseatic city of Stralsund.
Since the election night in Lower Saxony, SPD, CDU and Greens have tried to agree on a traffic light coalition.
The Greens also wanted to govern with the FDP.
But the FDP is not interested in red-green, but in traffic light.
Baerbock has already made it clear that the Greens would rather govern with the SPD than with the FDP.
The head of the Stralsund Greens district association also said in an interview with Spiegel that the traffic light coalition would benefit from the citizens of Germany.
The traffic light coalition wants to reduce the burden on the middle class and fight the climate catastrophe with a massive modernization of the economy.
The negotiations between the traffic light parties have now been ongoing for a week.
The basic paper is now on the table and a first version of the coalition agreement will be presented at the beginning of December.
"But now we have to fight the election campaign," says Baerbock.
It is now about electing as many representatives of the Greens as possible who could represent the coalition partner in the Bundestag.
But before the Greens, FDP and SPD can start coalition negotiations, the federal states need to make their voices heard.
The FDP is the only party that is really involved in the coalition negotiations and there is a serious question of whether the smaller party wants to engage in coalition negotiations.
The strong image of the Liberal Party is reflected in the election campaign.
From Brandenburg to Baden-Württemberg to Hamburg, the FDP wants to leave nothing to chance and ensure that its own voters are voted for again.
The FDP is thus pitting itself against the CDU, which is constantly winning over its own voters.
The party's election campaign, with Prime Ministers, is also associated with high costs and sophisticated election campaign material.
With this election campaign, the party wants to ensure that it wins the support of the voters in the larger cities and in the traditionally liberal areas in the south.
The election campaigns of the FDP and CDU are taking place in a completely different environment.
While the CDU election campaign is run on a shoestring budget, the FDP is using a huge campaign budget.
"The money isn't enough and the field service is struggling.
But in terms of strategy, we have always planned for the worst, that is, that the FDP would not participate in the traffic light coalition," says an FDP man from the Rhineland.
"But it is clear that the FDP will be an indispensable partner in the future, if there are only three in the new federal government," says another FDP man.
But even in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, there is some concern in the FDP because of the different levels.
In the election campaign in NRW, the FDP can build on the Prime Minister and Minister President Hendrik Wuest.
But in Baden-Württemberg and other states, the Prime Ministers are missing and are being replaced by candidates.
"But this is what the party has to do.
If we don't vote for as many people as possible, it will be harder to build a traffic light coalition," says an FDP man from the Rhineland.
Baerbock has made it clear that her party would be the "first choice" in a coalition with the FDP.
After the talks with the SPD have shown the possibility of a coalition, she does not see any reason to change the preference.
The Greens also want to bring their own federalism into the coalition negotiations.
"The CDU, after all, is also a federal party," says Baerbock.

We all have a part in the creation process.
It begins with Him, the potter, the Master Potter, if you will, who wears the title, 'Jesus'. He is the 'potter', the master who has the ability to mold us.
Once we are born into this world, we begin to grow, to learn, to take in the world around us. From start to finish, God has a plan and a purpose for us.
The idea of creation, was in the mind of God before even the beginning.
Once He created the earth and its' inhabitants, He let them go free to make their own choices, to love Him or hate Him.
No matter what choice you make, He is still in control and can create the best from it.
The thoughts that come to mind now, of creation and the end of the world, and all that is to come, are terrifying. I mean, really, it's scary. You know what I'm saying?
When I think of all the love that God has, to endure the disrespect that we give Him daily, I can't help but think of the emotion that must come over Him, to let His love keep flowing, as he carries us all.
I think of the verse, Psalm 23:4 "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me."
I have gone through some of my deepest valleys since I first read these words, and I must say, they are one of the most truthful verses in the Bible.
There will always be valleys in our lives, that we must go through.
He does comfort us in our valleys, with His rod and staff, that will guide us through.
For our love of Jesus, who gives us the most powerful gift, love. A love so powerful, that it can change us. Change us from a broken, scattered, sinner to an unbroken, whole, loving Christian.
In the end, it's not about who we were, but who we have become through the power of His love.
So today, I want to encourage you, to know that you are made for a purpose.
Don't be afraid to walk through your valleys, because God will guide you through.
With His rod and staff, He will guide you through.
Have a beautiful Sunday, and always walk in faith!

What

In a parallel universe where music is the only language, a tone-deaf ambassador must use the force of his personality to save his ship from disaster.

The silent film star's lost interview surfaced, revealing insights into his lasting popularity.
Gary Cooper kisses Doris Day in the 1953 film 'The Man Who Knew Too Much.'
Beverly Hills Film Festival/Wikimedia Commons
It turns out that you should never assume silence means consent. That's the takeaway from a newfound interview with Hollywood movie star Gary Cooper, who gave his thoughts on his wife and his career to gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in 1959, but never approved the interview for publication.
Hopper spoke to Cooper, who was a superstar in the 1940s, at his Los Angeles-area home in Beverly Hills. The columnist began with a few questions about his wife, Rocky actress Veronica Lake. The pair divorced in 1951, and Hopper asked Cooper if Lake would "be the same if she'd married Rock Hudson." Cooper said, "No, she would have probably married him, and she's the kind who would never divorce."
An actress by trade herself, Hopper asked Cooper if he ever felt the pull of Hollywood. "God, no, not at all. Not once. I've always just enjoyed acting," he said. "I'm not very good at sitting around."
And what did he think of the acting chops of fellow Hollywood legend Marilyn Monroe? Cooper called her "a fine actress," but not up to the caliber of performers like Humphrey Bogart, Jack Lemmon, Henry Fonda, and Lauren Bacall.
Gary Cooper, center, with his son, John, right, and Rocky Lake, 1952
Gene Lester/Wikimedia Commons
Perhaps Cooper's most revealing insights, though, were about the characteristics that made him a star. He said that while he didn't understand what "made me a success at all," he did know that "the biggest key to my success was the fact that I came from Montana and I was never smitten by Hollywood," he said. "If I ever went to bed and said, 'Gee, I wish I could be an actor,' I never told anybody."
It was that "almost stolid determination to get somewhere," he said, that made him appealing.
Cooper died in 1961, two years after his interview with Hopper. It wasn't until after his death that Hopper published her notes in her 1968 book The Good Times, which was compiled from her gossip column.
That book, as well as a recording of Cooper's interview, were discovered in the closet of Hopper's former home, which is now owned by director Francis Ford Coppola. The L.A. Times reports that the documents were discovered by archivists, who have not yet determined when the interview will be published or released to the public.
It's not the first time a star has been heard from past the grave. In January 2019, for example, newscasts aired a live broadcast of the late Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon. The 1969 audio was restored by The Apollo 11 Mission Control Center Restoration Project, which released a remastered version of the mission, with unused footage restored and slowed down audio.

The serene landscape of the countryside was dotted with more than 500 bright green, mushroom-shaped dwellings. They were actually modified quonsets originally constructed for the United States military, and now housing the artists of the Stony Lake Music Festival. Built to support the festival’s needs and provide ample shelter for performers and patrons in the sometimes harsh Canadian weather, they stood in relative silence, waiting for that weekend to come.
From a distance, the structures looked like the mushrooms from Alice in Wonderland, or, as several people remarked, like a village of Jabba the Hut's death squads. Whatever metaphor one decided to use, the fact remained that, each year, the musicians of the festival would populate these structures, turn them into intimate, acoustically perfect performance spaces, and play music for the nearby villagers of the small, but historic, town of Haliburton, Ontario.
The concept of such a festival is simple: The selected musicians were to provide all of the instruments (sans percussion), thereby leaving the village’s percussionist without a kit. Given the circumstances, Cully proposed the following solution: He would rent a travel-friendly kit and bring it to Haliburton, utilizing his drum parts for the musical performances, and the drum kit for the local jam sessions. Cully has become a fixture of the festival, a village elder of sorts who does so much more than just play drums.
Even though Cully set up the basic rhythmic foundation for each and every performance, he was also expected to play an essential role in many of the other activities that went on throughout the weekend. A naturally inquisitive, easy-going, and friendly person, he has, over the years, befriended a number of the other musicians and has become involved in numerous facets of the festival, to the point where he is considered a fixture, and his presence is anticipated. For him, the benefits go beyond the obvious role of facilitating the festival’s rhythmic foundation. His empathy has enabled him to get to know each of the participants in a more meaningful way. As he explains, “I've met musicians who don't do this kind of thing—who might not have the opportunity to play the guitar while a singer plays, for instance. I feel lucky to have these encounters, and to be able to facilitate musical experiences for them.”
Unlike a typical club engagement, where the drummer's performance is largely expected to support the lead singer, at the festival, there is no lead singer. The structures are acoustically and visually intimate, and the festival's goal is to foster an environment in which the musicians can develop a stronger musical bond.
One can’t overstate the power of the festival's sense of community. Artists who are already working together in the band environment will further develop their rapport over the weekend, creating something much more personal than a normal gig. Other artists—who might not get to play together on a regular basis—will learn new music and styles as they create a sound together. There’s a kind of serendipity to it all, and the musicians seem to really embrace the opportunity to get together, outside of the performance context, to just talk, hang out, and play music.
“There's a big difference between being a pro musician and being a musician who can play professionally, which I consider to be a higher calling,” Cully explains. “The festival, which provides a pretty equal setting for everyone, is a tremendous opportunity for artists to explore and expand. One of the things I try to do is support them in whatever direction they go—to facilitate their improvisation and let them explore as much as possible.”
Another added benefit of the festival is its focus on different musical genres. At a typical gig, the drummer is expected to play rock-solid, straight-ahead time. “It’s not a show unless I'm playing loud,” says Cully, laughing, adding, “I’ve been known to fill every little opening.” As a result of this variety of musical styles, Cully has been able to play music that he might not otherwise get the opportunity to play in a more traditional gig setting. “At this point, I’ve played with all kinds of musicians, from rock, folk, and jazz, to bluegrass, Celtic, and classical. I’ve been fortunate enough to be in all of those different settings,” he says. “But I love the ability to step out of that framework and explore other styles of music. It helps me become a more well-rounded player.”
After setting up his kit each day at the festival, Cully began learning the pieces that would be played that evening. Since each artist and band was allocated the same amount of time—a duration that was often, in the early years, an hour or so—the musicians would need to select only a handful of songs to play. These sets were expected to be a little bit more cohesive than the traditional, improvisational “jam.” While much of the music was unrehearsed, it was still not like a typical jam session, where each artist played whatever they felt like playing. In some ways, the musicians at the festival were expected to try and create a more cohesive musical narrative with one another.
Cully’s role in setting the rhythmic tone for the evening’s performances was significant. Having worked with so many different musicians in the past, he was often able to take musical cues from the other performers, and shape the music to fit the specific style that would be expected. As one of the more experienced musicians at the festival, he was often called upon to orchestrate the rhythmic structures of some of the pieces, although he was quick to point out that his role was to set the mood—not to dictate. “I don't think of myself as a sideman,” Cully says. “I’m a part of the rhythmic fabric of the music, and I try to be supportive of it—to get inside what the others are doing, and to figure out how I can best serve that music.”
As an artist, one of Cully’s greatest strengths is his versatility. As he explains, “Drumming, for me, is the ability to adapt. There’s no real reason to play the same thing over and over again.” So, in order to keep himself in the game, he is constantly working to perfect his improvisational skills. “For me,” he says, “it’s the little details, the subtleties, that really matter, and the only way to become a better drummer is to expand my playing vocabulary and understand how to change my parts to suit the piece.”
To help facilitate this development, Cully recently began working with drum teacher Derico Watson. For the past year, they have worked together, and Cully says that Watson’s influence has really helped him to focus on the fundamentals and to become a better reader. “I want to be able to sight-read music and to play different styles of music,” he says, “because, to me, music is really a language. The only way to get better is to understand how to speak the language.”
The morning of the last day of the festival began with its traditional breakfast barbecue, and Cully took the opportunity to do some sightseeing in the nearby town. It was at this point that Cully realized he’d forgotten his drumsticks at the village. The two-hour round trip was not really an option, so he did the next best thing: He improvised.
Grabbing a set of bushes from the side of the road, Cully ran back to the festival grounds, and set about finding some participants to perform. And, lo and behold, he found two very willing musicians, a drummer and a violinist, who agreed to participate in a spontaneous performance. There was, however, one major flaw in this plan: The only pair of drumsticks available belonged to the violinist. It was a perfect irony that the drummer at the festival could not play drums! The situation could not have been any better for Cully, though, who was able to spend the next hour demonstrating his new skills. “Improvisation,” he says, “is the key to being a good musician, and improvisation is all about being in the moment.”
Cully’s interaction with the festival has been incredibly fruitful, as he’s been able to foster some of the most meaningful musical relationships in his life. In addition to expanding his musical vocabulary, he’s also learned a lot about himself as a person. “The festival has been very beneficial for me as an artist,” he says, “and it’s been especially beneficial for my musical development. But I’ve also become a better person for it, because it’s brought me together with so many wonderful people.”

In the depths of the ancient forest, there is a girl named Sara who is on a long journey in search of the legendary witch of the woods. Little does she know she's being watched by the residents of the forest.
The residents of the forest don't feel safe around the girl. They have been persecuted by witch hunters in the past. The tension is high. The woodlands are empty. The girl has stopped at the witch's tree.
She's been there for a while. She's waiting for the witch to arrive. The forest is eerily quiet.
Then a tall old hag climbs out of the trunk of the tree, her black roots wrapped around her body like serpents. The witch smiles at Sara.
“Welcome child, to my home. I am the witch of the woods. Would you like to come inside and talk with me?” the witch says.
Sara follows the witch through the tree trunk and into her home. They sit by a fire and drink apple juice. They talk all night. Sara asks the witch all sorts of questions. When the sun rises, Sara knows the witch is a kind soul who wishes to help her.
“Thank you witch. I have decided to take you up on your offer. I would like to stay with you and learn your craft. But first I need to go home and get my things,” Sara says.
Sara finds a way out of the tree. She meets the witch by the waterfall. Sara puts on a dress and tries to walk in the witch's shoes. The witch takes her hand and leads her down a forest path.
The trail opens into a wide meadow. Sara sees a lake of glass with a reflection of a large tree in it. The witch takes Sara's hand and they walk down the path to the water.
Sara is about to step into the lake when she hears a sound from above. She looks up and sees a child standing at the tree's edge. Sara takes the child by the hand and helps her down from the tree.
“My child, I have found you. You have been lost for a long time. But I will not leave you here alone. I will take you with me,” the witch says.
“Why?” the child asks.
“Because I love you and want you to stay with me,” the witch says.
“I love you too witch,” the child says.
The witch and child embrace and Sara watches from the lake. She knows it is the right thing to do. She hopes the child will be safe with the witch.
The child and witch disappear into the forest. Sara returns to the witch's home. She sits by the fire and thinks about the day's events.
The witch comes home and sits by the fire. She stares at the flames. Her eyes reflect the light from the fire. She's deep in thought. Sara watches her silently.
“Why did you come to my home, child?” the witch asks.
“I heard about you and wanted to see if you were real,” Sara says.
“I am real, child. But I am also not what I once was. When I first became a witch I was strong and powerful. But I am no longer that witch. My powers have been weakened by a curse. I am all that remains of my past self,” the witch says.
“I don't believe you. Why would a witch like you need me?” Sara says.
“I need your blood, child. My power is tied to it. Without it I will fade and die,” the witch says.
“I don't understand,” Sara says.
“You will, child. I will explain everything when you come back with me,” the witch says.
The witch looks into Sara's eyes and sees her love for her child. She understands why Sara came to her. The witch places her hand on Sara's shoulder.
“It will all make sense, child. I will make it so,” the witch says.
Sara nods. She knows the witch is right. She follows her into the forest.
The witch and child walk down the path to the waterfall. They sit by the water and listen to the sound of the waterfall. Sara sits in front of them. She looks at the witch and the child. They look so different from each other.
“The child is mine, but the witch is yours. You are the one who will help me make my dreams come true,” the witch says.
“What do you mean? How will I help you?” Sara asks.
“You will become the witch's servant. I will teach you everything I know about magic and the supernatural. You will become my most trusted assistant,” the witch says.
“I don't understand. Why do you need me?” Sara asks.
“Because you are a gift from the gods. You are the chosen one who will guide me and lead me to my destiny,” the witch says.
The witch looks into Sara's eyes. She sees her love for her child. She knows Sara will help her.
“You have nothing to fear, child. I will keep you safe from harm. I will protect you and your child. Together we will rule this world,” the witch says.
Sara nods. She knows the witch is right. She follows her into the forest.
In the depths of the ancient forest, there is a girl named Sara. She is the chosen one. She will guide the witch and lead her to her destiny.
The Witch's Tale: Sara Rinaldi

The whispered legends of the haunted mansion spoke of secret panels, hidden chambers, vanishing room, poisonous gas, plague, death, a pale phantom—Laird of Lochmoore.
There was a time when Laird Jamison of Lochmoore roamed the Scottish highlands and fought in the fields of Bannockburn. During the madness of the fourteenth century he was master of his own fate—and that of his clan.
But that was long ago. The Laird was now a crippled old man—and death was near.
And now his daughter, beautiful Isleen—the houri of Lochmoore—was betrothed to the cruel Baron of Douglas, a man who loved only gold. Yet Isleen was in love with the poor Laird of Lochmoore, who would soon be dead. But Jamison would not give her to Douglas.
Yet there was a way to keep the treasure of the Jamisons from falling into the enemy's hand. Jamison had a map in his secret chambers showing the location of a great treasure—more than enough to buy an army. But, because of his betrothal, Douglas was in charge of Lochmoore—and he would do anything to get the gold.
Jamison, then, would die with his secret. And Isleen—for she would be lost to him forever.
Yet there was the whispered legend. Laird Jamison would not die. For the door to the secret panel that could lead to death would remain locked.
Jamison, crippled and broken, was wheeled into the secret room. And there, even as death came to him, a mocking voice asked him why he had not died. And now Jamison, knowing that death would come to his daughter, would know that he could not die—not as long as Isleen lived!
But death was near. And Isleen was now in the secret room with him, pleading for the secret of the locked door to be given to her.
She would enter the secret door if he would reveal the hidden key.
She would do that to save her people.
And then she would die!
Now Jamison laughed as he crushed the poisoned glass in his crippled hand.
"Isleen! She must die, too. My people must never suffer under the tyranny of the Barons of Douglas. I am their guardian. And I will lead them in battle! Together we will die!"
For, by dying, Isleen would free her father to live on forever—to be the legendary Laird of Lochmoore.
But then, as Jamison lay dying, a great treasure came to life before his eyes.
There was no longer any need for a ghost. The treasure had returned to life!
In the beginning there was the legend. The secret of the locked door. And Laird Jamison had a message to send through time to the boy, John Storm.

"Well," Alex laughed. "I wouldn't exactly call it a new life, but I do feel that the old life is over."

"It certainly is very different from life in the Mediterranean. The Red Sea is rather like a large bathtub—we are enclosed by mountains. And no wind. The Mediterranean, of course, is like an ocean."
"But the Mediterranean is never like an ocean," Jan protested. "It is as calm as this sea most of the time."
"Yes," Alex said, "and all the same I can't help feeling as if a wall has come down and we've entered a new world."

"They must be extraordinary," Jan agreed. "I can't wait. I've dreamed of the pyramids all my life."
"Maybe they'll make us feel very small," Alex said. "Sitting there so high and mighty, a million years older than we are. Maybe they'll look down on us as mere tiny bacteria."
"I suppose that's the difference between the ancient and the modern world," Jan mused. "The ancients never considered themselves small. They believed in gods and goddesses who created the world. They never realized that man is alone, an insignificant part of the universe."
"But that's what we are," Alex insisted. "Do you know that there are only some eight thousand human beings in all the earth for each square mile?"
"Aren't you forgetting about the other life forms? Most of which are far older than we are?"

He picked up the sliver of metal that dangled on a string from the rail. The sailing ship that had brought them across the Red Sea was an ancient smack—a sailing vessel whose boat was tied astern and was now being slowly pulled in.
Alex walked to the rail, rang the bell, and waved his piece of metal in the air. The boat came toward the _Maritza,_ and then the two crewmen aboard it threw out a rope. Alex caught the rope and tied it to the rail, and then he helped Jan to climb down into the boat.
The boat was a sailing dinghy, and in the center was a small mast from which a single triangular sail was suspended. The boat rocked and bobbed in the gentle swells of the Red Sea as Jan and Alex sat on a wooden bench at the bow.
"Pretty nice, isn't it?" Alex said.
"Except that we are going to be bounced around like marbles in a box," Jan said. "The Red Sea is very shallow, and we will be coasting on these sand bars all the way to Aden. It will be a slow ride."
The _Maritza_ was a modern motor ship, but they had agreed that they would leave her at the Red Sea port of Suez, the northernmost part of Egypt, and go the rest of the way to Cairo by land. They had made arrangements to join a motor coach for the remainder of the trip, but first they had planned to see something of Egypt before taking the coach. And that was why they had signed on to the _Maritza_ as stowaways, the night before she sailed.
The boat pulled away from the _Maritza,_ and Jan and Alex waved goodbye to the tall deckhands who had put them ashore.
"It's strange," Alex said, watching the modern ship fade into the distance. "I think I'm going to feel like a castaway for a little while. This isn't exactly the modern world we left."
"I don't know, Alex," Jan said. "There's something about the Red Sea that makes me feel as if I were one of the ancient pharaohs. I can imagine that we are crossing a holy place—the place between the worlds. It's a holy land—holy and mysterious."
"And I'm wondering if they still have pirates in the Red Sea," Alex said. "Do you know that a great deal of the trade that once went through the Mediterranean now goes through this sea? Reviewed by JimmyH 8 / 10
Being creepy and terrifying isn't the only thing that makes a great horror movie, or horror series for that matter. "Midnight Mass" sets the creep factor on a low burn, but makes up for it in good writing, engaging characters, and a story that makes you think about the meaning of faith, belief, and even what you will do to survive.
The series follows an out of work priest, Father Paul (Zach Gilford) who has returned home to an island on the west coast of Massachusetts. Paul has been stripped of his standing in the Catholic Church and is haunted by past tragedies and mistakes. Paul returns home to find his childhood friend Erin (Kristin Lehman) has taken up the responsibility of the local church, and while their mutual faith remains, Paul has become a doubtful and bitter man who distances himself from the town.
The town itself is mired in the death of local teenager James who was killed in a car accident that his drunk father survived. It is revealed that the town drunk (Ramon Tikaram) is a member of a cult who killed the boy in a sacrifice to a pagan god, and he is dragged out of the church in a grisly fashion by an angry mob. Father Paul is offered a job as a new pastor at the local church, and as the town's unrest begins to grow, a childhood acquaintance of Father Paul (Hamish Linklater) moves back home to the island as well.
"Midnight Mass" starts slow but builds a convincing case for a good story to follow. The acting is all on point, and I was especially impressed with Gilford and Linklater. The latter's performance feels particularly calculated but still genuine, making the character's background and arc all the more compelling. The island itself is almost a character of its own, given the brief glimpses of horrifying, parasitic creatures that we are shown in the first episode. These things are living monstrosities that are truly unlike anything that I have seen before, and the crew definitely did a good job bringing them to life on the screen. The island's own mystery also adds an air of intrigue to the overall story.
That being said, it is a bit of a trope to create a fictional town or location that is isolated from the outside world, where the evil happens to be trapped on the island and unable to escape, keeping the evil isolated. That being said, this trope allows for a low burn creepy atmosphere to build up as the story develops and leads us into what is sure to be an eventful and unsettling third act.
"Midnight Mass" is a strong story that builds a perfect atmosphere for a good horror series. I give "Midnight Mass" a 4 out of 5.

The detective pondered over the clues, which led to him drawing a conclusion, that the butler did it. (However, this could be a lie, which I cannot disclose the clues to prove.)

TheButler, Jan 29, 2008
Hello TheButler.
Yes, the clause "which led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it" is ambiguous. The phrase "led him to draw" can mean either "led him to think", or "led him to the actual drawing of a conclusion".
However, the use of the clause is completely normal and acceptable in this sentence, and it would be very odd to add "that the butler did it" after the words "led him to draw the conclusion", because in that position it is superfluous. It would be totally different if the person were to write "led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it" - which would be completely unacceptable in my opinion.
Yes, that's right. There are various things which can be done to a verb such as "pondered". You can add something which shows that you pondered on something (such as "over the clues"), or you can add "over" to "pondered" to show that you did not think about something.
Furthermore, does the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' have to elaborate on 'that the butler did it' and 'the detective pondered over the clues', since the clause 'which led him to draw the conclusion' has to elaborate on at least 'the detective pondered over the clues'? I was wondering if 'which led him to draw the conclusion that the butler did it' is ambiguous and that the reader does not know whether 'which led him to draw the conclusion' refers to 'that the butler did it' or 'the detective pondered over the clues'.
I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean here. If you are saying that "that the butler did it" refers to a specific event, then that is completely wrong. The "that the butler did it" is nothing more than a piece of information added to explain what the detective "pondered" or "drew a conclusion" about.
Hello TheButler!
I wouldn't say that the sentence is 'ambiguous' as much as it is 'potentially ambiguous'. As part of the general linguistic phenomenon called 'word hunting', there is a possible reading of the sentence that would equate the phrase "which led him to draw the conclusion" with 'that the butler did it'. In fact, there are a number of ways to achieve this meaning - either by word order, or through a few key additions/deletions to the sentence.
Thus, my preferred version (though not everyone agrees) would be to write: "He was led by the clues to conclude that the butler did it." This retains the sentence's intended meaning, but also removes any doubt as to what precisely the phrase "which led him to draw the conclusion" refers to.
The other way to achieve this meaning would be to combine the two clauses into one:
"He was led to the conclusion that the butler did it by pondering over the clues."
Although grammatically correct, I don't think it is necessary, as I do not think that the reader would be confused at all by the previous version.
farseer, Feb 2, 2008

eg: But at that time, I had no idea who was going to win, for I had no clue (led me to) what the match was about.
We can see that 'led me to' is a verb phrase that can also be a noun phrase, depending on what part of speech it is.
eg: I want to know what is this book about. (noun phrase)
When 'led me to' is used as a noun phrase, what is it the part of speech that it is a noun phrase of?

TheButler said: ↑
The fact that it could mean either does not indicate that it is either. It is grammatically a clause.
If the word "led" was the subject, it would clearly be a verb. If the word "to" was the subject, it would clearly be a verb.
The combination "led him to draw" can mean either "led him to think" or "led him to the actual drawing of a conclusion". The most probable meaning in the sentence is the former. This can also be demonstrated by the fact that the context of the passage relates to the gathering of information, and the formation of an opinion, by the detective.
Thanks for your reply. If I follow you, you are saying that in this sentence, "led him to draw the conclusion" is a verb phrase?
When 'led me to' is used as a noun phrase, what is it the part of speech that it is a noun phrase of? If 'led me to' is a noun phrase in the sentence 'I want to know what is this book about', what is the name of the noun phrase 'led me to'?
The noun phrase is simply the object of the preposition, in this case "about" (as in the following):
"I want to know what this book is about".
The phrase "what this book is about" is a noun phrase that refers to the content of the book.
Can you tell me what it is the noun phrase 'led me to' is referring to?
It is referring to the "content of the book". In other words, the "knowledge" that the book has, the "thing" it "is".
As far as the object, "what this book is about", is concerned, "about" is the preposition, and "knowledge" and "this book" are its objects.
You are right that I was not too clear. What I was asking is that if 'led me to' is a noun phrase in the sentence 'I want to know what is this book about', what is the name of the noun phrase 'led me to'? In other words, what is 'led me to' referring to?
There is no name. There is simply the phrase "what is this book about". The verb "to be" and its object "this book" are linked together by the preposition "about", which is equivalent to "concerning", "regarding" or "on".
What is the object of the preposition "about" in the following sentence?
"I don't know what to do about this problem."
Well, you have already answered that, haven't you?
What is the noun phrase 'led me to' referring to?
I have already said "the content of the book".

If 'I don't know what to do about this problem' is the object of the preposition 'about', does 'this problem' not form part of the noun phrase 'I don't know what to do about this problem'?

The novelist typed the final words of the manuscript on December 10, 1970, and marked it "FINIS." It was, for once, absolutely right: _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three_ was the end of it. The New York subway—the subject of all but three of the forty-six crime novels he had produced since the first one, _Death Wish,_ in 1972—was no longer viable as a setting. The books were still selling, but there was a growing sense of diminishing returns. Critics were less and less impressed with what were deemed perfunctory stories; characterization was increasingly sacrificed for plot. And the rabid fans who had packed his public readings as recently as 1972 were less and less interested in attending. He was, in short, out of ideas.
For all the attention paid to the 1974 film _Death Wish,_ it was the seventeenth novel Brown had written and the first that hit pay dirt—and perhaps even more remarkably, it was a sleeper. It was nominated for an Edgar, the award of the Mystery Writers of America; there were calls for it to be made into a movie, but it did not attract much critical attention until three years later, when a screenplay appeared. _Death Wish_ would prove to be the most popular and controversial book he ever wrote. While much attention has been paid to the film—which transformed the book into an explicit satire of gun-loving America—less notice has been given to the novel. It is an exciting, pacy book, written in an archly pared-down prose. Even though its roots go back to the 1930s and the novels of James M. Cain, _Death Wish_ also evinces Brown's familiarity with the works of the French crime novelist Frédéric Dard, particularly the Fred la Mayo series of paperbacks, _The Brain Goes Back to School_ (1966), _The Five Brains in the Pool_ (1966), and _The Brain Hangs Out_ (1966), published in America by the Graphic Press. The trilogy concerns a criminal mastermind who wakes from a coma with an IQ of 300, not all of it good. Brown was also a great fan of the comic books of Martin Goodman, later chairman of Marvel Comics, and it was perhaps this early exposure to a distillation of comic books that lay behind the stripped-down tautness of _Death Wish_ and its sequels.
In a way, the film was merely the last act of a great career in publishing. The British had had their day. The great explosion of the British New Wave, the overnight success of James Herbert, the extraordinary flourishing of the "crap"-shooters in the mid-seventies, all passed. Michael Moorcock died in the womb; his literary heirs failed to secure the deal on the distribution of their work. With Moorcock, Herbert, Brown, and John Lange, the British New Wave had seemed the way forward. In the event, none of these novels, particularly those written under the name of James Herbert, has aged well. But if the mid-seventies fad for horror novels was silly, even Brown's friends concede that _Death Wish_ is an unforgettable book. Its raw vigor echoes a more confident, less cautious period in publishing, when it was possible for books to become best sellers without the support of advertising. Even in America it was not unknown for readers to find a new author in their local library. Such was the case for _Death Wish_.
The quality of Brown's fiction began to decline in the seventies. This was perhaps unsurprising, given the violence of his break with Ballantine Books, but even the books he wrote during his tempestuous relationship with Random House founder Harry Evans showed a lack of focus. Having persuaded Random House to create a new house for his publishing, Evans Books, he attempted to replicate the Ballantine model, hiring editors from the publishing giant who had rejected him and paying them less. Of the five novels he wrote for Evans, only _The Snake,_ the first, and _Death Game,_ the third, could be considered successful. _The Snake,_ based on a six-page idea by a Texas fan, was so good that when Brown moved to Fawcett in 1975, he asked them to reprint the book as a two-dollar Fawcett Gold Medal special. To the end of his life, Brown called it the best book he ever wrote. It is indeed a wonderfully lean piece of work, one of his most claustrophobic and intense novels, a study in the psychology of paranoia and survival that ends with a stunning twist in the last line.
_The Snake_ and _Death Game_ are exceptional in Brown's fiction: as much as anything else, they belong to the pulp crime and horror novels of the fifties. But in a sense, Brown had made his peace with the British in the mid-seventies and had found a new way to make a living out of the subway. The next book he wrote, after _Death Wish,_ was _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three,_ which still sold in great numbers. It would become one of his most adapted films, but _The Taking of Pelham One Two Three_ is almost surrealist in its suspension of reality. The criminal, Bernard "Bug" Kaplan, is appalled by the public's casual misinterpretation of the title, which he thinks should be "The Taking of Pelham 2-3-4," the name of the actual train. He is an aficionado of the language, and of theater, and has much in common with Aramis, the criminal mastermind in the French graphic novel, in his conviction that crime and art are intertwined. Brown's choice of name— _Pelham One Two Three—_ evoked the location of the station on the Lexington Avenue line.
With _Murder on the Eighth Floor_ and _Cop Out,_ Brown began to revive the series he had started with _The Snake,_ about the two professional thieves Darryl and Terry. Both _Murder on the Eighth Floor_ and _Cop Out_ are thoroughly dismal works, and the film of _Cop Out_ (1978) was no better, though Robert Aldrich's direction gives the script some bounce. Yet Brown had found the new form he was looking for. There was still good, readable stuff in him, but at a time when people were beginning to take crime fiction seriously, it was no longer good enough.
One of the main themes of _Death Wish_ is one that Brown returned to obsessively in later novels: the thin line between crime and justice. In the book, Paul Kersey does not pretend that he is right, he does not even believe in a higher law, or his own actions. He knows that he is doing something wrong, yet he cannot stop himself, and each killing makes the next one more likely. At the end of the book, Kersey is held in a state of purgatory: he is neither completely guilty of murder, nor able to exonerate himself. Brown's admiration for Joseph Conrad is plain, in particular for the novel _Under Western Eyes._ Brown found _Under Western Eyes_ a highly constricting book, yet Kersey's moral torment echoes that of Razumov in the Conrad book. Both Razumov and Kersey are intelligent, reflective men who suffer under the pressure of conscience, each tortured by the dilemma of their actions. Like Razumov, Kersey tries to set right the wrong he has done, even to the point of destroying his family.
Kersey was an outsider, more comfortable with his instincts and imagination than with people, which makes his sudden and dramatic reaction to the brutal attack on his wife and daughter a stark contrast to his manner before the event. When the vicious attack occurs, he is tipped over the edge into a self-righteous terror. And in his search for justice, he becomes as much a part of the monster as the criminals who rob, rape, and murder.
Kersey's quest for justice is intensified by a further frustration. He is one of the few characters in Brown's fiction who is a complete failure at one of the things he does best: he is a miserable architect. In one sense, he is a contradiction in terms: a crime novelist who disliked violence. He was horrified by what he saw in _Death Wish,_ that it turned out to be the kind of novel that readers loved to see come true. In this regard, he was similar to his friend Michael Moorcock, who found his reputation as a "magician" thoroughly distasteful. The central character of Brown's _City of the Dead_ was, in

Deep in the ocean's abyss, where light and air and sunshine do not penetrate, is a most strange and curious plant, which grows and lives by drawing from its environments that which is of use to it. It has no roots, but instead, cables, long threadlike tendrils, which go out and search until they touch the sandy bottom. There are thousands of these tendrils, reaching and feeling around in the darkness, one on top of the other, some touching, some passing, but all feeling, searching, and straining for something to fasten to.
Then, when one of these cables feels what it needs, if only for a moment, something to hold to and draw strength from, it will clasp on and never let go. The rest will go out and search again. If another comes in contact with the same thing, it will grasp it also, and again the process goes on until every one of the cables has a firm hold on something. Then the cables get thicker and thicker and blossom like a beautiful rose, and they surround their object as a castle would its drawbridge.
When a breeze comes up or a wave strikes, the tendrils clasp tighter, and some more tendrils will grasp on to the clasping ones, if they happen to come in contact with them. And so on, until, if a big breeze or wave should come, the whole mass will be held as fast as a mountain might hold, or a huge castle.
There are in the ocean a thousand wonders, and strange things we cannot understand, and none is more strange than this plant which grows and lives on the bottom of the ocean, without light, and yet knows how to live. You cannot live without air and sunshine, but this strange thing does. And, if it lives in the darkness, it is also beautiful. When the sun is out it sends a beautiful color into the sea, and in the night, when the moon comes up, it sends a beautiful reflection in her light. But these are only its happy times; for many days and nights go by, and it clutches on for strength, while the sun and the moon do not even know it exists.
Now I have told you a story, and this strange plant is no more than a story, but it has a purpose.
There are many people in this world, who do not need to live in the light, who live their whole lives on the bottom of the ocean, grasping something for strength, but never bringing anything into the light that is worth while.
Some have good voices, and have the talent to sing, but never sing the right kind of songs.
Some have skill in painting, but have no conception of right and wrong, and paint things that would not do to look at, and which never help anyone to be good.
Some have ability in writing, and write books and poems, but are all wrong.
There are many, many who have talents of some kind or other, and bring them all to the wrong places. They think only of themselves, and forget to consider others.
All this is wrong. A talent is a gift of God. It is one of the things which we are given by the Great Father, that we may do something with it. It is not ours to do as we please with, but it is to be used and not abused. A talent is like a sturdy oak tree. If we plant it in the right place it will grow and become great and noble, a shelter and a guide for those who pass it by. But if we plant it in the wrong place, in a dry, arid, barren spot, it may grow there, but it will never be a grand old oak, with mighty branches and strong, wide-spreading roots. So it is with a talent. If we plant it in a dark, unproductive spot, and use it for selfishness, it may grow there, but it will never be a grand and useful talent. It will always remain weak and selfish, and all its growth will be used in selfish ends.
If we have talents we ought to use them. We cannot change them; we cannot throw them away, so why not put them in the right places and see how they will grow? We do not know what they may be, but we do know that, if we plant them in the right places, they will be strong, and we shall have the satisfaction of knowing that we have done our best with our talents.
The next time a sunbeam or moonbeam comes, and we are tempted to think we are so bright, let us think of that strange plant which is bright in the darkness of the sea. It shows that we can be bright without the sun or moon, and it helps us to know how we can be right in our lives, even in the absence of the sun and the moon. And if we are right in the absence of the sun and the moon, we may safely be right when they shine brightly upon us, and we will know that, no matter where we are, whether on the bottom of the ocean, or on the top of the earth, we have done our best with our talents, and that we are living up to our duties as children of the Great Spirit.

Maybe you feel like I do and have also decided to look for a way to answer your question: "How do I talk to someone after having a bad experience with them?"
I'm going to give you a sure-fire method that will help you talk to anyone without even asking one question of the person you want to ask.
How you can answer that question, "How do I talk to someone after having a bad experience with them?"
You need to realize one thing before you start. You need to realize that you are not going to be judged by the other person when you talk to them. That is a big one, and that is not what you think.
Now when you talk to someone you don't like after a bad experience you are making yourself feel better.
You are telling them that you are better than them.
In reality, they may be just as bad as you are or they may be worse. But you are not really talking to them, so you can't really tell if they are worse or not.
That is why you can't judge the other person.
You can't judge the person you are talking to by judging them based on what you have seen and heard.
In the eyes of the person you are talking to, you may be a great person.
If you are going to be judged by them, then you will lose the point of the conversation. If you lose the point of the conversation, then you are wasting your time.
So the question, "How do I talk to someone after having a bad experience with them?" becomes, "How do I talk to someone after having a bad experience with them without being judged?"
