The scientist's groundbreaking discovery challenged the established scientific theory and gained him the title of "father of the transistor" - a semiconductor device that changed the way the world produces, stores and transmits information.
The prize was awarded to the 95-year-old scientist during a ceremony at the Nobel Center in Stockholm. His wife and son were present at the ceremony, and they were congratulated by President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Professor Göran K. Hansson.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 was awarded to John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science”.
In a paper presented in the journal Nature, Professor Göran Hansson and the Nobel Committee said: "The three laureates have found different ways of following and exploiting the quantum state, even when the object being measured has been separated from the measurement apparatus. This breakthrough made it possible to explore a new kind of quantum mechanics in which reality does not exist until it is measured. This has helped to develop quantum computers and quantum encryption."
This year's winners, John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger, "have, along with colleagues, conducted fundamental studies of the so-called quantum entanglement, wherein two or more quantum objects can be linked in such a way that one quantum object can affect another quantum object even if they are separated by large distances".
The prize citation mentioned that "if you do the same experiment twice in a row, you will get the same result each time. This is a classical way of thinking about nature, based on cause and effect and basic predictability".
This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, followed by the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 3.
The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on October 7, and the winners of the prizes in literature, economics and serenity will be announced on October 10.
The committee mentioned that the studies conducted by John F. Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger were important steps in the development of quantum computing, as well as the development of quantum encryption.
“Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory in modern physics. In the middle of the last century, it was realized that quantum-mechanical phenomena could be used for information technology. In recent decades, quantum information science has paved the way for a new generation of quantum computers, the development of secure quantum encryption and a revolution in metrology. The three laureates have laid the foundation for this development”, the committee said.
“John F. Clauser and Alain Aspect have, along with colleagues, conducted fundamental studies of the so-called quantum entanglement, wherein two or more quantum objects can be linked in such a way that one quantum object can affect another quantum object even if they are separated by large distances. In the 1960s and 1970s, John Clauser and Stuart Freedman constructed an experiment to study whether two photons, which always behave like particles, could be entangled so that one photon could be used to transmit information about the other photon.
Alain Aspect performed the essential experiments at the beginning of the 1980s. However, it was not until 1982 that the rules of quantum mechanics were formulated with such clarity that their predictions could be tested experimentally. The quantum theory is thus regarded as the most powerful tool that humanity has for understanding many phenomena in modern physics.
“Anton Zeilinger and colleagues have, in the early 1990s, performed a series of experiments on entangled photons that were decisive for quantum information research. The experiments demonstrated that information can be encoded not only in the states of individual particles, but also in the relationships that particles have to each other.
This was followed by experiments that led to new insights about the nature of entangled states, to the so-called Bell-tests. Alain Aspect and colleagues and Robert A. Cowan and colleagues carried out important Bell-tests in the late 1980s.
In the 1990s and 2000s, Anton Zeilinger and colleagues developed Bell-tests to a high level of precision, but it was not until 2015 that the so-called loophole-free Bell-test was first performed, using entangled photons, by Delft University of Technology, the Netherlands. With the work of the laureates, the field of quantum information has made enormous strides. Today, practical quantum computers are nearing the horizon, and countless additional applications are being developed.
Quantum information is also used for revolutionary methods in the measurement of molecules and radiation", the committee mentioned.

The vintage car raced down the open highway. I found it to be more comfortable than my dentist's waiting room. I saw it as a good omen that I arrived back to the present, and in better shape than when I left.
My senses returned to normal levels. The techno-chill dance music no longer shook my fillings loose. I kept my smile tight. I hoped my invisible cosmetic dental work was passable. I was ready to dive back into the past.
My first stop was to visit a friend. He had returned to Seattle after a six-month trip to Asia.
The mysterious drugs placed my friend in the witness chair. I found a new drug delivery system. The drug turned a large area of the brain into a radar scanner. I directed the radar to detect the location of my friend.
"I'm here." He wasn't. He was nowhere to be found. The radar scanner told me where he lived, but not where he was living.
His neighbors told me they'd last seen my friend standing at the mailboxes. They assumed he was off to work at the post office, or perhaps on an early morning coffee run. They'd mistaken my friend for a postman.
It was still early.
I used the scanner to pinpoint the location of the coffee shop. I saw my friend at the counter, dressed in a postal worker's uniform. I shook my head in disapproval.
I entered the coffee shop. "Hey, Seymour."
He didn't hear me. His head was in the clouds. I walked up to the counter. I grabbed the coffee mug out of his hand. The acid stains burned my palm.
"You were better off making coffee for the post office."
He looked at me with a blank stare. He still had the wild look of a serial killer. He'd escaped from the psych ward, and was still on the run from the law. The coffee shop was on the most wanted list. The coffee shop owner was one of the finest criminal minds that ever lived. He'd done time at several institutions, including The White House.
The coffee shop owner was infamous for robbing the rich to give to the poor. He considered the government to be the rich, and deserved to be robbed. He created his own postal system to be able to deliver his ill-gotten goods to those in need.
The worst part was that my friend was the coffee shop owner's trusted sidekick. The trusted sidekick was like the minion of a super villain, but with a shifty grin, and a fondness for red bikinis.
"Give me my coffee." My friend grinned.
"That was some drug trip you were on. I'm back now."
"Not so fast."
I saw the grenade. He was going to shoot me for making a clean cup of coffee. I ran.

I found my friend unconscious at the coffee shop door. A vintage car passed by on the street. I'd seen it before. I was fairly certain it was the one that sent me through time.
He'd arrived from a different time. He'd slipped through the cracks in the fabric of the universe. He'd come to erase us from existence.
I rushed into action. I grabbed my friend, and raced him into the car. I put him in the back seat. I drove away before he could awake. I was aware of the vintage car's actions.
I sped to the airport. I hid the car, and hopped a flight to New York. The last time I was there was in the mid 1980's. Things had changed in a big way.
My friend woke up. The medical pills weren't working fast enough to control his actions. He ran down the street. He saw a young woman walking down the sidewalk. He chased her.
The woman turned to see who was chasing her. She saw my friend. She ran faster. He chased her.
He caught up to the woman. He knocked her to the ground. He straddled the woman's chest. He slapped her cheeks.
The woman screamed for help. I rushed over to help her.
"Get off of me." She threw him off. I'd found her weapon.
"What were you going to do with that?" I asked her.
"I don't know." She replied. "I'd probably use it on you."
My friend woke up. He took off after her. I started to run after my friend.
The vintage car stopped me. The car gave off a dangerous vibe. I recognized the murderer in the driver's seat. I also saw the ice cream, or rather the murder weapon.
The vintage car went full throttle. The car passed my friend. The vintage car made the turn at the corner.
I ran after the vintage car. I saw my friend at the cross walk. The vintage car sped away.

Exploring the depths of the ocean reveals an extraordinary wealth of marine life and incredible landscapes, and those willing to take a deep dive can find fascinating locations worldwide.
This is the journey of the Galapagos Aggressor, a liveaboard vessel exploring the waters around the islands of Galapagos, in Ecuador. Scuba divers are welcomed onboard the ship which offers a range of fantastic dive sites, including spots for advanced divers.
Divers can explore a wide range of dive sites around the islands. The Galapagos Aggressor takes dives of two tank dives to the maximum depth of 130 ft (40 m). The ship makes six dives per day, and some spots only allow for one tank dives due to their depth.
The ship is a large liveaboard and is decked out with everything you could need for an unforgettable diving experience. The cabins include ensuite bathrooms and are split over three decks. All rooms have air-conditioning, TV and DVD. The dining room offers a wide range of cuisine, catering for those with special dietary requirements.
The main deck contains a salon, library and dining room with large windows. The onboard video system means you can see the incredible marine life even when you’re not on a dive. There’s also a spacious sun deck complete with sun loungers, and an onboard gym. The ship is a tech friendly vessel, and divers are provided with a PCR laptop and cameras for underwater photography.
Galapagos is one of the best diving destinations in the world and features a large range of marine life. The area has not been exposed to pollution or damage, and its waters are home to a wide range of fish and sea life. Galapagos has wrecks and reefs, and even seamounts.
Divers can enjoy colourful corals and an abundance of marine life. Frogfish, sea horses, dolphins and schools of hammerhead sharks are all common. Diving Galapagos can be a thrilling experience, and is a wonderful way to get to know one of the most unique and beautiful areas on the planet.
The Galapagos Aggressor is the perfect place to explore the deep, and dive a host of spots in the area. The diving offers a wide range of experiences from reefs, swim-throughs and pinnacles, to seamounts, shipwrecks and caves. It’s a fascinating adventure, and an exciting opportunity to dive some of the best spots in the world.
The most famous dive site in Galapagos is Kicker Rock. It’s a rock in the shape of a shoe, rising out of the water and reaching up to 130 ft (40 m) above sea level. There is a huge colony of marine birds nesting here. The site is the best place to see large schools of hammerhead sharks, as well as sea lions, dolphins, turtles, barracuda and snappers.
The Aggressor dive sites are spread out across the Galapagos region. Dive sites around San Cristobal Island include Cerro Brujo, Kicker Rock and Punta Pitt. For the more advanced divers, the Lion’s Hill dive offers an exploration of depths up to 130 ft (40 m). Santa Cruz Island boasts one of the best dive spots around, Cousins Rock. The Galapagos Aggressor also takes divers to Punta Carrión and Sea Lion Rock, both home to large schools of hammerhead sharks. Bartolomé is another famous spot, and takes divers to its reefs and rocky pinnacles.
Further out, there is Darwin Island, one of the most famous sites in Galapagos, known for its schools of hammerheads. The Western Isles region, which is home to Fernandina Island and Pinta Island, boasts some great sites such as Cousins Rock and Lava Flow.
Diving Galapagos is an adventure that offers spectacular sights and experiences. Divers should be aware that there are strong currents in the area, so the experience isn’t for everyone. The Galapagos Aggressor provides an excellent opportunity to explore the area and access some of the best spots. The Galapagos Aggressor offers a once in a lifetime adventure.

The winding path through the mountains offered little reprieve from the sun's relentless assault. Icara's party, led by the barbarian Thramark and his wife Morg, seemed to be following a trail that was at once footpath and drainage ditch. The party followed the wide, baked swath that marked the trail as long as the baked mud offered some measure of shade.
The journey grew harder with each step. The endless miles of dusty trail and constant sun had sapped the party's strength. Several of them had fallen, unable to continue. They were far from fresh or hungry—yet they trudged on.
Behind them trailed a young man of just seventeen summers. He wore dark leathers and carried a slender blade. The young man's face was gaunt and his eyes were full of hard, burning determination. His hair was tangled and sun-bleached, his skin brown and reddened by the sun. From his back and shoulders dangled a scimitar—the ruined tail of a beast he had slain months before.
The dwarf Baryth led the charge. The blacksmith carried a set of ornate keys and the weight of the dragon-slayers' heritage upon his shoulders. He looked every bit the dwarf, his arms swung from his short stature, his beard wound tightly back from his square chin and eyes that gleamed with the mischievous fire of battle. In his right hand he clutched a gargantuan mace, its massive head studded with runes of fire.
A half-dozen bowmen surrounded the pair of humans and dwarf, their bows drawn and at the ready. These men were mercenaries, drawn from the ranks of the King's army by Baryth, who was known throughout these lands as the finest blacksmith in Icara.
Thramark crested a low ridge and surveyed the jagged peaks that surrounded the party. "We cannot return," he whispered.
"No," said Baryth, "we must press on."
Thramark nodded and crested the hill, signaling for the party to follow.
Following the dwarf and his vanguard of mercenaries, the barbarian pressed forward along a trail of broken stone. The path was ancient and much of it had been washed away. The arrows of the mercenaries sank deep into the ground ahead of them. The ground was rough and shifting beneath their feet. The stones were perilous and broken—the result of thousands of years of winters and floods.
Thramark followed the mercenaries down the jagged path. Beneath his feet the ground seemed to shift and give way, but the barbarian pressed on. Thramark knew this path—these were the edges of Squirreling Forest, and in the midst of this strange landscape a small temple had once stood.
The land here was barren, pocked with geysers and sinkholes, studded with stones and honeycombed with the tunnels of the squirrelfolk. It was a treacherous and bizarre environment. The thought of reaching the temple and finding safety there—even if only for a day—had kept Thramark on his feet and pushing ahead. He would risk anything to reach safety and safety, Thramark knew, was found in that ancient temple.
The land changed and the water turned warm. Thramark felt something stir inside him, as if he had stepped upon sacred ground. The wind stirred and the dust flew in gusts like smoke. Thramark looked around and saw that the strange forest had begun to encroach on the path. The trees shifted and stalked, moving ever closer to the trail.
He heard a guttural shriek, and he turned. He saw one of the men-at-arms, a man he knew to be a strong swordsman. Thramark saw the man's knee begin to bend backward, bone screaming in protest.
Without thinking, Thramark charged forward, swinging his broadsword. As he moved, the ground seemed to shudder and a rumble filled the air. The barbarian raised his blade and brought it down upon the ground—striking hard into the rock. The blade shattered against the ground and the world shifted and seemed to darken.
When the world stopped shifting, the men-at-arms were gone. The ground was smoking and steaming, as if struck by lightning. Thramark looked around—he and his companions were alone. The whole of Squirreling Forest had surrounded them, cutting off their escape. It was as if the squirrelfolk had swarmed from every corner of the forest, suddenly appearing in the surrounding terrain.
"Get down," Baryth shouted. The party fell to the ground, the bowmen darting for cover behind rocks and boulders.
Morg grasped the mace in her hands and called out, "I stand."
Baryth cursed, "The ground is weak, it will collapse—"
"I stand!" Morg shouted, pointing the mace at the surrounding trees. "The blast is coming!"
The dwarf looked at Thramark, "Cover your ears."
The barbarian complied and as he did, Morg screamed and the sky seemed to open in a surging wave of golden light. The world shuddered and a wave of darkness passed. When the barbarian opened his eyes, he saw that Morg was gone.
"How long?" Thramark asked, his mind grappling for control.
"Five minutes," said Baryth, "after that they will be upon us."
Thramark looked around and saw that Baryth's eyes were full of tears. The dwarf was overcome by loss.
"We will not die here," Thramark said, remembering Morg, his wife, his partner.
The barbarian grasped his fallen blade and rose.
"Cover your ears," Baryth said.
"Not yet," Thramark said.
As he stood, the barbarian turned and he saw them, in the distance.
The squirrelfolk were upon them.

MORG, TREASURER OF THE FORTRESS, slung her crossbow over her shoulder and steeled her grip upon the chain-wrapped handle of her mace. The house she called home was in turmoil, the dust stirring in thick clouds. A decade's worth of treasures were packed tightly into a wagon—the booty of thirty sieges and a hundred battles—the spoils of a thousand conquests. It was the greatest treasure ever known to mankind.
Her lover, Thramark, the barbarian, stood at her side. He was sweating and his arms shook. The great beast that he had slain, the dragon's ruined tail, dragged in the dust behind him. A satchel, empty and filled with nothing more than a worn, cloth map, lay at his feet. It was one of the dragon's hoards and it was the last of their loot. All that remained was the world's most valuable treasure, the Singing Blade—the most precious sword in all of Icara.
Thramark picked up the satchel and looked into it, as if seeing his home for the last time. He could barely speak, his throat and lips were caked with dry, crusted blood.
"Thramark?" Morg said, "It's time to go."
He looked up, a dazed look upon his face. "I am ready."
Morg looked around at the treasures, now nearly gone. It seemed impossible that this treasure could have come to this, that this—all of it—had been given to her. They had managed to steal all of this loot, they had slaughtered a dragon—one of the greatest of the Age of the Dragon—but the treasure was going nowhere. "I am sorry," Morg said. She had learned that from Thramark, a man of few words, a man whose strength was matched only by his vulnerability. She touched his hand and he turned and nodded.

"Because we must," Morg had replied.

"Yes," Morg had said, "because he asks it of me."

The old librarian discovered a forgotten letter between the pages of an old book in the library.

At the world's most awkward family reunion, the entertainment is a mind-reading machine that knows what its customers want to hear.
I Was There! I Don't Care About You!
I have news. The reviews from Edinburgh are in, and the touring production of The Book of Mormon did not get good notices. From the reviews I’ve read, I can safely say that, while I disagree with all of them, they are written with a polite, respectful humor that doesn’t quite match the production’s.
The show’s a flop, of course. But not quite the hit it was at the Eugene O’Neill. Now in Los Angeles and rolling into San Francisco and DC, it’s not selling out, and the posters are already down on the Tube stations. How could it be anything else? We’re in the middle of a recession, and the show itself is antagonistic to religion, an expensive ticket (for London standards), and a very specific, high-spirited brand of humor that by definition will play to some but not all audiences. It didn’t matter that I loved it.
In fairness, the show seems to be a textbook example of critics following the consensus. Of the seventeen critics I’ve found who reviewed it, twelve gave it some form of rave, three rated it favorably, and two thought it was good, though they weren’t sure why. Only one, the most up-to-the-moment of them all, gave it a completely negative review. To their credit, they acknowledge they might be wrong, as it is such a popular show, but they are mostly defensive. The chief argument against the show, in terms of reviews, seems to be “It doesn’t have the same magic as when it first premiered.”
Of course, the thing about theater is that it doesn’t need magic, and while I was watching The Book of Mormon, I didn’t miss it at all. It’s actually rare that I ever walk out of a musical and go “You know, that was amazing,” because the miraculous feels too much like magic, and is usually done as part of a too-slick show that doesn’t have a lot else to say. When I walked out of The Book of Mormon, I went “You know, I like this show. I can’t wait to tell my friends.” Which may be one of the best compliments I can give, because it means I’ll be able to be snarky about it.
As with anything else, though, there’s a difference between what it is and what it’s trying to do. And what it is is a frenetic, relentless musical that constantly has you on the edge of your seat. The show follows two naïve Mormon missionaries who get sent to a dangerous part of Africa and their struggle to get past the local tribe’s distrust of the Mormons. The entire set-up, as one character explains, is so that they can get through the indoctrination necessary to be Mormons, and it’s packed with clever but easy to follow references to the religious con, and some very entertaining songs.
Most of the songs are sung by two members of the tribe, Nabulungi (Taylor Iman Jones) and her friend, Pumas (Cody Jamison Strand). They’re an entirely invented character, whose songs echo the values of the show as well as traditional Broadway as a whole. “Sal Tlay Ka Siti” is an entire story told with choreography and a song, very much a throwback to the golden age of showmanship. “Turn it Off” is the catchiest tune I’ve heard in years, sung by a very funny J. Anthony Crane as Mafala Hatimbi, the colonel of the Ugandan military, who wants to kill the two Mormons. But perhaps my favorite song is “Hasa Diga Eebowai,” sung by Nabulungi, wherein she asks if she can hear all the wrong things about God, and Elders Eaton and Cunningham quickly deny this, and Nabulungi then goes on to list all the things that are wrong about God.
Some of the songs are very catchy, others surprisingly clever, and the entire production is a delight. The sets are ingeniously constructed, the dancing is excellent and at times daring (if a little too close to the audience at points), the actors are amazingly good. If there is a weakness in the show, it is that at times it comes close to overstaying its welcome, at times too relentless for its own good. The momentum can slow down, and every now and then it seems to be stretching just a bit too far to maintain its own self-respect, and that comes when it seems to be putting in padding to get to its conclusion. I also don’t think they quite know what they’re trying to say, if anything.
But then, when a show’s so much fun, it hardly matters. The Book of Mormon isn’t trying to make sense or send a message. It’s not trying to say anything profound or change your life. It’s a very cleverly written musical, full of good songs and excellent acting. It’s a blast.
Which is exactly why I disagree with those critics who think it’s not as good as the first time they saw it. It’s not meant to be the kind of show that changes your life and forces you to think about the human condition, because its primary strengths are its production values, its cast, and its humor. I don’t think a show that ends with an act of genocide and the mutilation of a young girl as she’s dragged away can be written that way. That, to me, is a criticism of its ambition, which is both high and admirable, and that’s not really what the show is about.
I'm an amateur theater critic who lives in the South Bay of Silicon Valley. I've been writing about theater since I was about eleven, when I figured out the magic of hyperlinks and starting putting up amateur reviews of local theater. I'm an actor in the area (and no, I'm not as bad as you think I am), I'm a software developer, and my ultimate goal in life is to someday see The Book of Mormon.

An alien visiting Earth for the first time becomes obsessed with knitting, eventually starting a new business to help the inhabitants of the planet stitch up their wounded psyche.
The Craft and art of the Fleisher MFA Show 2019
Knitting is a handicraft, a time honored practice which has been passed down from mother to daughter for hundreds of years. In this series I have challenged this tradition and brought this feminine, domestic craft into the street, a male dominated space, where it has been seen as an anomaly. By combining the contrasting worlds of yarn craft and street art, I have brought these two practices together, connecting traditional craft, something which is learned by repeating the same movements time and time again, with street art, something which is constantly changing and evolving as it deals with the modern world. Through this juxtaposition I have created a space where the viewer must reconcile these two worlds and confront the reality of their existence, both as a craft, and as a technique for communication.
In 1993, Grafton, NZ born Christopher Ruck was very happy to escape the “sheep infested” city of his youth and move to Canada to study film production. In 2002 Christopher, at the age of 27, entered the workforce as an editor at CBC.
Although Christopher had a steady job, a loving wife, and two beautiful daughters, he was not happy. After 15 years of editing for news organizations Christopher made the leap to fine art photography.
Since Christopher first dabbled with a digital camera in 2009, he has been studying photography at all levels, and in 2014 received his bachelor’s in Photographic Arts at OCAD University.
In his short time in the photography world Christopher has had solo exhibitions in Canada, the US, and France. In 2016 he participated in the ‘Biennale Internationale de l’Art Contemporain’ in Bordieres, France and in 2018 he took part in the ‘Yellow House Festival’, taking home the Bourse d’Excellence in the Panelled Exhibition.
In the last year Christopher has been involved in multiple international artist residencies, working with a variety of photographic media, and has been teaching photography since 2014.

The first snowfall of the year blanketed the town in a sheet of white. The second day of snow drew out crowds for snowball fights and sledding down Hester Street Hill, leaving behind a new layer of fluffy snow.
The snow brought the beloved Christmas Festival from Dec. 1 to Dec. 2. Many local artists and crafters sold their holiday products and creations in the Municipal Complex. Everyone was invited to pick up a warm cup of hot cocoa and take a walk through the glowing, decorated park.
“The craft fair, the lights and the Christmas parade were the highlights for my children,” Matt Anderegg, Bloomfield resident said.
Dec. 2 was a chance for children to come to the Bloomfield United Methodist Church for the Christmas cookie walk. The cookie walk is a fundraiser for the church. Tickets are sold for $5, and people select their own variety of cookies.
The cookie walk is set up like a cookie buffet; cookies are grouped by variety. The cookies are homemade and grouped by weight, so you can pick up as many as you can carry. Tickets are for sale at the Bloomfield United Methodist Church, Church Boutique and Gift Shop, State Farm Insurance offices, Ben Franklin store, Mainstreet Market, Community State Bank, Bloomfield Library, Happy Home Cooking, Spalding County Chamber of Commerce and Ager’s Garden. The baked goods will be available for purchase on Saturday, Dec. 2.
“Our entire community is invited to celebrate the Christmas season with us. We will have coffee and hot chocolate, a cookie walk and baked goods,” Beth Hanlin, chairman of the church’s outreach committee said.
Food was also on sale at the Annual Christmas Parade on Dec. 2. Bloomfield FFA members sold concessions, such as hot dogs, nachos and chips. The concession stands, located at both entrances of Town Square Park, kept the children and adults warm as they waited to be dazzled by the decorated floats and the entertaining activities.
In the parade, one of the best-known floats in Bloomfield is the vintage fire truck. Local resident Lamar Hutcheson owned a truck company in Alabama. He bought an antique fire truck with the money he made from his business. Hutcheson passed away in 1989 and gifted the truck to the City of Bloomfield.
The city restored the truck and presented it as a float in the Christmas parade.
“It takes a lot of hard work to restore and maintain the truck,” Billy Williams, Bloomfield fire chief said. “We will have to replace the water hoses, add new paint, put new tires on and make the lights brighter.”
Williams said the truck will not only be in the parade.
“It is the Bloomfield Fire Department’s mission to not only put the fire truck in the Christmas parade, but to put the truck out on the streets during the Christmas Festival.”
The Bloomfield High School Band also put on a show for the crowd. The band’s performance was choreographed with dance performances, the firetruck float and a variety of beautifully decorated floats.
Following the parade, some local businesses were lit up by Christmas trees. The Christmas in Bloomfield float entry was also decorated with lights. The decorations were donated by Vick’s Lighting and Christmas in Bloomfield decorated the tree.
The Bloomfield Christmas Festival is always in the first weekend of December. Everyone is encouraged to bring their children to the Christmas Parade and Town Square Park to join in on the activities.
Bloomfield United Methodist Church to host Christmas cookie walk
Bloomfield will be filled with the sounds and sights of the holiday season Dec. 1 and Dec. 2 as the town hosts its Christmas Festival and Holiday Parade.
Each year, the Bloomfield United Methodist Church Women and Outreach Committee host the cookie walk at the church, located at 105 W. Spring St. The cookie walk will take place from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Dec. 2.
“The cookie walk is a lot of fun,” Jennifer Moore, head of the committee, said. “We have a lot of fun doing this and look forward to this time of the year.”
The cookie walk has been a long-time tradition at the church, but the committee has been trying to make it even more successful. Moore said that the United Methodist Women members will bake the cookies from scratch to make sure they are fresh.
Each year, the committee purchases new cookie sheets to be used to display the different cookie varieties. The baked goods will be arranged according to the types of cookies, and the best part is that patrons can pick their own cookies from the trays.
Moore said the cookie walk is a way for people to give back to the church. The committee and women of the church help plan the cookie walk and donate their time to the cause. They say that the event is also a great way for the community to come together.
The cookie walk is a great opportunity for people to purchase some great-tasting cookies, support the church and support their local community.
“The cookie walk is a special time for the community and the church,” Moore said. “It is important to keep the tradition going.”
There are also several other events scheduled during the weekend of Dec. 1-2, including the annual Christmas Parade, the Christmas Open House and other activities at the Bloomfield Town Square.
For more information about the cookie walk, contact Jennifer Moore at (912) 659-7117.
The Bloomfield United Methodist Church and Outreach Committee will host a cookie walk from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Dec. 2.
Santa to bring cheers to Bloomfield
Santa Claus is coming to Bloomfield this Saturday!
In conjunction with the Bloomfield Christmas Parade, Santa Claus will be available to hear the holiday wishes of children. Santa will be located at the North end of the Town Square Park beginning at 11:30 a.m. Saturday. Children can tell Santa what they would like for Christmas, and parents can take pictures. There will be no charge for having Santa’s picture taken.
The parade is also a chance for children to write letters to Santa. Following the parade, letters to Santa will be collected at the Bloomfield Public Library. Letters will be forwarded to Santa Claus in a timely manner.

The parade will also feature several floats. Some of the floats will be themed with Christmas decorations, while others will be tied to the parade theme, “Christmas in Bloomfield.” The parade is sponsored by the Bloomfield Chamber of Commerce, which invites everyone in the community to participate. The judges will award a first-place prize of $100, second-place prize of $75, third-place prize of $50 and honorable mention prizes of $25.
Vehicles, floats, walking groups and other entries must be a minimum of 6 feet wide and 10 feet long. There is no limit on the number of people who participate in the parade, and walkers will be available at the park to direct traffic. There will also be an announcer to let everyone know the names of the floats and other participants.
For more information, call the Chamber at (912) 659-6613 or email to bloomfieldcoc@gmail.com.
Parade registration forms are also available at City Hall and online at www.spaldingchamber.org.

On a distant planet, scientists discover a lake, not unlike our own. It’s the color of aquamarine, shimmering in the light, rippling beneath a soft breeze. What they don’t know is that the lake, its water and bottom, is laced with a form of copper, one not found on Earth.

Wandering through the old city, one finds oneself absorbed by the splendor of the copper-domed shrines and tombs, the maze of caravansaries and mosques, the beauty of the palaces and the bazaars. Around every corner in the ancient Persian city of Shiraz, new treasures await. It is a place like no other.
Shiraz was one of my favorite cities in Iran and it was easy to see why so many poets and artists have been inspired by this beautiful city. We spent a couple of days in Shiraz before heading to Persepolis. While most visitors may only explore a few of the most notable sites, I prefer to see what I can while I am in a city. In this post, I will go over the best places to visit in Shiraz.
Shiraz is known as the city of poetry, as many of the famous poets in Iran such as Hafez and Saadi were born in Shiraz. In fact, many houses in Shiraz were the homes of poets in ancient times, and while they are now museums, you can go inside and see the walls covered in the famous poetry of the residents.
In addition to being a poetry-loving city, Shiraz is known for its gardens and flowers. Shiraz is actually the Persian word for rose, and the city is a hub for rose-scented products.
If you are looking for great places to visit in Shiraz, check out these top things to do in Shiraz, Iran.

One of the most impressive buildings in Shiraz is the Karim Khan Citadel, which dates back to the 18th century. It is a small citadel, but it is still one of the most important landmarks in Shiraz.
The citadel was built by the Zand dynasty in the 18th century, and it has been used as a military base, a prison, and even a movie studio. The building was damaged in an earthquake in 1778, and it was restored in the 19th century.

Whispered secrets of the forest are not what they seem.
“Mother,” Brynn’s mum said.
“Yes, dear?” I responded in our long-standing role play.
“I don’t want to go to England for the summer vacation,” she said.
“Why?” I asked, now playing the oblivious parent to her predicament.
“The Elders are going to meet.”
“That’s right. It’s been years since they last met. The prophecy is coming true. Your father, the Elders, and I will be away.”
I expected her response and had prepared a set answer. “The best way to show your support is to continue living your life as usual. We are strong and smart. We will always find a way to solve our problems.”
“But what if we can’t? I feel so helpless. We are going to lose everything we have.”
“It’s okay. It’s all going to work out. Do you understand me?”
I must’ve sounded like every parent in the world. I felt my inner voice struggle to get my attention. It wouldn’t go away. I ignored it. It persisted.
“Mother,” Brynn said again.
“Yes,” I answered. She was speaking too softly for me to hear. I leaned in, cupping my hand over her mouth.
“Mother, the sirens are calling again,” Brynn said.
“I hear them.”
“We should take refuge in the garden. This house is too old to be safe. The sirens might call us into the water.”
“Brynn, listen to me.” I cupped my hands around my mouth, the most effective way to get her attention when I spoke to her. “If the sirens call us, we will go to the garden.”
Brynn nodded. “That’s the plan.”
“Now, be a good girl and get ready for your picnic.”
I kissed her and left for work, knowing the sirens were calling, but I kept thinking of the fresh flowers in my garden. I kept thinking of what would happen if Brynn and I weren’t together. The sirens wanted me. It was my fate.
I knew this was our last summer together. I had felt this deep down for months. Now I was sure of it. The sun began its ascent into the sky. I was heading home from work. The sky was slowly turning pink as my car pulled into the driveway. The driveway was dark and unkempt. The forest was dead. Everything was dead. The sky was eating the sun. All I could hear were the sirens calling. I ran inside the house.
“Mother,” Brynn said as I reached the door.
“They are calling. We have to go to the garden. This house isn’t safe.”
“You’re right.” I didn’t have to reassure her. “Now get your sister. We’re going to the garden.”
“Get the kids. It’s time to leave. If we stay any longer, we won’t survive. We’re leaving right now.”
Brynn nodded. “Okay, Mom.”
“You have to understand me,” I said. I had learned how to make my thoughts clear, but it was a hard process. It was like writing in graffiti.
I took off my black boots and crossed the forest, moving farther away from the house. The leaves of the trees were dead and had begun to form puddles of water. All I heard were the sirens calling. I remembered this from the last time the sirens called me. I tried to move quickly so I could find Brynn and the kids. I got farther and farther from the house. Brynn and the kids never showed up.
“Mother, are you okay?” Brynn’s voice sounded miles away.
“I’m in the garden.”
“Hurry up,” she said.
I found a half-eaten strawberry at the end of the garden. I searched everywhere in the forest, in the garden, but there were no signs of Brynn and the kids. I called out to them, but no one answered. I lay down in the grass and watched the sun as the sky swallowed it. I didn’t know what to do.
Then I heard the voices of the sirens. They were in my garden. I could hear them singing.
All I want is your eyes, your body, your kiss.
I thought I was ready to see them again. I felt I was ready to be called by the sirens. But I hadn’t expected their beautiful voices to cut me to the bone, like some sort of poison. I wanted to kiss them, but I also wanted to run.
Then I remembered Brynn’s voice. She was somewhere in this forest. I felt like I needed to get back to her, but I didn’t know where to start. The sirens were singing again. Their songs were confusing me. I couldn’t help but fall in love with them. I fell asleep. The last thing I remember was the sun sinking into the water.
I dreamt of the ocean. The water was calm, and the fish were swimming happily. I felt peaceful and content. I felt at peace. I didn’t know why I felt so much contentment. I felt like I was being called by a higher power.
The sirens were singing again. I heard their song and wanted to be with them forever. I fell asleep again, but the dream became more peaceful. I wanted to go back to the ocean. I wanted to be a siren forever.
My eyes fluttered open. I saw Brynn, my daughter, standing in front of me. She was holding a beautiful bouquet of flowers. I got up and hugged her. I didn’t want to lose her ever again.
“Brynn, I love you,” I said. “I’ve missed you so much.”
“I’ve missed you, too. I’ve been looking for you everywhere.”
“Brynn, I need you to do me a favor.”
“Brynn, you have to do this for me. You have to understand me. Please, please, please.”

“Mom, what’s going on?”
“You have to understand me. You have to do this for me. I’m begging you.”
“Mom, what’s wrong with you? What are you talking about? What are you asking me to do?”
“Please, Brynn. Please.”
“Please, Mom. Please, Mom.”

The decision to embark on a solo travel adventure leads to life-changing experiences in places around the world.
Although solo travel in itself can be extremely empowering, the experiences and people that solo travelers have brought to their lives is what really impacts them the most.
We spoke to female solo travelers across the globe to find out about their journeys and their experiences with Solo Travel Society to learn what motivated them to take this big step to travel alone.
Who is the solo traveler?
Jenna is a 28-year-old from Ontario, Canada. She first traveled solo when she was 20 years old, having signed up for an excursion through a Toronto-based company for a two-week trip to Costa Rica.
Jenna said she’d always felt a strong desire to travel and even as a child, she was fascinated by the idea of exploring other parts of the world. She found herself spending a lot of time on the internet looking at maps and cities.
“I’d leave my laptop unattended at home and find things online,” she told us, adding that the internet allowed her to be anywhere in the world without being there.
With that in mind, Jenna took the plunge and spent time planning her first solo travel adventure. Although she didn’t immediately feel confident in the decision to go alone, she felt excited and knew that she wanted to pursue solo traveling in the future.
What inspired her to go alone?
“What first started as a weekend trip to NYC (New York City), it really just turned into something much more,” Jenna explained.
Jenna said that she was working on her own business and working a lot of overtime at a job she didn’t particularly like. This left her feeling like she needed a change, and her weekend trip to New York City provided that.
“I was very much in the thick of things at work, and then my boss quit and I was left with this time off. I was like, ‘Alright, I guess it’s time for me to go see the world.’”
Jenna said the choice to go was an easy one. She had saved up enough money for the trip, and she had no family or friends in the area. It also gave her an opportunity to try something new and to make new friends.
“I had never really had much time to explore on my own, so it was a new experience,” Jenna explained.
What was her first solo travel adventure like?
Jenna’s first trip was to New York City, which she had been planning for a few years. She had planned to take a one-week trip, but ended up staying for three.
“I stayed in a hostel in Brooklyn and met some amazing people who were also solo travelers. I learned so much about the city, the people, and the culture.”
Jenna also had a great time exploring the city, and she was pleasantly surprised by how friendly people were and how easy it was to meet people.
“I felt so welcomed and comfortable with everyone I met. It was a great experience,” Jenna said.
How did she prepare for her trip?
Jenna spent time researching her trip and learning about the city she was going to visit. She also looked at travel guides and asked around for advice on where to stay and what to see.
“I also looked at TripAdvisor and found some interesting things to do. It was just a fun way to get around and meet new people. I didn’t have any trouble getting around and I felt really comfortable there.”
How did she overcome her fears and doubts?
Jenna said that it wasn’t easy at first, but she learned to trust herself.
“There were definitely moments where I felt like I couldn’t do it, but I just pushed through,” she said.
Jenna said she felt confident in her ability to handle herself and that she wasn’t afraid of what was ahead of her.
“It was just so exciting,” she said. “I felt like I could do anything I wanted.”
How did Solo Travel Society help her on her journey?
“The staff was super helpful and encouraging, which was really great,” Jenna said.
“I had a lot of questions and they answered them all. The staff was also very friendly and made me feel at home.”
What advice does she have for other solo travelers?
Jenna said that she would recommend planning a trip with friends first and then going solo.
“I would tell them that they can go and have a great time,” she said.
“I think it’s so important to make new friends and meet new people. It’s so easy to be in a bubble, but when you go and meet new people you’ll be surprised at how much you can learn.”
Jenna said that she was so excited to get back to the place she’d been and that it was a great feeling.
“I just feel so much better about myself and who I am,” she said. “I’m so happy that I made the decision to go and I would definitely do it again.”
Read more about Jenna’s solo travel experiences at Jenkosworld.com.
Isabel is a 36-year-old freelance writer and photographer who has been traveling for the past five years.
She first traveled alone to New York City in 2012 for the Women’s March on Washington.
“I always wanted to go to NYC, but I never thought I’d get there on my own,” Isabel explained.
Isabel said that the march had been something she wanted to do for years, and she finally decided to take the plunge and book the trip on her own.
“I’d never been to New York before, so I didn’t know what to expect,” she explained. “It was just the first time I’d ever been to the city and I wanted to be there when it happened.”
What inspired her to go solo?
Isabel said that she had wanted to travel alone for years, but she had never actually done it before.

During the world's quietest concert, the audience realizes the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
During the world’s quietest concert, the audience realizes the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
During the world's quietest concert, the audience realizes that the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
Their voices faded to whispers, their senses calmed and their breathing slowed. Now, the audience of roughly 200 people sat quietly, eyes closed, as the orchestra began to play.
For the next 45 minutes, the musicians performed in near silence, creating music with few words — and maybe fewer sounds. The vibration of the bass echoed through the room, but the crowd never heard a note.
“We tend to identify music with sound, but sound is just a byproduct of music,” said composer Jason Treuting, who joined composer Adam Sliwinski to perform the world’s quietest concert in New York City on Friday. “When you’re not aware that you’re hearing anything, you’re acutely aware of this other body.”
For the first time, SONOS Studio in New York City hosted the Composers Concert series. The two-hour show, now on tour, featured music from Treuting and Sliwinski, Yo-Yo Ma and So Percussion.
Each performance was part of a larger experience that featured ambient noise and darkness. The audience wore blindfolds to adjust to the dimness, according to the website.
“This is our first time presenting these three pieces in New York, so we’re going to take our time and really dig into them,” said John Bence, curator of the series and executive producer of SONOS Radio. “We really wanted to create an experience that would inspire and allow our audience to reflect.”
The event was part of the Composers Concert series, which SONOS launched in 2016 to showcase new music.
Bence said the series is a “window” into the artists and their work. In addition to the pieces performed by Treuting and Sliwinski, a work by so-called ‘silent’ musician Bobby McFerrin, who is also on tour, was featured.
“Our concerts feature artists who have a strong connection to our community, but we also want to bring a unique view to the New York concert experience,” Bence said.
He added: “These concerts are a great opportunity for New Yorkers to experience the wonderful world of music through composers who are not always represented on our airwaves.”
For those who attended the show, it was an experience that was “a little eerie, a little enlightening and very beautiful,” said Robert Kastenbaum, who attended the concert.
“I think it was a real pleasure to be able to go and experience the music in that kind of environment,” he said. “I thought it was really wonderful.”
Kastenbaum, 59, had never experienced the concert series, but said he’s always been a fan of modern music.
He added: “I just think it’s such a treat to be able to see these people in person, as opposed to hearing them on a recording.”
In addition to the concert, the series also included an interview with Treuting and Sliwinski about the performance. The two performers spoke about the compositions, their creative process and how they have evolved as artists over the years.
They also shared some thoughts on the future of the music industry and its impact on the concert experience.
“We’re in the middle of a musical renaissance,” Treuting said. “What we’re seeing is that the musicians are taking more of an active role in how their music is performed and recorded, and they’re able to create a lot more of an immersive experience for their audience.
“It’s all about the live experience. It’s all about the audience being able to feel the music, rather than just hearing it.”
Sliwinski said the show allowed the audience to be more engaged with the performers, while also giving the performers an opportunity to perform in a different way.
“This concert allowed us to be more active, rather than just sitting back and watching a performance,” he said.
“We’re able to have a conversation with our audience, and that’s really what the Composers Concert series is all about.”
The Composers Concert series, which is presented by SONOS and The New Yorker magazine, will continue to tour through the end of March.

A mysterious artifact uncovered in Egypt revealed a huge potential energy source. If only they could charge it…
… that’s how it all started. It has been more than twenty years since the researchers from our world first uncovered the artifact in Egypt and tried to use its power to meet the energy needs of our growing population. The Great Pyramid was a giant tool that gave a continuous supply of energy that seemed to match the needs of the current civilization.
But the reality was not as simple as it seemed. The artifact, or the pyramid, as the researchers called it, was a very complicated machine that used different ways of giving energy from that we were used to: it was not generating electricity like our power plants, it was not producing heat like our boilers and it was not producing light like our lamps. The pyramid was giving energy in a way that was completely new to the world.
Researchers tried to imitate the ways of the pyramid, but it turned out to be much more difficult than they thought: the system used by the artifact is far beyond our scientific knowledge of today. Even though they tried to reproduce its function, they could never make it work with their own devices, not even a small part of it. In fact, they never succeeded in understanding how it worked, and that in itself is a marvelous piece of engineering.

Under the starlit sky, the campers gathered around the glowing campfire, and one after another they took the sacred pipe, or kinnikinnik. When the calabash was passed around, they didn’t talk about the usual things, but stories about the dream life. In my dream, I am in the middle of a massive forest, alone. I hear rumbling noises, as if an avalanche is coming. Then an elephant appears, and begins to run towards me. I try to run away, but I am paralyzed, and just as the elephant is about to trample me, the wild boars suddenly appear and run at it. The elephant flees, and I am finally free.
The old men laughed. Dreams could be interpreted in different ways, they said, but the elephant was a clear sign of a great wisdom, even though it was very young. The wild boars, however, were a sign of an early death, so it was lucky that you had escaped!
On my way back home the following morning, a young badger suddenly jumped out of the ditch and landed right next to me. Even though I am terrified of badgers, I gave the badger a hug, and he followed me home. I continued to follow the bear path. At the place where the tracks were the freshest, I cleared away the snow, and buried the badger. Then I continued my hike.
Once the crowing of the rooster woke me. I was on my own small island, I had dug a hole and lived in it. The rooster told me that it had found a message in a bottle, which told of how the man in the cockpit had put out to sea. The rooster took off with the bottle, but had landed in the wrong place, and had fallen into the ditch where I was walking. I realized I had to continue my journey, and so I returned to the mainland.
A bluish light from a large, beautiful sparkling hut streamed into the forest. I felt like I could wander around freely in the fairy-tale world of books, and so I entered the hut. I was amazed when I discovered the hidden entrance. It was dark inside, and I fumbled in the darkness. I was surprised to feel silky hair under my hands. I realized it was a huge nest full of birds’ eggs. I felt the eggs carefully with my hands, and when I couldn’t find anything at all, I put my head into the nest and saw the eggs shimmering in the bluish light.
Then I realized that I must have wandered out of the forest. I was standing on a steep hillside. The snow was bluish and it was clear that there was a river at the bottom. I continued to walk on the hillside, where it was the steepest. The bluish snow became red, and finally I saw that there was actually blood on the hillside. When I looked at the red, icy snow, I realised that I was not alone. There was someone with me.
Even though I couldn’t see his face, I knew who he was. He looked like a man, but he was very young, with a beautiful blond hair, the kind you get in fairytales. His hair was so fair that the snow reflected in it. It was an angel. He lifted his hand, and waved with it like a bird.

The artist's brush danced across the canvas, creating a whimsical scene of butterflies dancing among the lush green leaves.
The brush stroked, hesitated, and then created a flourish of orange and yellow, bringing the butterflies to life.
I watched in awe as the artist created a work of art before my eyes. But who was this artist? And why did I feel as if I knew him from somewhere?
I was drawn to the painting, as if it held a secret that I needed to uncover.
The sun was just beginning to set, casting a warm glow over the streets. It was then that I noticed a young boy standing in the shadows, his eyes fixed on the artist.
He was tall and thin, with dark hair and a serious expression. I watched as he approached the artist, his eyes never leaving the canvas.
As he reached out to touch the painting, the artist spun around, startled.
"Who are you?" he demanded, his voice low and menacing.
"I'm just an admirer," the boy replied, his voice calm and confident. "I just wanted to see your work up close."
The artist scoffed. "I don't sell my work to anyone," he said, his eyes narrowing. "And I certainly don't give it away."
The boy looked at the artist for a moment, then nodded. "I understand," he said, "but I have to say that I'm impressed with your work. It's beautiful."
The artist frowned. "You don't know what you're talking about," he said, his voice rising. "This is my livelihood. I need to make a living from my work, not give it away for free."
The boy shrugged. "I guess I'll just have to settle for looking at it from a distance," he said.
The artist's eyes narrowed. "You're not going anywhere," he said, his voice threatening. "Not until I get paid."
The boy didn't flinch. He just stood there, his eyes fixed on the painting.
Suddenly, the artist lunged forward, grabbing the boy by the arm. He dragged him towards the painting, and before I knew it, the boy was pulling a sharp object from his pocket.
The artist stopped dead in his tracks. He stared at the boy, his eyes wide with shock.
"What are you doing?" he asked, his voice trembling.
The boy looked at the artist for a moment, then nodded.
"It's time for you to die," he said, and with that, he plunged the sharp object into the artist's chest.
The artist fell to the ground, blood pouring from his chest.
The boy stared at the body for a moment, then turned and walked away.
I stood there, frozen in shock.
"Who is he?" I heard someone ask.
I turned to see a man in a dark suit and tie standing next to me.
"I don't know," I said, my voice shaking. "I just saw him stab the artist."
The man nodded. "I saw it too," he said. "Let's go. The police will want to speak with us."
I followed the man as he walked towards the police station.
"Who do you think he is?" I asked. "And why did he kill the artist?"
The man shrugged. "I don't know," he said, "but I have a feeling we're going to find out soon enough."
At the police station, we told our story to the officers. They listened intently, taking notes and asking questions.
"What did the boy look like?" one of the officers asked.
"He was tall and thin, with dark hair and a serious expression," I said.
The officer nodded. "Do you remember what he was wearing?" he asked.
"I don't remember the exact clothes," I said, "but he was dressed like a professional. Maybe a suit or something similar."
The officer frowned. "What do you mean by that?" he asked.
"I don't know," I said. "I just mean that he didn't look like a typical person on the street. He looked like he was from a different world."
The officer nodded. "Okay, that's all we need for now," he said. "Thank you for your help."
As we left the station, I couldn't help but think about what had happened.
Why did the boy kill the artist? And who was he?
"I'm glad you're here," the man said, giving me a warm smile.
"I'm glad to be here too," I replied. "I can't believe we got away with it."
The man nodded. "It was a close call," he said, "but we managed to pull it off. And now, we can finally relax and enjoy ourselves."
I smiled back at the man, enjoying the warmth of his smile.
But as we settled down on the beach, I couldn't help but feel a sense of guilt.
I knew that what we had done was wrong, and I couldn't shake the feeling that we would be caught sooner or later.
But for now, I would enjoy this moment and forget about the consequences.
I watched as the sun set over the horizon, casting a warm glow over the ocean.
The man next to me stirred, breaking the silence.
"It's time for me to go," he said. "I have a flight to catch."
"Oh, I see," I said, my heart sinking. "So this is goodbye, then."
The man nodded. "I'm sorry," he said, "but I have to go. I have a job to do."
I nodded back. "I understand," I said. "Thank you for everything."
The man smiled. "It was my pleasure," he said. "Good luck with your life."
And with that, he got up and left.
I was alone once again, staring out at the ocean.
I knew that what we had done was wrong, and I felt guilty for what I had done.
But at the same time, I couldn't deny that it had been exhilarating.
The man next to me had shown me a world that I had never imagined before.
A world of crime, where anything was possible.
But now, that world had been left behind.
And I had to face the consequences of my actions.
As the sun set over the horizon, I knew that I had to make a choice.
Would I turn back and try to make things right, or would I move forward and try to forget about what had happened?
As I watched the sun dip below the horizon, I knew that my choice had already been made.
I would move forward, and try to forget about what had happened.
But as I walked away from the beach, I couldn't help but feel a sense of guilt.
I knew that I had done something wrong, and I couldn't shake the feeling that it would catch up with me sooner or later.
But for now, I would focus on moving forward and forgetting about the past.
As I turned the corner, I felt a wave of relief.
I had made it back to my apartment, and I could finally get some rest.
I had been through a lot in the past few days, and I was exhausted.
But as I lay down in bed, I couldn't help but feel a sense of guilt.
I knew that what we had done was wrong, and I couldn't shake the feeling that we would be caught sooner or later.
But for now, I would try to forget about it and move forward.
I drifted off to sleep, hoping that my guilt would fade with the passing of time.
But as I lay there, I couldn't help but think about what we had done.
And I knew that I would always remember it, no matter how much I tried to forget.

Within the walls of the castle, hidden passages, forgotten stories and secret rooms unfold, as we, the characters, remember, and discover new truths about ourselves. Each play in The Oxford Cycle is inspired by the writing of a contemporary playwright, whose work sets the tone and begins the exploration of the themes of memory, desire, choice and redemption. The Architect – conceived by Greg Boyd – is loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s story, The Overcoat.
As the play begins, the Castle is a maze of corridors and chambers, populated by the inmates who had been expelled from the World in time immemorial for their various offences. In the eternity of the Castle, they are alone, banished from the outside world. Only the walls and the ceilings are real. The Castle is a 360 degree set. There is no front. There is no back. There is no up or down.
In The Architect, Phineas Ward, an eccentric scholar has chosen this inert and exhausted community as the perfect place to live. He decides to offer them a new profession: to design buildings, using only their memories. First to step forward is Effie, a defrocked priest, brought low by the passing of time and the decline of the Church. Phineas has invited Effie to imagine his new cathedral. As Effie retreats into his recollections and starts to rebuild the cathedral in his mind, he not only reinvents his past but creates a new identity and a new purpose.
The first production of The Architect was staged in the East Wing of Limerick City Museum, on Bedford Row, and performed on the same site where the ancient churches of the Cathedral Quarter had once stood. The play was devised by a company of ten professional actors and twelve community members, in workshops with Greg Boyd, over a two-month period. The Architect, set in the town where Gogol worked as a clerk in a law office in 1832-33, is the second play in The Oxford Cycle and will be followed by The Master Builder in 2013.

The young inventor's new device promised to revolutionize the war, and he was more than willing to display it. But while watching the contraption, the two officers spied an odd angle—what if the pilot could aim his gun in any direction?
"Why, my boy," the stunned old man said, "that is the secret of war!"
What a brilliant, ludicrous invention the Wright Brothers must have invented.
That kid with the wind-up toy is the inventor of the machine gun.
If only the U.S. military was as up-to-date as the British military. If only America would dedicate our riches to weapons instead of to the education and health of the people.
If only that boy with the wind-up toy would sell his invention to the government and help end the war.
If only the young inventor would not fight against American military intervention in World War I. If only he did not dedicate his genius to peacetime instead of to the war. If only he and his brothers had not been drawn in. If only that boy had been born into a family of inventors rather than fliers. If only he had done anything other than defy the inevitable, that path, like all paths, is a path to violence.
If only humanity was not moving toward a grand war, toward the need for a massive, devastating war.
In that 1912 speech, Orwell invokes the visionary sinking ship of modernity, the global system set to collapse, calling upon society to devise new mechanisms of control and "improve" the human being.
And who was the target of the first, greatest weapons, the crushing instruments of a major power struggle? Women, people of color, the working class. Those of us who were told that our bodies, our minds, our souls, our spirits were expendable in the fight for democracy.
Our lives were not valued by the American government. We were to fight on the front lines while the men who, in civilian life, bossed us around sat back and dodged the draft, using their economic and political power to stay safe, sound, and employed.
When it comes to war, the few who gain most, and the many who die.
When it comes to war, the few who gain most, and the many who die.
But there is an interventionist model to control and surveil that has nothing to do with physical strength or physical warfare. Indeed, there is another waging of war, a different way to occupy, subjugate, and control the world that is peaceful and quiet. It is polite, civil, inviting, even domestic. It is that of a world controlled by technological innovation and marketing, where the rule of technology has become the new empire, the new war machine, a war machine of symbols, of persuasion, of seduction.
This is not the traditional modernist vision of Empire, based on military domination and imperial rule, but the postmodern empire of marketing, technology, and consumption, the empire of business. But it is Empire nonetheless.
The softer and more palatable method of controlling the world is through the use of symbols, the wielding of images, the mastery of visual displays that speak to an entire generation, an entire world, and wage a war on human senses and human consciousness. That war is fought with great success every day of our lives. As an active propagandist, Orwell understood that symbols were powerful tools for the manipulation of reality. Like Orwell, we must understand that marketing strategies are war strategies.
Modernism, the rush to industrialize and control the world through technological modernization, did not see itself as a culture of war and a culture of occupation. And yet in the wake of World War I, all modernism was suspect, including the technological modernism that was the embodiment of its time.
This is where the paranoia began—the idea that what is new is dangerous. This paranoia, inherent in technology's paradoxical nature, spawns utopian fantasies and cynical deconstructions. Technology will save us or destroy us.
The culture of war that engulfed the 20th century, a culture that left as many as 100 million dead, was a culture that brought to us a new world, a world of televisions, radios, iPods, and the Internet. These seemingly new, even exciting, things brought to our lives a new consciousness, a new knowledge, and a new voice, but they also brought a new way of subjugating.
Orwell reminds us that any time the state is able to take an action that it would not have been able to take before, then we are in the realm of realpolitik. Before the war, the American government simply could not get the entire population of the country on board with foreign intervention. Our technological advances brought with them a new way of getting the masses behind the rhetoric of intervention and foreign adventurism.
This new medium—television, for one—helped the American government sell the need for the Korean War to Americans. And with the invention of the new medium of mass communication, the need to control the media was the driving force behind the Vietnam War, an unpopular war fought to protect a failing media regime, a regime that was struggling to keep its power amidst the advent of technological change.
The power of technology, specifically television, to create a culture of intervention is an important part of Orwell's analysis in his 1948 essay "Politics and the English Language," where he warns about the importance of political language in a time of new media.
The decadence of our language—and with language, the imprecision of thought—is a result of our failure to keep pace with a changing culture. Whereas we once fought physical wars, we now wage symbolic wars, we fight for senses, for consciousness, for perception. To do this we require a new language, a new way of communicating. Our language today seems to serve our traditional goals: it is to persuade.
The tyranny of marketing, the tyranny of entertainment, are the realms of the most powerful technological innovations. They, too, are, in fact, weapons of mass control, weapons that wage a new kind of war on our senses, our consciousness, our intellects.
This is not only about the degradation of language, it is also about the transformation of language. If language—and therefore knowledge, thought, and thinking—is evolving, then the question becomes, are we evolving with it? Is our consciousness evolving? Does our brain evolve in concert with technological innovations? And if not, if our brain does not evolve, how do we have an honest conversation about the impact of television on our brain and on our consciousness?
For Orwell, the culture of technology is a real culture, not simply a symbolic one. It is a culture whose power is so great it can transform our society, our consciousness, and our world.
This is the great power of technology, which we saw most dramatically in 1999, when 80 million people participated in a live event, in a live webcast that took place online. The technology was too new. It was unknown territory. This was a challenge to the power of television. This was a failure of the medium. In fact, this was a success.
While many television-based broadcasts have failed, the online broadcast was successful. The idea that millions of people could actually be watching the same thing was so unusual that we, the technologists, did not know what to expect.
The fact that people could be "watching" something, but not necessarily watching it on a television set, was new, different, exciting, and threatening. It is the same reaction we had to the radio and television in the 1920s and 1930s, and we saw that same reaction with the Internet.
We were caught in the crossfire of technological innovation.
These were new technologies of war that were not about waging a literal war.
Television is a medium that delivers images and information. Television was not invented to change our consciousness, to create a new kind of society. Television was invented to deliver pictures and information.
Television was invented as a vehicle for news, as a vehicle for education, as a vehicle for culture, as a vehicle for entertainment. It is an important tool of communication, but it is also an important tool of control.
And yet television does not merely deliver information. It creates it. It creates an image of the world. It creates a world in our minds. It creates a world in our consciousness. It creates a world in our thoughts. It creates a world in our imagination.
But it does not stop there. Television creates a world in our actions. It creates a world in our behaviors. It creates a world in our interactions. It creates a world in our language.
And it is that world that we must understand.
It is the world that we must recognize.
It is the world that we must know.
And it is that world that we must shape.

At the worst zoo in the world, the main attraction is an invisible giraffe that’s stolen the heart of a young girl who’s just turned four. She goes by the name of Adelia. She dreams about the giraffe every night. She makes up stories about the giraffe, and how happy it must be to be invisible.
There’s a contest at the zoo, and Adelia wins, as the only child who shows up. So she gets to go with the zookeeper to feed the animals.
Adelia and the zookeeper go to the elephant cage, and they’re just about to feed the elephant when Adelia is nearly electrocuted, and the elephant is electrocuted, and all the elephants die, and the zookeeper dies, and everyone dies except Adelia, because she’s invisible.
Adelia goes to the giraffe cage, where the other giraffe, who is not invisible, is sitting all alone. Adelia can’t talk, so she writes on the cage, “If you were invisible, would you love being invisible?” She writes and writes and writes, and the giraffe reads what she’s written, and slowly starts to read back, and she writes, “Yes,” and then Adelia writes, “Me too!”
This is a fragment of an actual fairy tale I wrote. It’s a story I’ve been meaning to write for some time now, and I think I’ve been drawn to it for as long as I can remember.

Thirteen-year-old Max Adams wants to get the attention of his classmate Rachel by obtaining something rare and special. At the market for enchanted items, he purchases a magic carpet that takes him to the cloudlands above, where he is threatened by an angry gargoyle before being saved by the beautiful Cora, the daughter of the king of the fairies.
Cora leads Max to her father, who has lost his memory. When Max offers to help him regain his memories, he is told that the gargoyle he had confronted is protecting the fairies, and that Max and Cora are in danger.

In a world powered by laughter, a comedy show becomes the unlikely battleground for the heart of a nation. The Masked Entertainer was the outlandish character, created by award-winning playwright Noël Coward, who captured the hearts of audiences in the 1920s, with his revue, The Gaiety Girl. The artist who plays The Masked Entertainer at a New York performance in 1941 is a refugee from the Spanish Civil War, haunted by the death of his lover, the Spanish actress, Estrella Cabeza de Vaca. And the show that brings him to the States becomes his psychic shipboard voyage, transporting him back to a shared past that transcends time and war, and the love he once knew. When the soldier and the actress re-emerge on stage, the audience is transfixed by their reunion. But which one will live to tell the tale?
"Compelling...what's most striking about the piece is Coward's stunning mastery of the power of dramatic irony, underscoring the conviction of a man who has always been in control, even of his own contradictions." - Kathryn Haughland, Drama-Logue, February 1994
"A simple, deeply moving love story...'Audience' deals with some of Coward's most poignant themes, as he portrays the soldier's struggle to 'recapture love,' often so elusive in his plays. All of Coward's satirical instincts come into play in the performers' confrontation with the artistic and commercial problems of the stage." - Clive Barnes, New York Post, February 3, 1994
"Audience plays well with our desire to be enraptured and entertained...a beautiful and touching reminder that Noël Coward's range was far broader than we might have thought. He is a master of the psychic backstage, as here, and in brilliantly comedic works such as Private Lives, Design for Living and Blithe Spirit." - Christopher Isherwood, London Observer, December 12, 1993
"What most captivates the audience in this Coward play is the potent spell of the theatre itself...Like those beloved nineteenth-century melodramas which The Masked Entertainer spoofs, Audience generates a special excitement, a set of intense suspended emotions, a feeling of gripping uncertainty." - John Gross, London Sunday Telegraph, December 12, 1993
"It all works brilliantly...Coward's deft touch, his brilliant ear, his mastery of the genre, as well as his theatrical brilliance, make the show a delight. Not least, of course, is the great theme that runs through the work, which brings the audience and cast together with such compassionate empathy." - Michael Billington, London Guardian, December 12, 1993
Noël Coward's first comedy, I'll Leave It to You, premiered in 1920. His first hit, The Vortex, opened in 1924, with Design for Living (1932) and Blithe Spirit (1941) to follow. His first starring role in a musical, Set to Music, opened in London in 1939. He also appeared in two of his own plays, Hay Fever (1925) and Present Laughter (1942). He acted and directed in films from the 1930s on. Coward has been honored with two knighthoods, a Nobel Prize nomination and a National Book Award. He died in 1973.

In an alternate universe where socks are the currency, a mismatched pair could be the key to your survival.
A life of adventure comes with risks and I’m happy to take them. When an excursion from camp takes a dangerous turn, the last thing I expect is to be kidnapped by a wild horde of mud-covered sock men. When they look at me, they see my stuffed flamingo, Marshmallow, and with him, they’re determined to collect a ransom.
A wild and wacky adventure in a world where socks are the currency. Kids will enjoy the story and adults will get a good chuckle, or maybe even a full blown belly laugh.
Don’t let the words kidnapping and ransom scare you, this is a tale for the younger set, and it’s a fun one.
The story is fairly simple: an excursion into the woods turns sour when Sara and her friend end up captured by Sock Men. It’s strange, but weirdly humorous. The twists are quite entertaining, such as the Flamingo’s wishing well.
The prose is fun to read, the flow is good, and the book is clearly designed to be read aloud. The illustrations are vibrant, and work well with the story.
A quick read that’s entertaining and a nice diversion from life’s troubles.
It’s a delightfully fun story with marvelously unique illustrations.
I had a little trouble with the two heroes’ names sounding alike, but the vivid descriptions of the sock men and the colors and textures of their socks more than make up for it.
Whether the parents read the book or the kids read it on their own, this is a good addition to any kid’s library.
