During the world's quietest concert, the audience realizes the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
During the world’s quietest concert, the audience realizes the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
During the world's quietest concert, the audience realizes that the music is not heard, but felt through vibrations
Their voices faded to whispers, their senses calmed and their breathing slowed. Now, the audience of roughly 200 people sat quietly, eyes closed, as the orchestra began to play.
For the next 45 minutes, the musicians performed in near silence, creating music with few words — and maybe fewer sounds. The vibration of the bass echoed through the room, but the crowd never heard a note.
“We tend to identify music with sound, but sound is just a byproduct of music,” said composer Jason Treuting, who joined composer Adam Sliwinski to perform the world’s quietest concert in New York City on Friday. “When you’re not aware that you’re hearing anything, you’re acutely aware of this other body.”
For the first time, SONOS Studio in New York City hosted the Composers Concert series. The two-hour show, now on tour, featured music from Treuting and Sliwinski, Yo-Yo Ma and So Percussion.
Each performance was part of a larger experience that featured ambient noise and darkness. The audience wore blindfolds to adjust to the dimness, according to the website.
“This is our first time presenting these three pieces in New York, so we’re going to take our time and really dig into them,” said John Bence, curator of the series and executive producer of SONOS Radio. “We really wanted to create an experience that would inspire and allow our audience to reflect.”
The event was part of the Composers Concert series, which SONOS launched in 2016 to showcase new music.
Bence said the series is a “window” into the artists and their work. In addition to the pieces performed by Treuting and Sliwinski, a work by so-called ‘silent’ musician Bobby McFerrin, who is also on tour, was featured.
“Our concerts feature artists who have a strong connection to our community, but we also want to bring a unique view to the New York concert experience,” Bence said.
He added: “These concerts are a great opportunity for New Yorkers to experience the wonderful world of music through composers who are not always represented on our airwaves.”
For those who attended the show, it was an experience that was “a little eerie, a little enlightening and very beautiful,” said Robert Kastenbaum, who attended the concert.
“I think it was a real pleasure to be able to go and experience the music in that kind of environment,” he said. “I thought it was really wonderful.”
Kastenbaum, 59, had never experienced the concert series, but said he’s always been a fan of modern music.
He added: “I just think it’s such a treat to be able to see these people in person, as opposed to hearing them on a recording.”
In addition to the concert, the series also included an interview with Treuting and Sliwinski about the performance. The two performers spoke about the compositions, their creative process and how they have evolved as artists over the years.
They also shared some thoughts on the future of the music industry and its impact on the concert experience.
“We’re in the middle of a musical renaissance,” Treuting said. “What we’re seeing is that the musicians are taking more of an active role in how their music is performed and recorded, and they’re able to create a lot more of an immersive experience for their audience.
“It’s all about the live experience. It’s all about the audience being able to feel the music, rather than just hearing it.”
Sliwinski said the show allowed the audience to be more engaged with the performers, while also giving the performers an opportunity to perform in a different way.
“This concert allowed us to be more active, rather than just sitting back and watching a performance,” he said.
“We’re able to have a conversation with our audience, and that’s really what the Composers Concert series is all about.”
The Composers Concert series, which is presented by SONOS and The New Yorker magazine, will continue to tour through the end of March.

The gentle hum of the city at dawn brought a contented smile to his lips. The peace he felt within was heightened by the rising sun. The sky, covered with soft mist as thick as cotton, turned shades of rose and gold as the sunlight swept across the hushed streets of the city. He felt more alive than he ever had. His mind was sharp as a newly honed blade, and he felt clean and pure. He drank in the morning air, exhilarated by the promise of a new day.
He heard the soft click of his wife’s heels on the wooden floor of the foyer and closed his eyes with contentment. His sleep that night had been perfect, a calm, restful sleep filled with dreams of blue skies and beautiful women and the smell of a campfire. His wife’s footsteps stopped, and he heard her sigh softly.
“Morgan,” she said in a low, throaty voice.
He didn’t move. He felt her near. He could almost feel the softness of her curves pressed against him as she turned her body toward him. He could almost taste the softness of her lips as she began to speak.
“I have a surprise for you.” She stopped. “It’s something I thought you would like.” Her voice held a whisper of mischief.
He heard the rustle of her dress and then her warm body against his. He felt her breasts pressed against him, and her cheek moved softly against his. He closed his eyes and savored her soft breath on his cheek, then felt her lips, warm and wet, against his own.
He sat up and stared into her face.
She stared back, her dark, unreadable eyes softened by a smile. “Your wife, a pirate?” she asked.
She laughed. “A pirate who loves to please you. We’re going on an adventure. I’ve been saving for weeks.” She stood and began to pull at her dress. “Ready?”
He waited for the dress to fall from her shoulders. He expected her to slide off the bed naked, or nearly so, her hair cascading down her shoulders, her body radiant in the soft morning light. Instead she was fully clothed, dressed in a simple, nondescript brown dress.
“This will come off,” he said, not understanding.
She laughed again and stared at him with those dark, unreadable eyes. “You’ll see. I have a plan for us.”
He watched as she slid out of the bed, still fully clothed. She waited for him to get up and then led him to the door. The sun was now higher in the sky, and he could see the shapes of the buildings beyond the windows of their apartment. His wife opened the door, then looked back at him. “It’s time.”
He felt the anticipation rising in him as he followed her. They left their apartment and stood on the walkway of the third floor of their building. He felt her arm come around his waist and then her hand grasped his. She held tight, and he understood that he was not to let go of her. He felt the wooden steps beneath his feet as they descended to the street. The streets were empty, the sun rising behind him. They could see the world as God made it, uninterrupted by the filth of the city. He felt the light breeze on his face as they approached the long dock that stretched out into the lake from the foot of the hill on which the city was built. The long docks housed all manner of boats, from grand yachts to the small, one-mast fishing boats used by the locals. The fishermen had begun the day’s work already, and he could see the lake as it reflected the rising sun. His wife stopped at the end of the dock. He saw the shape of a small, one-mast fishing boat, waiting patiently for them.
“Surprise,” she said with a smile. She had her hand on the railing. Her hair was not bound up; her long hair flowed over her shoulders in loose strands, falling softly over the red rose at her throat. She seemed to glow in the morning light.
“What is this?” he asked, still not understanding.
“You’ll find out soon enough.” She laughed and pulled him toward the boat. “Get on. I’ve got it all set up.”
He stopped, suddenly unsure. “I don’t understand,” he said again.
She leaned into him and kissed him softly on the lips. “Trust me,” she said.
He felt her eyes on him as she turned away and sat on the bench of the boat. He let go of her hand and stepped onto the wooden boards. He felt his shoes slip a bit as the boat rocked on the water. He grabbed the railing, his eyes wide. “Where are we going?”
“Pirates,” she said. She was grinning, her white teeth flashing in the morning light.
“I’m a pirate?” he asked, incredulous. He’d been a sailor all his life, and had always felt most at home on the open sea. But pirates? It was not something he ever thought he would do. He’d heard the stories about them, the tales of greed and treachery, but he’d never imagined himself as one of them.
“Well, not exactly,” she said. “But it’s the next best thing. It’s going to be great. We’ll be at the lake for most of the day. We’ll have a picnic on one of the islands, maybe even a swim. I’ve got all the food and drinks. The sun is going to be shining, the air is going to be warm. It’s going to be perfect.”
“But the lake…” he began. He stopped, realizing how ridiculous he sounded. “Oh, well, I’m not sure I can be a pirate…”
“You’ll be fine,” she said, her dark eyes twinkling with mischief. “I’ll teach you. You’ll be a natural.”
“A pirate?” he said again.
“A pirate,” she said.
He climbed on board, his wife holding the boat steady. She helped him sit down, and he watched as she untied the rope from the dock and threw it over the side of the boat. He felt the boat move as she let out the rope, and then it began to glide silently across the lake.
“Look,” she said, pointing to the rising sun.
He turned and watched as the sun crested the lake, and the water below it became like a sheet of gold. He felt the breeze on his face and the sun on his arms, and he felt the gentle rocking of the boat. He felt his wife’s body against his, and he knew that this was exactly what he wanted to do.
“It’s going to be a perfect day,” he said.
He felt her smile against his cheek. “I knew you’d like it.”
The lake shimmered like a lake of liquid gold, and he knew it was going to be the perfect day.
Author’s Note: “Pirate” is a short story that tells the story of a man and his wife. The man is a sailor who has always wanted to be a pirate, and the woman is a woman who wants to give her husband the perfect day. The story is set in the late 19th century, when the Chicago World’s Fair was held, and the world was about to change.
It is a story of adventure, love, and self-discovery.

But for now, I would try to forget about it and move forward.
I drifted off to sleep, hoping that my guilt would fade with the passing of time.
But as I lay there, I couldn't help but think about what we had done.

Within the walls of the castle, hidden passages, forgotten stories and secret rooms unfold, as we, the characters, remember, and discover new truths about ourselves. Each play in The Oxford Cycle is inspired by the writing of a contemporary playwright, whose work sets the tone and begins the exploration of the themes of memory, desire, choice and redemption. The Architect – conceived by Greg Boyd – is loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s story, The Overcoat.
As the play begins, the Castle is a maze of corridors and chambers, populated by the inmates who had been expelled from the World in time immemorial for their various offences. In the eternity of the Castle, they are alone, banished from the outside world. Only the walls and the ceilings are real. The Castle is a 360 degree set. There is no front. There is no back. There is no up or down.
In The Architect, Phineas Ward, an eccentric scholar has chosen this inert and exhausted community as the perfect place to live. He decides to offer them a new profession: to design buildings, using only their memories. First to step forward is Effie, a defrocked priest, brought low by the passing of time and the decline of the Church. Phineas has invited Effie to imagine his new cathedral. As Effie retreats into his recollections and starts to rebuild the cathedral in his mind, he not only reinvents his past but creates a new identity and a new purpose.
The first production of The Architect was staged in the East Wing of Limerick City Museum, on Bedford Row, and performed on the same site where the ancient churches of the Cathedral Quarter had once stood. The play was devised by a company of ten professional actors and twelve community members, in workshops with Greg Boyd, over a two-month period. The Architect, set in the town where Gogol worked as a clerk in a law office in 1832-33, is the second play in The Oxford Cycle and will be followed by The Master Builder in 2013.

The young inventor's new device promised to revolutionize the war, and he was more than willing to display it. But while watching the contraption, the two officers spied an odd angle—what if the pilot could aim his gun in any direction?
"Why, my boy," the stunned old man said, "that is the secret of war!"
What a brilliant, ludicrous invention the Wright Brothers must have invented.
That kid with the wind-up toy is the inventor of the machine gun.
If only the U.S. military was as up-to-date as the British military. If only America would dedicate our riches to weapons instead of to the education and health of the people.
If only that boy with the wind-up toy would sell his invention to the government and help end the war.
If only the young inventor would not fight against American military intervention in World War I. If only he did not dedicate his genius to peacetime instead of to the war. If only he and his brothers had not been drawn in. If only that boy had been born into a family of inventors rather than fliers. If only he had done anything other than defy the inevitable, that path, like all paths, is a path to violence.
If only humanity was not moving toward a grand war, toward the need for a massive, devastating war.
In that 1912 speech, Orwell invokes the visionary sinking ship of modernity, the global system set to collapse, calling upon society to devise new mechanisms of control and "improve" the human being.
And who was the target of the first, greatest weapons, the crushing instruments of a major power struggle? Women, people of color, the working class. Those of us who were told that our bodies, our minds, our souls, our spirits were expendable in the fight for democracy.
Our lives were not valued by the American government. We were to fight on the front lines while the men who, in civilian life, bossed us around sat back and dodged the draft, using their economic and political power to stay safe, sound, and employed.
When it comes to war, the few who gain most, and the many who die.
When it comes to war, the few who gain most, and the many who die.
But there is an interventionist model to control and surveil that has nothing to do with physical strength or physical warfare. Indeed, there is another waging of war, a different way to occupy, subjugate, and control the world that is peaceful and quiet. It is polite, civil, inviting, even domestic. It is that of a world controlled by technological innovation and marketing, where the rule of technology has become the new empire, the new war machine, a war machine of symbols, of persuasion, of seduction.
This is not the traditional modernist vision of Empire, based on military domination and imperial rule, but the postmodern empire of marketing, technology, and consumption, the empire of business. But it is Empire nonetheless.
The softer and more palatable method of controlling the world is through the use of symbols, the wielding of images, the mastery of visual displays that speak to an entire generation, an entire world, and wage a war on human senses and human consciousness. That war is fought with great success every day of our lives. As an active propagandist, Orwell understood that symbols were powerful tools for the manipulation of reality. Like Orwell, we must understand that marketing strategies are war strategies.
Modernism, the rush to industrialize and control the world through technological modernization, did not see itself as a culture of war and a culture of occupation. And yet in the wake of World War I, all modernism was suspect, including the technological modernism that was the embodiment of its time.
This is where the paranoia began—the idea that what is new is dangerous. This paranoia, inherent in technology's paradoxical nature, spawns utopian fantasies and cynical deconstructions. Technology will save us or destroy us.
The culture of war that engulfed the 20th century, a culture that left as many as 100 million dead, was a culture that brought to us a new world, a world of televisions, radios, iPods, and the Internet. These seemingly new, even exciting, things brought to our lives a new consciousness, a new knowledge, and a new voice, but they also brought a new way of subjugating.
Orwell reminds us that any time the state is able to take an action that it would not have been able to take before, then we are in the realm of realpolitik. Before the war, the American government simply could not get the entire population of the country on board with foreign intervention. Our technological advances brought with them a new way of getting the masses behind the rhetoric of intervention and foreign adventurism.
This new medium—television, for one—helped the American government sell the need for the Korean War to Americans. And with the invention of the new medium of mass communication, the need to control the media was the driving force behind the Vietnam War, an unpopular war fought to protect a failing media regime, a regime that was struggling to keep its power amidst the advent of technological change.
The power of technology, specifically television, to create a culture of intervention is an important part of Orwell's analysis in his 1948 essay "Politics and the English Language," where he warns about the importance of political language in a time of new media.
The decadence of our language—and with language, the imprecision of thought—is a result of our failure to keep pace with a changing culture. Whereas we once fought physical wars, we now wage symbolic wars, we fight for senses, for consciousness, for perception. To do this we require a new language, a new way of communicating. Our language today seems to serve our traditional goals: it is to persuade.
The tyranny of marketing, the tyranny of entertainment, are the realms of the most powerful technological innovations. They, too, are, in fact, weapons of mass control, weapons that wage a new kind of war on our senses, our consciousness, our intellects.
This is not only about the degradation of language, it is also about the transformation of language. If language—and therefore knowledge, thought, and thinking—is evolving, then the question becomes, are we evolving with it? Is our consciousness evolving? Does our brain evolve in concert with technological innovations? And if not, if our brain does not evolve, how do we have an honest conversation about the impact of television on our brain and on our consciousness?
For Orwell, the culture of technology is a real culture, not simply a symbolic one. It is a culture whose power is so great it can transform our society, our consciousness, and our world.
This is the great power of technology, which we saw most dramatically in 1999, when 80 million people participated in a live event, in a live webcast that took place online. The technology was too new. It was unknown territory. This was a challenge to the power of television. This was a failure of the medium. In fact, this was a success.
While many television-based broadcasts have failed, the online broadcast was successful. The idea that millions of people could actually be watching the same thing was so unusual that we, the technologists, did not know what to expect.
The fact that people could be "watching" something, but not necessarily watching it on a television set, was new, different, exciting, and threatening. It is the same reaction we had to the radio and television in the 1920s and 1930s, and we saw that same reaction with the Internet.
We were caught in the crossfire of technological innovation.
These were new technologies of war that were not about waging a literal war.
Television is a medium that delivers images and information. Television was not invented to change our consciousness, to create a new kind of society. Television was invented to deliver pictures and information.
Television was invented as a vehicle for news, as a vehicle for education, as a vehicle for culture, as a vehicle for entertainment. It is an important tool of communication, but it is also an important tool of control.
And yet television does not merely deliver information. It creates it. It creates an image of the world. It creates a world in our minds. It creates a world in our consciousness. It creates a world in our thoughts. It creates a world in our imagination.
But it does not stop there. Television creates a world in our actions. It creates a world in our behaviors. It creates a world in our interactions. It creates a world in our language.
And it is that world that we must understand.
It is the world that we must recognize.
It is the world that we must know.
And it is that world that we must shape.

At the worst zoo in the world, the main attraction is an invisible giraffe that’s stolen the heart of a young girl who’s just turned four. She goes by the name of Adelia. She dreams about the giraffe every night. She makes up stories about the giraffe, and how happy it must be to be invisible.
There’s a contest at the zoo, and Adelia wins, as the only child who shows up. So she gets to go with the zookeeper to feed the animals.
Adelia and the zookeeper go to the elephant cage, and they’re just about to feed the elephant when Adelia is nearly electrocuted, and the elephant is electrocuted, and all the elephants die, and the zookeeper dies, and everyone dies except Adelia, because she’s invisible.
Adelia goes to the giraffe cage, where the other giraffe, who is not invisible, is sitting all alone. Adelia can’t talk, so she writes on the cage, “If you were invisible, would you love being invisible?” She writes and writes and writes, and the giraffe reads what she’s written, and slowly starts to read back, and she writes, “Yes,” and then Adelia writes, “Me too!”
This is a fragment of an actual fairy tale I wrote. It’s a story I’ve been meaning to write for some time now, and I think I’ve been drawn to it for as long as I can remember.
I wrote it this morning, after sitting on it for a year. And as I wrote it, I was suddenly overcome with a profound sense of my own invisibility. It was like a bucket of ice-cold water in my face, a way of jolting myself awake to how deeply in hiding I’ve been, and how much I’ve been hiding.
I haven’t been living my life. I haven’t been living my life. I haven’t been living my life.
Such a simple idea. And yet it hasn’t been making its way into my everyday awareness at all.
Yesterday, my daughter said to me, “But, Mommy, you don’t do anything. You don’t have any friends.”
I could have argued with her, and defended myself, and explained that it wasn’t true. But she’s right. And I haven’t done anything for a long time.
I have spent much of the last year in solitude. I know some people would say that’s the most spiritual place to be. And perhaps it is. But I am not finding it very spiritual. I am lost. I am stuck in a hole.
I am hiding from my life. I am hiding from my life. I am hiding from my life.

In a world powered by laughter, a comedy show becomes the unlikely battleground for the heart of a nation. The Masked Entertainer was the outlandish character, created by award-winning playwright Noël Coward, who captured the hearts of audiences in the 1920s, with his revue, The Gaiety Girl. The artist who plays The Masked Entertainer at a New York performance in 1941 is a refugee from the Spanish Civil War, haunted by the death of his lover, the Spanish actress, Estrella Cabeza de Vaca. And the show that brings him to the States becomes his psychic shipboard voyage, transporting him back to a shared past that transcends time and war, and the love he once knew. When the soldier and the actress re-emerge on stage, the audience is transfixed by their reunion. But which one will live to tell the tale?
"Compelling...what's most striking about the piece is Coward's stunning mastery of the power of dramatic irony, underscoring the conviction of a man who has always been in control, even of his own contradictions." - Kathryn Haughland, Drama-Logue, February 1994
"A simple, deeply moving love story...'Audience' deals with some of Coward's most poignant themes, as he portrays the soldier's struggle to 'recapture love,' often so elusive in his plays. All of Coward's satirical instincts come into play in the performers' confrontation with the artistic and commercial problems of the stage." - Clive Barnes, New York Post, February 3, 1994
"Audience plays well with our desire to be enraptured and entertained...a beautiful and touching reminder that Noël Coward's range was far broader than we might have thought. He is a master of the psychic backstage, as here, and in brilliantly comedic works such as Private Lives, Design for Living and Blithe Spirit." - Christopher Isherwood, London Observer, December 12, 1993
"What most captivates the audience in this Coward play is the potent spell of the theatre itself...Like those beloved nineteenth-century melodramas which The Masked Entertainer spoofs, Audience generates a special excitement, a set of intense suspended emotions, a feeling of gripping uncertainty." - John Gross, London Sunday Telegraph, December 12, 1993
"It all works brilliantly...Coward's deft touch, his brilliant ear, his mastery of the genre, as well as his theatrical brilliance, make the show a delight. Not least, of course, is the great theme that runs through the work, which brings the audience and cast together with such compassionate empathy." - Michael Billington, London Guardian, December 12, 1993
Noël Coward's first comedy, I'll Leave It to You, premiered in 1920. His first hit, The Vortex, opened in 1924, with Design for Living (1932) and Blithe Spirit (1941) to follow. His first starring role in a musical, Set to Music, opened in London in 1939. He also appeared in two of his own plays, Hay Fever (1925) and Present Laughter (1942). He acted and directed in films from the 1930s on. Coward has been honored with two knighthoods, a Nobel Prize nomination and a National Book Award. He died in 1973.

In an alternate universe where socks are the currency, a mismatched pair could be the key to your survival.
A life of adventure comes with risks and I’m happy to take them. When an excursion from camp takes a dangerous turn, the last thing I expect is to be kidnapped by a wild horde of mud-covered sock men. When they look at me, they see my stuffed flamingo, Marshmallow, and with him, they’re determined to collect a ransom.
A wild and wacky adventure in a world where socks are the currency. Kids will enjoy the story and adults will get a good chuckle, or maybe even a full blown belly laugh.
Don’t let the words kidnapping and ransom scare you, this is a tale for the younger set, and it’s a fun one.
The story is fairly simple: an excursion into the woods turns sour when Sara and her friend end up captured by Sock Men. It’s strange, but weirdly humorous. The twists are quite entertaining, such as the Flamingo’s wishing well.
The prose is fun to read, the flow is good, and the book is clearly designed to be read aloud. The illustrations are vibrant, and work well with the story.
A quick read that’s entertaining and a nice diversion from life’s troubles.
It’s a delightfully fun story with marvelously unique illustrations.
I had a little trouble with the two heroes’ names sounding alike, but the vivid descriptions of the sock men and the colors and textures of their socks more than make up for it.
Whether the parents read the book or the kids read it on their own, this is a good addition to any kid’s library.

The local legend spoke of a treasure buried beneath the sandy plains of the kingdom of Raptash. There were various theories as to who buried it, and how. There were wild ideas as to what the treasure actually was. It was said to be the burial chamber of an immortal vampire, who had feasted upon the young and strong and the beautiful. Many had theorized that the treasure was a combination of the vampire’s fangs, and a sacred artifact, the Crystal of Ages. It was said that the vampire would have, in his blood, the secret to immortality, the age slowing serum. The sacred crystal would have, trapped within its depths, the ages to come.
Whatever the truth may have been, the treasure had been sought after for centuries. Many had died in the process.
The last leg of my journey had been an easy one. I arrived at the local inn, and after an hour or so I found myself on the beach, midnight, storm clouds filling the sky. It looked as though it were going to be a night of heavy rain. I donned my armor and strapped on my weapons. The digging would have to wait. I quickly jogged to the top of the cliff overlooking the beach. When I looked down upon the sand, I could see a pair of eyes shining back at me. The creature appeared to be a man, dressed in a black suit and tie. The glaring and sparkling eyes were the only feature I could make out in the moonlit night. As I leaned over the cliff to get a better look, I felt a stab in my side. It was as though a creature had scratched me with a short but dull spike. I stumbled back and my left hand touched something wet and soft. It was blood. I looked down and saw the blood running down my left side, dripping from my armpit and down my ribs. I tore my shirt open and stared down at my rib cage. I hadn’t been struck by the creature, the creature was me. With its right hand I had stabbed myself. The creature tugged at my shoulder and I stumbled down the cliff. As I crashed to the ground, I realized that I had fallen face first onto the beach. I had fallen down so close to the edge of the cliff that the wave of my crash was absorbed into the ocean. I was now knee deep in the water. I shoved my hand inside the wound and pulled out the small shard of metal that had done the damage. It was a nail, from my boot.
I suddenly realized that I had two options. I could either go back to the inn and heal my wound, or I could follow the creature that had lured me to the cliff and continue the search for the treasure.
In retrospect, the choice was easy. The creature was a legend, an unknown entity. There would be countless more treasure hunters searching for the Crystal of Ages and the Vampire’s Fangs. There would be no way that a creature like myself would ever be able to find such treasures. The creature in me was far more skilled than I was. I would follow the creature.
I jogged through the desert, gliding through the loose sand like a shadow. I darted through the darkness like a lion stalking its prey. I knew where the creature would go next. I knew I had a fair amount of time to get there before it arrived. I also knew that it was traveling more slowly than I was. I was willing to race it to the treasure.
There is a fine line between dedication and obsession. I am determined to make certain that I don’t cross that line.
I realized that I was panting. It was hot. I was used to the hot climate of the desert. The creature had been traveling the desert for far longer than I had. I was surprised that I had managed to keep up. I felt that my mind was clear. The creature could change its course if it wanted, it could avoid me. It could also detect the phantom trails of other creatures that might also be searching for the treasure. I knew that the creature was not stupid. It had waited for me to lose my balance and fall off the cliff. Had I not been wearing my armor, I would have died. I pulled out my sword and held it in my hand. I looked into the desert and saw the silhouette of another creature moving in the sand. It appeared to be carrying a large bag over its shoulder. I figured that this creature was most likely a treasure hunter. I could imagine that it was aware of the creature ahead of me. If it had been aware of my presence as well, it would have already turned its back on me. The fact that it hadn’t, led me to believe that it was completely unaware of the creature ahead of it.
It was only after I had dashed past the creature in the sand that I realized that the creature I had passed was not moving on its own. It was being carried by two smaller creatures. They were human, though not like me. I studied their clothes. They were not wearing the clothing of the inhabitants of the desert. They were wearing the clothes of the kingdom of Raptash. I knew that they were two of the many treasure hunters that had come to this area in search of the immortal vampire’s treasure. If they had been alone, I would have made certain that they never found what they were looking for.
After what I figured to be a quarter of a mile of travel through the desert, the creature turned and ran towards the base of the cliff that faced the sea. It raced to the edge of the cliff and plunged into the water. When I reached the edge of the cliff I couldn’t see anything. I could hear the waves crashing against the cliff, the waves must have been strong. The creature had dove into the water and was nowhere to be seen. I stepped out onto the edge of the cliff, and carefully crept towards the edge. I could see the surface of the ocean, nothing. I turned my body around so that I was facing the sand, and noticed that the two men that I had passed had made their way to the top of the cliff. I turned my attention back to the ocean, and at that very moment I felt a hand slap the back of my head. The two men were dragging me away from the edge of the cliff. I turned my head to my right and saw the creature that had led me there, laying motionless on the ground. There was a wooden cross protruding from its back.
I could hear the sound of wooden planks being dragged towards the edge of the cliff. I suddenly realized that I had the freedom to run off into the desert. I pulled out my sword and prepared myself for the battle ahead of me. I was ready to fight two men, with or without my sword. I was surprised that they had not tried to stab me, they had taken my sword from me. I was sure that they didn’t want to provoke me. The creature had been leading them to the treasure. They had followed it to the edge of the cliff. It was now possible that the creature had led them here and would now lead them back to the treasure.
I saw the first man turn to the second and point down at my body. They had found a way to break my armor. I realized that I had probably fallen on my sword as I had landed on the ground. My sword was embedded deep into the sand. I looked down at my sword and saw that the blade was slightly bent, and the handle was broken off.
I couldn’t afford to get caught by the men. I began to move towards the edge of the cliff. The second man began to run towards me. I stabbed at him with my broken sword, and missed. I pulled out my other sword and rushed towards the man. He didn’t move. I was able to stab him in the back. The man didn’t fall to the ground. I had missed his heart. He fell forward and collapsed. I stabbed him in the back again and he finally fell to the ground. I dragged him back into the shadows of the cliff and began to walk towards the second man. I could see him standing at the edge of the cliff, looking at the ocean. He turned to look at me. I was ready to fight him, and I realized that he was also ready to fight me. I stood there and watched him for a moment. He looked at me for a moment and then turned to look at the ocean again. He turned back to me and I stabbed him in the back. I didn’t know why I had done it. I had never killed anyone. I didn’t know what I was doing. I just knew that I didn’t want to be taken prisoner. I dragged the second man into the shadows of the cliff and watched as he fell to the ground.
I knew that I couldn’t let the creature out of my sight. I walked back towards the creature and stabbed it in the back. I pulled out my sword and stabbed the creature in the back. I watched as the creature fell to the ground.

The grand opening of the new museum attracted art enthusiasts from all over Europe, including the American expatriate Charles Henry Devol who saw the new institution as a possible outlet for his collection. Père Charles, as he was called, was the son of a wealthy family, but he chose not to take his place in the business world, preferring instead to devote himself to art and historical research. Devol had acquired a wide variety of original artworks, many with religious themes, and he envisioned the new museum as a way to share his collection with the public.
After securing the support of the city council, Devol met with municipal director Boissaye. Boissaye expressed excitement about the project but made it clear that the museum would need a permanent home. With that in mind, Devol purchased a large tract of land that was just outside the city limits. The land had been part of the king’s domain and had once been a hunting ground, but it had been abandoned for many years. It was little more than a marshland populated by wild swans, deer, and large piles of hay. Not deterred by the lack of modern infrastructure, Devol constructed a small building where he could house some of his artworks. The new institution opened its doors to the public in 1906.
He named his new venture the Domaine de Kerguéhennec.
What does “Kerguéhennec” mean?
Charles Henry Devol liked the Latin-sounding name, but what did it mean? In ancient Breton, Kerguéhennec meant “quiet valley,” a name that seems to fit the rustic setting of the property. Devol called it the first “outdoor museum in France” and developed it in the spirit of a romantic rural landscape park. He envisioned a place where visitors could stroll through the forest and discover sculptures nestled in the undergrowth.
To this end, he began collecting statues and other artworks and dispersed them throughout the surrounding woodland. Guests followed a mile-long path that meandered through the picturesque setting. Soon, word spread about the charming art oasis, and curious visitors began making the pilgrimage to the woodland paradise.
Making a garden of art
The growing popularity of the museum inspired Devol to plant over 1,000 trees and install some 30 fountains to create a picturesque setting for the growing number of artworks. He dedicated the collection to Jean Macé, a French politician who advocated for the preservation of Breton culture.
When Devol died in 1915, Kerguéhennec was taken over by the city of Lorient. It became a city-owned museum that attracted artists and art enthusiasts from all over the world. During the First World War, it was used as a rehabilitation center for wounded soldiers. The museum continued to thrive under municipal management, but eventually, due to financial pressures, the city of Lorient decided to close it in 1926.
A number of prominent figures, including some in the French cultural establishment, were horrified at the thought of the museum being shuttered. Fortunately, the city council reversed the decision, and the museum reopened. But during World War II, the situation became dire once again when the German army invaded France. Lorient was a strategic port that the Germans used for their military operations and as a result of the Allied bombings, the museum was damaged and some of the artworks were lost.
Modern museum and international collection
After the war, the museum reopened again, this time with a new emphasis on modern art. It was in the 1960s that Kerguéhennec began collecting contemporary art from around the world, and it became a major outlet for exhibiting avant-garde works. The museum’s contemporary collection includes pieces by prominent figures such as Yves Klein, Sam Francis, Karel Appel, and Pol Bury.
Today, the museum continues to showcase artwork from the 20th and 21st centuries. Visitors can view the contemporary works in the indoor galleries, while the outdoor sculpture garden is a perfect place to enjoy a leisurely stroll and admire the beauty of the natural setting.
The Domaine de Kerguéhennec is a unique institution that combines a historic art collection with the natural beauty of the Breton countryside. With its commitment to contemporary art, it remains a vital cultural resource for the people of Brittany and beyond.

THE BOY AND THE BLACKSMITH.

BY FRANCIS FARLEY BROWNE.

The boy came by the smithy to hire a day's work, and so he stood by and saw a horse shod. "Would you like to be a blacksmith?" said the smith, when the work was done.

"Would you like to be a watch-maker?" said the boy.

"No, no, a watch-maker, hey? There's no life in that for me. Give me horseshoeing, I say, when I'm old and grey."

So the boy went away, and took service as a watch-maker.

Next day, as the smith was shoeing a horse, it drew its foot in the fire and was badly burned. The master had to be sent for, and the watch-maker went to call him. But he did not know the smith's house, and stopped at a cottage by the road. There he heard a horse stamping and grinding its teeth. So the watch-maker opened the door and looked in, and there was the smith asleep in his shirt, with a great iron shoe hanging from his thumb. The horse was tied to his leg with a lasso, and it was trying to get free.

"Why don't you get up and shoe my horse?" said the watch-maker.

"Hoity toity!" said the smith. "I'll do no such thing."

"I have a watch," said the watch-maker. "Look! It's open. Watch away!"

So the smith looked, and then he wanted to see the watch wound up.
"You'll have to show me how to wind it," he said.

But when the watch-maker put his hand into his pocket, the watch was gone.

"Where's my watch?" cried the watch-maker.

"Ha! ha!" laughed the smith. "I've just seen you shoe my horse! That's what I call business."

"I wouldn't take service of you," said the watch-maker, "for all the world!"

A little English school-boy, as his name, would say, once asked me why I, an American, was so fond of French.

"The French people," I answered, "must be very lovable. They are much given to praising their country; and, therefore, to making known to others the virtues and excellences of their native land. It is quite common for them to show a marked friendliness towards the stranger and visitor. But I do not think that even French affection is such a sure thing as yours; because a Frenchman may be merely exhibiting his nationality, while you are exhibiting your personality. You have adopted the language of a foreign country; you live where you were not born; you do not belong to the land in which you were reared; but you have a wider friendship than a Frenchman has. You are not so narrow as a German, because you have found something more outside your own language and country. But a Frenchman is such a complete Frenchman, that he has no other friendship than that of Frenchmen. You take a man as a whole, but the Frenchman takes him only according to a part of him. He has not sympathy enough to take a man, but only sympathy enough to take the man's natural qualities."

"What is it?"

"Two in the bush."

_bourgeois_, but because it is the story I mean to tell you."

"You have forgotten the question. You have not told me the question."

"No matter. It does not matter. You have forgotten it, and now I have forgotten it; and that is better than if you had it, because we would not be able to answer it. The question was not important, only the answer was; and so the question is forgotten, because it has been answered."

He was to be the old man's grandson for six months, and then to come back to him. And that was the way that he had his two birds. The old man had a big estate, and his grandson had a little one, and so they went on being two.

Drifting through the cosmos, the comet harbors the Earth's only hope. It is a lucky comet because, in a most unexpected way, it carries with it something indestructible and eternal that can be a new beginning for the Earth. Alas, this spectacular encounter is not without a price: the fateful accident that sets in motion the final impact. At this point, time has ceased to exist; the Earth is left helpless in the hands of nature.
Comet, a feature film by director John Putch, is a stunning display of expertise in a field that is very close to my heart, amateur astronomy. Starring William Devane as Dr. Alan Harrington, along with a stellar supporting cast, Comet has all the right stuff to qualify as a hit with any crowd. I was lucky enough to see a screening of the film recently at Paramount Studios in Hollywood. After the screening, I was able to meet and chat with Mr. Devane and Mr. Putch as well as William Katt and Cynthia Watros, also stars in the film.
Mr. Devane gave me his autograph in my copy of Scientific American's January 2001 issue and agreed to be photographed with me and my poster of the comet colliding with the Earth. The only thing I was not able to do was to photograph the back of my shirt with Mr. Devane's autograph. With the bright sun outside of Paramount Studios, I was not able to bring out the detail. Still, I am excited to own his autograph in one of my favorite magazines!
The following evening, I had the privilege of attending the film's Los Angeles premiere. We were picked up by a limousine at my hotel and brought to the Paramount Theatre on Hollywood Boulevard. It was a surreal experience being chauffeured to a premiere screening of a movie that I had just seen only a few hours earlier.
Comet received a standing ovation from the audience upon the ending of the film. After the credits rolled, the three principle actors, John Putch, William Devane and William Katt came out to do a Q&A with the audience. I took the opportunity to get a second autograph from Mr. Devane on my screening ticket.
Comet opens on September 22, 2001, in theatres in the US. It is a must-see film that will appeal to a wide variety of audiences: from the amateur astronomer to the lover of science fiction. It has been rated PG and is most suitable for children and adults who are at least 9 years old. Comet is the most realistic and most accurate film about a comet collision with the Earth that I have seen. It is an extremely realistic and yet entertaining display of the effects of such an impact on our planet.
For more information about the film and its star William Devane, I invite you to check out his official web site at http://www.williamdevane.net/.
Comet may be the last film in a decade that approaches the theme of an impact with Earth and provides a true-to-life view of such an event. The last film of this genre that I can recall was the made-for-television film Meteor released in 1998, starring Jason Alexander and Natalie Wood. That film was made with scientific advisors and a mostly accurate impact scenario that involved a meteor not an actual comet (although a comet is sometimes called a "dirty snowball"). Unfortunately, meteor crater in Arizona was not used to film Meteor. The location was actually filmed at San Bernardino, California and the impact site had been destroyed for another filming prior to Meteor's.
The next impact film that comes to mind is actually a scene from Deep Impact, a film coming out in July 2001, starring Morgan Freeman. The scene that I refer to was filmed at Meteor Crater, Arizona and it features Tea Leoni (her character is a paleontologist, by the way) and she tries to give a description of the impact with a grandparent type figure to her daughter, a teenager. Unfortunately, Tea Leoni's description is inaccurate and very sensationalized. First of all, the impact would have caused an inferno and a large dust cloud. There would have been no mist in the desert, as she claimed.
The inferno would have vaporized any water in the vicinity and, based on current evidence, that region would not have had an abundance of water to begin with. (It's been believed that the area was very dry and arid 50,000 years ago). The shock waves from the impact would have weakened Earth's crust and the land itself would have been shattered. The teenager in the scene asks the logical question: How could you possibly vaporize the planet? The character's grandparent replies that the impact has actually "vaporized" all of the water on the planet and only the bare rock is left. She then implies that Earth is no longer inhabitable. She states that the sudden removal of Earth's water has "changed the balance of nature."
She and the teenager look at each other, in a very emotional moment, as they contemplate the total destruction of the planet. Such an impact would not have removed all of Earth's water and it would not have "changed the balance of nature." The planet would not have been destroyed and it would have remained habitable. I would not have wanted to live through an impact, but we would not have ceased to exist, as the movie implies.
Such an impact would have destroyed the rockets that Deep Impact claims to be able to launch. In the film, a large comet is discovered orbiting the Sun and the space shuttle gets launched with an orbiting space station. A second shuttle launches to the Moon to uncover the secrets of a mysterious monolith that was left behind by an alien race (similar to 2001: A Space Odyssey). The shuttle is destroyed by a meteor that apparently came out of nowhere and manages to avoid the station. The meteors intensify and Earth gets pummeled with debris. An ingenious solution is found to send a large drill-like machine into the center of the comet. The machine "sprays" the core of the comet with cold gas and the comet is shattered, to the delight of the planet and all of its inhabitants.
This is where Comet shows the importance of science in science fiction and why I want everyone to see this movie. I applaud the makers of Deep Impact for hiring a science consultant, Dr. Everett L. Lasher of The George C. Marshall Institute, Washington, D.C. Unfortunately, I do not believe that Dr. Lasher was able to convince Deep Impact's writers to make the film more accurate. For example, Dr. Lasher recently told me that there is no way that a comet could be manipulated to hit the comet's nucleus and shatter the comet. Comet, on the other hand, shows the opposite to be true and shows that comets are much more fragile than astronomers previously thought. If an impact occurs, then the comet would likely be shattered.
Deep Impact has a premiere screening in Los Angeles on June 19, 2001, and will open nationwide on July 12, 2001. The film stars Morgan Freeman, Robert Duvall, Tea Leoni and Elijah Wood.
I don't want to get in trouble with MGM/UA by being compared to a film critic. As an amateur astronomer, I can tell you that I have seen both movies and can say that, scientifically speaking, Comet is the most accurate impact film that I have seen in the last 20 years. I will be writing more about this film in a future issue of the Electronic Asteroid and Comet Gazette.

The game was inspired by a real-life incident involving the breeding of an orchid called Angraecum sesquipedale. First sighted in 1822, Charles Darwin immediately recognized the importance of the discovery. The flower had a 10-inch long nectar spur. This length was exactly what pollinators needed to reach the nectar inside, and yet no animal was ever seen visiting the flower.
In 1862, British botanist Sir Richard Owen paid a visit to the British ambassador in Mauritius and found orchids for sale in his garden. He was given an Angraecum plant, which he carried with him back to London. After several years of care and some effort, he managed to get the plant to bloom. It finally proved his theory. The Angraecum sesquipedale was pollinated by the now-extinct Eudoxia, a moth with a 10-inch-long proboscis.
The orchid's name means "quarter foot" in Latin, since its spur was "half a foot" long. But it was a Dutch scientist who came up with the name of its pollinator: Eudoxia - the largest genus of moths in the world, so-named for its beauty.

The ancient tree stood tall, bearing witness to centuries of change and to many a life, a silent witness who had witnessed wars and peace, rejoiced in victory and lamented defeat, many who had stood before it were gone, but it remained, a symbol of life itself.
There came a time, when the tree started to fall, some blamed it on time, some blamed it on change, some blamed it on the advancement of man, on his ever growing greed, the ever growing desire to possess, to conquer, to take what was not his, but in reality, all these were merely symptoms of the root cause.
Whether time, greed, desire or possession are the root cause or not, remains to be seen, as yet, the tree remains, a witness, a mere witness, a mere silent witness to the beauty of life, to the beauty of man, to the beauty of love and hate, to the beauty of all that can be seen, to the beauty of all that cannot be seen.
As long as it exists, it serves as a witness to the on going wars between the destruction of one man and the creation of another, it exists as a witness to those who would like to claim it, for the benefit of man, as a harbor, as a haven, as a shelter for the destitute, to those who would see it destroyed in the name of progress, in the name of advancement.
Its silence has long been broken, the world has heard it voice, its call has resonated through the lands, its call for help is heard, but like most great things, those who do not understand it, simply cannot see it, those who understand it, see the wisdom in it, in its wisdom, lies a voice which can no longer be denied.
I have no right to say what is right and wrong, all I can do is stand before it, and listen to its voice, for it is no longer the silent witness, it is now, the voice of the world, the voice of wisdom, the voice of truth, the voice of love, the voice of life, to those who would oppose it, I wish them all the best in what they do.
To those who would listen to its voice, its call, it is my wish that you listen to its voice, its wisdom, and live, live in harmony with the world around you, for you are the world, the world is you, so live with wisdom, live with peace, live with the intention of building a better world, for you, for those around you, for those not yet born, as in the end, we are all, a witness.
